options.label: Adopt it. If indignation degrades judgement, the fix is structural — you cannot ask people to feel less, only to decide later and elsewhere.

evidence.says: Madison held that passionate factional majorities cannot be cured by improving citizens' motives, only by institutional design that filters a decision through people the passion has not reached.

options.label: Adopt it, and expect it to fail. A committee of three at one remove will reproduce the mood of the room while feeling procedurally clean about it.
Reject it. Judging one another is what a community is; outsourcing it to a week later and a subcommittee is how obligations become paperwork.
The rule treats anger as the problem. The problem is what anger is for, and a practice built on payback will be unjust however calmly it is administered.

evidence.says: Nussbaum argues that the payback wish inside anger is incoherent, since another person's suffering repairs nothing, and that justice should be built on forward-looking repair rather than on the sentiment of desert.

outcomes.label: The Feeling Is the Evidence
outcomes.text: You treat the enjoyment in the room as data about the room rather than about the accused, and you audit your own share of it first. This is Russell's actual counsel and it is unusual in being self-directed. The cost is a chronic difficulty acting: if every strong moral feeling is provisionally suspect, you will hesitate in the cases where hesitation is itself a decision, and the person harmed by the delay is rarely the one you were being careful about.

outcomes.label: What Is Owed Regardless
outcomes.text: Your attention goes to what the accused is owed — an accurate finding, a hearing, a correction entered whether or not it changes the vote — and none of it is contingent on how anyone feels. Strawson is partly with you: indignation is not a defect, it is what holding someone responsible looks like. The exposure is that your standard can be satisfied on paper. A process can be scrupulous in every particular and still be a room enjoying itself, and your framework has no way to see that.

outcomes.label: Watch the Sentence, Not the Verdict
outcomes.text: You separate the question of what he did from the question of what will now be done to him, and you expect the corruption to show up in the second. That is a sharper instrument than most people bring, and it survives the discovery that he is guilty. What it costs is standing: once you have granted the finding, you have little to say against a proportionate punishment administered with obvious relish, and relish was the thing you set out to object to.

outcomes.label: Build the Delay In
outcomes.text: You do not expect people to feel less, so you move the decision — later, elsewhere, to someone who did not bring the complaint. This is the only answer here that survives the fact that everyone thinks they are the exception. Its weakness is that procedure launders as easily as it protects: a subcommittee at one remove can deliver the same verdict with a clean conscience, and now nobody in the building feels responsible for it.

outcomes.label: Someone Should Tell Him
outcomes.text: You keep returning to the man in the corridor who does not yet know what has happened to him, and you think the relationship survives the offence. That is the correction a disciplinary process most needs and least invites. It is also the position most easily used: the wish that this remain between people who know each other is exactly the instinct that has protected offenders in small institutions for as long as small institutions have existed.

entries.title: Shigalyovism
entries.gist: In Part Two of Dostoevsky's *Demons* (serialised 1871–72) a group of provincial conspirators gather at Virginsky's house. One of them, Shigalyov, has written a book. He explains its argument to the room, apologising in advance: he set out from the principle of unlimited freedom, he says, and he has arrived at unlimited despotism. He adds that no other solution to the social problem is possible.

questions.prompt: The most rigorous egalitarian in your group presents a worked plan for making the group genuinely equal. It requires a standing committee that can override any member, a compulsory work rota, and members reporting on one another's compliance.

options.label: The plan refutes the premise. If following the reasoning honestly lands here, something in the reasoning was wrong several steps back.

evidence.says: Berlin traced how a doctrine of freedom as self-realisation licenses coercing people toward the self they would have chosen if they were wiser, which puts liberation and tyranny on the same road.

options.label: The plan is what equality actually costs, and everyone who claims to want equality while refusing the machinery is bluffing.

evidence.says: Rousseau held that a citizen who resists the general will may legitimately be compelled by the whole body, on the grounds that this only forces him to be free of his own private dependence.

options.label: Nothing follows about equality. It follows that plans of this kind always produce an enforcing minority, whatever they are plans for.

evidence.says: Michels argued from the study of avowedly democratic mass parties that organisation itself generates a governing minority, so the outcome is a property of the structure rather than of the ideology it serves.

options.label: Keep the goal and drop the completeness. Equal basic liberties come first, and any distributive scheme has to fit inside them rather than override them.

evidence.says: Rawls ordered his principles so that equal basic liberties take priority over distributive gains, precisely to block trades of freedom for equality however favourable the arithmetic looks.

questions.prompt: A second member — bored by the theory, ruthless about people — has spotted that the committee could be used to remove anyone she dislikes, and begins quietly saying so to the people whose votes she needs.

options.label: This is the real objection to the plan. A structure is what it can be used for, not what its author intended it for.

evidence.says: Hayek argued that centrally directed schemes select for the people willing to do what direction requires, so the unscrupulous rise not by accident but because the structure has work only they will take on.

options.label: Separate them. Her opportunism is a fact about her; the plan should be judged on whether it is right, then defended with safeguards against people like her.
She is the point. The theorist supplies the vocabulary and someone like her always supplies the will; that pairing is the actual historical mechanism.

evidence.says: Camus argued that rebellion turns murderous when it is handed a total justification, and read Dostoevsky's conspirators as the case where an abstract logic finds the men who will carry it out.

options.label: Deal with her directly and leave the plan alone. Naming what she is doing, in the room, to her face, is the only thing that stops it.

questions.prompt: When the committee's first act is to expel a member, the author of the plan objects that this is a wasteful deviation from his system, declines to take part, and goes home. The expulsion proceeds without him.

options.label: He is responsible for it. Designing the mechanism and then declining to operate it is not distance; it is the division of labour working as intended.
His walking out is the most useful information anyone has. A designer who will not stay in the room has told you what the design is.
He is not responsible, and pretending otherwise makes every theorist liable for the worst reader they ever had. Blame belongs to the people who voted.
Forget him. There is a person being expelled tonight and the interesting question about the author of the plan can wait a week.

questions.prompt: Someone objects that this whole line of argument is a conservative alibi: point at the committee, and every proposal to share anything out gets shelved forever while the existing distribution — which nobody designed and nobody voted for — carries on.

options.label: The objection is right. The status quo is also a coercive arrangement, and it is exempted from this scrutiny only because it is old.

evidence.says: Cohen argued that equality and community are plainly desirable when we test them on a small scale we all understand, and that objections almost always concern feasibility while presenting themselves as objections to the ideal.

options.label: The objection is right about the alibi and wrong about the lesson. Redistribute by rules that apply to everyone, and refuse any scheme needing a body above them.
The warning survives the alibi. The distinctive danger is the complete plan, not the redistribution — piecemeal changes can be reversed, blueprints cannot.

evidence.work: The Open Society and Its Enemies
evidence.says: Popper distinguished piecemeal reform, which can be checked against results and undone, from utopian engineering, which needs a long horizon and therefore needs to suppress the criticism that would interrupt it.

options.label: Both sides are arguing about systems. What settles it is who ends up holding a key to somebody else's door, and that is visible without any theory at all.

outcomes.label: Follow It to the End
outcomes.text: You judge a proposal by where it lands rather than by what it declares, and you treat the committee, the rota and the reporting as the actual content of the plan. This is the reading that makes Shigalyov worth arguing with. Its price is conservative by default: since almost any arrangement can be shown to terminate somewhere unpleasant if you extend it far enough, this instrument will nearly always be available to whoever wants nothing to change.

outcomes.label: Some Things Are Not Tradeable
outcomes.text: You hold that a person's standing is not an input to a distribution — that no arithmetic about the nine tenths licenses anything over them — and you will say so before you know what the alternative costs. That is the position Shigalyov's own argument was constructed to embarrass, and it survives the embarrassment. What it costs is that you must accept the existing distribution's victims as the price of refusing the machinery, and you owe them a reason that is not merely that their suffering is traditional.

outcomes.label: Rules, Not a Body Above Them
outcomes.text: Your test is whether the scheme needs somebody standing outside it with a power of override. If it does, you refuse it; if it can be run as rules that bind their authors, you will consider almost any content. This is the most workable answer in the file and the one that most nearly separates redistribution from Shigalyovism. Its weakness is that rules are administered, and the discretion you refused at the door tends to reappear in the person deciding what counts as compliance.

outcomes.label: Watch Who Volunteers
outcomes.text: You read the situation through the people in it — the theorist who cannot stay for the consequences, the opportunist who has found her instrument — and you think the pairing, not the doctrine, is what does the damage. Dostoevsky's novel is built on exactly that observation. The limitation is that character is not a check: the plan will still be adopted, and having correctly identified everyone's motives leaves you with nothing to propose at the meeting.

outcomes.label: There Is a Person at the Door
outcomes.text: You keep the argument anchored to whoever is actually about to lose something tonight, and you decline to let the general question postpone the particular one. That instinct is what keeps such rooms honest, and it is the thing every complete plan is designed to make you feel embarrassed about. Its cost is scale: the harms done by an arrangement to people you will never meet do not register on this instrument, and those are usually the larger ones.

entries.title: The Crystal Palace
entries.gist: *Notes from Underground* (1864) is narrated by a retired civil servant, nameless, forty, living in a corner of St Petersburg and addressing an imagined audience he despises. The first half is his argument; the second half is a story from his life that undermines it. Both halves are Dostoevsky's, and neither is his doctrine — the book opens with a footnote saying the narrator is invented, and that people of this sort must nevertheless exist.

questions.prompt: A scheduling system has demonstrably raised everyone's pay and cut injuries. One driver has begun taking the slower route on purpose. It costs him money, it costs him nothing else, and asked why, he says only that he felt like it.

options.label: He is asserting that he is a person and not a component, and the fact that it costs him is the entire content of the assertion.

evidence.says: Dostoevsky gives his underground narrator the argument that a man will deliberately choose against his own advantage in order to establish that he is not a piano key, and that this capacity is the advantage he prizes above all the ones that can be tabulated.

options.label: He is telling you something about the system that the metrics cannot register, and he may not have the words for it himself.

evidence.says: Scott argued that schemes designed from a central vantage systematically discard the practical local knowledge of the people inside them, and that resistance often carries exactly the information the design has thrown away.

options.label: Doing something because you felt like it is not freedom. Freedom is acting on the wants you would endorse on reflection, and caprice is the opposite.

evidence.work: Freedom of the Will and the Concept of a Person
evidence.says: Frankfurt located freedom in the agreement between what a person wants and what he wants to want, so an impulse acted on without endorsement is not liberty but the absence of a self doing the choosing.

options.label: It is his money and his afternoon. The question of what it means does not arise until he does it with someone else's.

evidence.says: Mill's principle restricts interference to conduct affecting others, and his defence of individuality holds that a choice made because it is one's own has a value that a better choice made for one does not.

questions.prompt: The designer proposes locking the route: deviations simply become impossible. She is transparent about it and has the figures. Twelve fewer injuries a year, and an end to the argument.

options.label: Lock it. Twelve people not in hospital is a real thing; the ability to take a worse road for no reason is a feeling about oneself.

evidence.work: An Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation
evidence.says: Bentham treated the reduction of suffering as the only intelligible standard for institutions, and regarded appeals to dignity that cannot be cashed out in someone's pain or pleasure as decorative.

options.label: Keep the deviation available and expensive. What matters is that the door is not welded shut, not that anyone walks through it.

evidence.who: Richard H. Thaler and Cass R. Sunstein
evidence.says: Thaler and Sunstein argue that some arrangement of choices is unavoidable, so the defensible design steers toward the better outcome while leaving the option to depart genuinely open.

options.label: Refuse it. A person who cannot do the wrong thing is not doing the right thing either, and the injuries do not buy back what the lock removes.
Ask the drivers, and abide by it. Whatever they decide will be better founded than either the figures or the principle, because they are the ones inside it.

questions.prompt: The firm extends the model: guaranteed hours, childcare, a clinic, housing at cost. Households can decline the package, but declining means declining all of it. A neighbour says he will decline, and cannot explain why beyond not wanting to be inside it.

options.label: His refusal is intelligible and he does not owe you a reason. Wanting one's life to be one's own is not a preference that needs justifying to a committee.

evidence.says: Nozick's experience machine was built to show that people want to do things and to be a certain kind of person, not merely to undergo the best available sequence of states, however expertly the states are arranged.

options.label: His refusal has a cost his children will pay, and the fact that he cannot articulate it does not make the cost theoretical.
The all-or-nothing bundling is the problem, not the package. Make each part separately refusable and the objection largely dissolves.
Take the package and stay awkward inside it. Gratitude was never required, and nobody is asking him to believe in it.

questions.prompt: Three months on, four other drivers are deviating in imitation. The efficiency gain is gone, and a colleague who counted on it — she had told her landlord — loses the raise it was funding.

options.label: That ends it. The gesture was defensible while the bill was his own; it is not a right to be paid for by a woman who never made the gesture.
It does not end it. A freedom that evaporates the moment anyone has arranged their life around your compliance was never a freedom.
The imitation is the answer to the whole question. Four people found the thing worth losing money over, which is evidence about the scheme and not about them.
The wrong done to her is a wrong done by a person to a person, and it should be settled between them rather than by amending the system.

outcomes.label: Not a Piano Key
outcomes.text: You take the driver's side, and you take it at the point where it stops being convenient — when the deviation has no upside, cannot be explained, and looks merely perverse. That is the Underground Man's actual position, and it is a serious one: a self that never departs from the optimum has no way of knowing whether it is a self. The cost is that you have adopted a principle that cannot distinguish between a man asserting his personhood and a man being a nuisance, and Dostoevsky's own novel spends its second half showing you the difference.

outcomes.label: Twelve Fewer Injuries
outcomes.text: You weigh the gains, find them real, and decline to trade them for a feeling about one's own personhood that nobody has been able to state without metaphor. This is the strongest position in the file on any given Tuesday. Its exposure is the long run: every particular restriction will pass this test, none of them individually will look like tyranny, and there is nothing in the method that tells you when the building has been finished around you.

outcomes.label: Leave the Door Unwelded
outcomes.text: Your test is not whether people deviate but whether they could, and you will pay a real efficiency price to keep the exit open. This is the most defensible compromise available and it is roughly how liberal institutions actually justify themselves. Its weakness is that an exit which costs enough is not an exit, and you have no principled way to say how expensive is too expensive — which is exactly the lever a designer with good intentions will reach for first.

outcomes.label: The Lock Is the Wrong
outcomes.text: You object to the welded door as such, independently of what lies behind it, and you will not let the injury figures buy it. That keeps you clear of the trap where each improvement is individually reasonable. What it costs is that you must say the twelve injuries out loud and accept them, to people who will ask you which twelve, and the answer that a person must be able to do wrong will not sound like an answer in that room.

outcomes.label: The Woman Who Told Her Landlord
outcomes.text: You keep the argument attached to whoever is holding the bill, and you notice that grand gestures about freedom are usually costed by somebody who did not make them. That is the objection the Underground Man never answers and cannot. Its limit is that it can be run against any refusal at all: someone is always relying on your compliance, so a rule that the reliance wins is a rule that nobody may ever step out of line.

outcomes.label: What Caprice Makes of You
outcomes.text: You distinguish freedom from mere unpredictability, and you want to know whether the driver would stand behind the impulse afterwards. Frankfurt is with you, and so is the second half of Dostoevsky's novel, where the narrator's unfettered will turns out to be exercised mainly on a woman who was kind to him. The risk is that this standard is easy to hand over: once freedom means acting on the wants you would endorse on reflection, someone will offer to tell you which ones those are.

entries.title: Smerdyakov's Inference
entries.gist: In *The Brothers Karamazov* (1879–80) the middle brother, Ivan Fyodorovich, is credited with a formula he never quite states in his own voice at the moment it matters. It is reported at the monastery by Miusov, who says Ivan has argued that virtue depends on the immortality of the soul, so that if belief in immortality were destroyed nothing would be immoral and **everything would be permitted**. Ivan, present, does not disown it. Rakitin repeats it to Alyosha. It circulates around the novel as a thing Ivan is known for, which is the first thing to notice about it: a doctrine loose in a household.

questions.prompt: A man kills someone, and tells you afterwards that he did it because of an argument you had made in public and repeated in front of him. You believe him. You also believe the argument is true, and you gain materially from the death.

options.label: You are guilty. Not in the way he is, but really — you supplied the reasoning and the permission, and the fact that he pulled the trigger does not undo that.

evidence.says: Jaspers separated criminal guilt, which attaches to the act, from moral and metaphysical guilt, which attaches to those who supplied the climate, and refused to let the second dissolve because the first belongs elsewhere.

options.label: He is guilty and you are not. He heard an argument and made a choice; treating him as something your words operated is a worse insult than blaming him.

evidence.says: Sartre took Dostoevsky's formula as the starting point of his own position and drew the opposite conclusion from it — that without a given standard a person is wholly responsible for what he makes of what he is handed.

options.label: What matters is not guilt but what you do now. Guilt is an accounting exercise; there is a family, an inheritance you should not take, and a public argument that has been shown to do something.
Look at what you gained. Until you can rule out that you wanted this, your verdict on your own responsibility is not evidence about anything.

evidence.work: Fifteen Sermons Preached at the Rolls Chapel
evidence.says: Butler's sermon on self-deceit argues that partiality to ourselves operates precisely where our interest lies, so a self-acquittal issued in a case one profits from is the least trustworthy judgement a person can make.

questions.prompt: He puts it to you directly: he was only the pupil. You were the one who believed it, said it, and lived as though it were true; he simply took it seriously enough to act.

options.label: He is right about you and wrong about himself. Both of those can be true, and a man who claims to be a mere instrument has just made one more choice.
The charge that stings is the one about living as though it were true. Saying it and not meaning it would have been the worse fault, not the lesser.
It is a manipulation. He needs you implicated so that he is only half a murderer, and you should not accept a role because it is offered persuasively.
He is right, and the reason is that you spoke to him as though he were not really listening. You were performing an argument in front of someone you had decided did not count as an interlocutor.

questions.prompt: You are asked to retract the argument publicly. You still think it is true. A retraction would help the family, cost you your standing, and be a lie.

options.label: Do not retract. An argument is not refuted by someone acting on it badly, and a public lie about what you believe corrupts the only thing you had to offer.
Retract, in the sense that matters: say publicly that you were wrong to say it the way you said it, to whom you said it, without the parts that restrain it.

evidence.says: Mill protected opinions absolutely while denying protection to the same words delivered as an instigation to a particular audience, locating the wrong in the circumstances of the utterance rather than in the content.

options.label: Retract fully, and accept that it is a lie. The family's need is concrete and your intellectual consistency is not, and you would not be the first person to pay for a death with a humiliation.

Do not retract, because the argument was false and should be refuted rather than withdrawn. Obligation does not need a transcendent ground, and saying it does is what made the inference look valid to him.

evidence.says: Foot grounded moral evaluation in facts about what human beings need in order to live well, arguing that the standard is as objective as the one applied to a plant or an animal and requires no religious backing at all.

questions.prompt: Before any of it becomes public he kills himself, leaving a note taking sole responsibility. Nothing you say now can be corroborated. You confess anyway and are told, kindly, that you are not well and should rest.

options.label: Keep confessing. What you owe is the truth about what happened, and whether anyone credits it is not a condition on the debt.
Stop. A confession nobody believes is not truth-telling, it is a performance of remorse that costs the family another week of the story being about you.
Neither confess nor stop. Live differently — give up what you gained, and take the work you would not have taken. Words are what got everybody here.
The confession is owed regardless of the audience, because the wrong is not exhausted by what any court could establish. Being disbelieved is part of it.

evidence.says: Dostoevsky gives the elder Zosima the doctrine that each person is guilty before all for everything, a responsibility that is acknowledged rather than adjudicated and does not wait on anyone else's verdict.

outcomes.label: You Wrote the Permission
outcomes.text: You hold that supplying the reasoning is itself an act, and that responsibility does not evaporate because a second free agent stands between you and the body. That is a hard line and it survives the obvious replies. Its cost is that it generalises badly: every teacher, every editor, every person who has ever argued a position in front of a stranger falls under it somewhere, and you will need a stopping rule that does not simply track how much you happen to regret this particular case.

outcomes.label: He Chose, and So Did You
outcomes.text: You refuse to let either party dissolve into the other. He is not a mechanism your words operated, and you are not innocent merely because he acted; both of you made something out of what was available. Sartre took Dostoevsky's own formula in exactly this direction. What it costs is an answer to the asymmetry — you had the education, the standing and the money coming, and a doctrine of equal freedom is very convenient for whoever already had more of it.

outcomes.label: What Is Left to Do
outcomes.text: You treat the allocation of guilt as an accounting exercise that helps nobody, and you go looking for what can still be affected — the inheritance, the family, the way the argument gets made next time. This is the answer most likely to do some good. Its exposure is that it never has to settle the question, and a person who is always busy repairing has found a socially admired method of not thinking about what he did.

outcomes.label: The Kind of Person Who Says It
outcomes.text: Your attention is on what the arguing was for — whether you believed it, whether you were performing, whether you noticed who was in the room. That is the register the novel itself works in, and it catches something the guilt calculation misses. Its weakness is that it can be conducted entirely inside your own head: self-examination is unfalsifiable, and it makes no difference to anyone that you have understood yourself better than they have.

outcomes.label: The Man You Were Not Listening To
outcomes.text: You locate the wrong in the relationship — that you talked past someone you had decided did not count as an interlocutor, and that this is why he heard permission where you heard an argument. It is the most specific diagnosis available here and probably the truest to the case. It also risks making the murder a communication failure, and there is a point past which attending to how you spoke to him becomes another way of keeping the subject on you.

outcomes.label: Guilty Before All
outcomes.text: You think the debt is real whether or not it can be established, and that acknowledging it is owed regardless of who believes you. Dostoevsky gives that position to Zosima and clearly means it, which is worth knowing: it is the novel's answer, not a neutral reading of it. The difficulty is that a guilt everyone bears for everything is hard to act on and easy to enjoy, and it can leave the person who actually did the thing standing in a crowd of the equally culpable.

entries.title: The Onion
entries.gist: In Book VII of *The Brothers Karamazov* (1879–80), Alyosha goes to Grushenka's house on the worst night of his life. His teacher, the elder Zosima, has died, and the body has begun to smell — which the monastery takes as a verdict on the man. Grushenka, who has arranged to have Alyosha brought to her intending to ruin him, hears about Zosima and gets off his knee. Then she tells him a story she says she had from her cook, Matryona.

questions.prompt: A woman who has treated the people around her badly for forty years did one generous thing, once, a long time ago, and the person she did it for is now the only one arguing that she should be helped.

options.label: The one act counts, entirely and without discount. A kindness is not cancelled by the forty years around it, and it is the only thing here anybody actually did.
One act does not make a person generous. Character is a settled disposition built by repetition, and a single exception is evidence of very little.

evidence.says: Aristotle held that virtue is a stable disposition formed by habituation, so that doing one just thing no more makes a person just than one swallow makes a summer.

options.label: What matters is why she did it. If it was a mood, or vanity, or a debt she was settling, it tells you nothing about what she is owed now.

evidence.work: Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals
evidence.says: Kant argued that an action has moral worth only when done from duty rather than from inclination or advantage, so a benevolent impulse that happens to help is praiseworthy but not, strictly, good.

options.label: Her record is beside the point. Ask what helping her costs and what refusing costs, and treat the forty years as a fact about her rather than a sentence.

questions.prompt: Offered a private deal that saves her alone and weakens the case for the other forty households, she takes it, and says openly that she was offered it and they were not.

options.label: That is the end of the claim. Whatever the one kindness was worth, she has just spent it — and spent it on exactly the thing it was supposed to prove she was not.
It is not the end of anything. She is seventy-nine and frightened, and taking the offer in front of you is not a moral position she is adopting.
Nothing about her changes what you owe. You do not calibrate your conduct to hers, or you have made her the author of your behaviour as well as her own.

evidence.work: Otherwise than Being, or Beyond Essence
evidence.says: Levinas, who returned repeatedly to Dostoevsky's line about being guilty before all, held that responsibility for the other is prior to any reckoning and does not depend on the other reciprocating it.

options.label: Everyone in the building would take that offer, and most of them would tell themselves a better story about it. What is being punished is her candour.

evidence.says: Mandeville argued that public displays of charity and public condemnations of selfishness are largely governed by pride and reputation, and that people claim motives their conduct does not support.

questions.prompt: The man she once helped wants to keep supporting her, at real cost to the campaign the other households depend on. He says he owes her, and that a debt is a debt.

options.label: He is right. Particular obligations to particular people are not overridden by arithmetic about strangers, and a person who drops them is not more moral.
He is wrong, and being used. Forty households against one debt is not a close question, however much the debt feels like a debt from inside.

evidence.says: Singer argued that proximity and personal connection carry no moral weight in themselves, so an obligation is not diminished by the beneficiary being a stranger nor inflated by their being close at hand.

options.label: He should pay the debt himself and not out of the common fund. Gratitude is his to honour with his own money and his own time, not with theirs.
Look at what he is actually doing — sitting with someone nobody else will sit with. That is the whole of moral life and the campaign is the abstraction.

evidence.says: Murdoch located moral progress in the patient attention one person gives another rather than in choices between options, and treated the just regard for a particular person as the substance of goodness rather than its ornament.

questions.prompt: To move quickly, the campaign must drop one household. The lawyer is indifferent which. Someone proposes dropping the one who has behaved worst; someone else proposes dropping the one who will manage best without it.

options.label: Drop by conduct. A group that will not distinguish between its members' behaviour has no standards, and the standards are what made this a campaign.
Drop by resilience. Desert is unknowable and need is not, and you would be building the whole judgement on gossip about forty years of somebody's temper.
Drop nobody. Take the slower route and lose two months. The moment this group starts ranking its own, it becomes the thing it was formed against.
Draw lots. It is the only method that does not require anyone to be judged, and the only one everybody could still look at afterwards.

evidence.says: Broome argued that when claims are comparable but cannot all be met, a lottery gives each claim a proportionate hearing in a way that direct selection does not.

outcomes.label: The Onion Is an Onion
outcomes.text: You hold that a kindness is real when it happens and stays real afterwards, and you will not let a ledger of forty years cancel it. You also stay with the frightened old woman rather than with the principle she has offended. That is the reading of the fable most people take from it, and it is the warmer one. Its cost is that it has no way to refuse anybody: the person who kicks is exactly the person this instinct will keep on helping, and the forty households are also particular people whom you happen not to be looking at.

outcomes.label: One Swallow
outcomes.text: You want to know what the act came out of, and you are unmoved by a single exception in a long record. Aristotle is behind you, and so is the shape of the fable — it is not the smallness of the onion that breaks it. The exposure is that this standard is nearly impossible to meet from outside: you are assessing a character you have only heard about, and the people whose dispositions are legible to you are mostly the ones who are already like you.

outcomes.label: What Is Owed Anyway
outcomes.text: You detach what you owe from what the other person deserves, which means the side-deal, the forty years and the kicking change nothing about your conduct. Levinas holds that position seriously and so, in his own idiom, does Zosima. It is the hardest line here to knock over. What it costs is that you will be used, that you have no way to say so, and that the people who cooperate at their own expense are subsidising the people who do not.

outcomes.label: Count the Households
outcomes.text: You keep the arithmetic in view — forty tenancies against one debt of gratitude — and you decline to let the vividness of the person in front of you set the price. That resistance is genuinely difficult and usually right about scale. Its price is that it can justify dropping her, and the reasoning that drops her will be available again next month against someone else, at which point the group has acquired a method for deciding who is expendable.

outcomes.label: Terms Everyone Can See
outcomes.text: Your instinct is to fix the rule before the case: who is in, what a member owes, what happens to someone who takes a private deal. That is what actually holds a campaign of forty households together, and it is the only answer here that does not depend on everyone being decent. Its weakness is the fable's own point — a rule about who may hold on to the onion is still a rule about letting go, and the woman in the lake did nothing that any constitution forbids.

outcomes.label: Everybody Would Have Taken It
outcomes.text: You suspect the judgement more than the conduct: the building is condemning a woman for doing what almost anyone would do and saying so without a cover story, and the standard being applied is a standard nobody in the room could survive. Mandeville would recognise the point, and it is a useful corrective in a meeting that has begun to enjoy itself. Its difficulty is that it disarms you completely — if every standard is really about reputation, you have no ground left from which to object when the company does the same thing to all forty-one of you.

outcomes.label: Nobody Earns It
outcomes.text: You take the fable as being about grace rather than accounting: the onion was never payment, it was a handhold offered to someone with no claim at all. On that reading the question of what she deserves was always the wrong question, and the sin is not the thinness of her record but her insistence that the rescue be hers alone. It is probably the reading Dostoevsky intended. Its difficulty is practical: an unconditional rescue is easy to affirm and expensive to run, and the forty households cannot be saved by a doctrine that declines to choose.

entries.title: The Pillars of Support
entries.gist: Gene Sharp's claim, argued at length in *The Politics of Nonviolent Action* (1973) and compressed into the pamphlet *From Dictatorship to Democracy* (1993), is that political power is not a possession. A ruler does not *have* power the way a person has a coat. What a ruler has is the ongoing cooperation of a large number of people — tax collectors, soldiers, judges, teachers, railway workers, the men who print the currency — and that cooperation can be withdrawn.

questions.prompt: A government you consider illegitimate has held power for nine years. You have a week's warning of a crackdown. You can spend that week organising a mass rally, or quietly persuading forty mid-level tax officials to slow their work to a crawl.

options.label: The officials. A regime that cannot collect revenue cannot pay the people who enforce it, and that is where its power actually lives.

evidence.says: Sharp's central claim is that rulers depend on the cooperation of bureaucrats, police, soldiers and business, and that withdrawing that cooperation is more decisive than any confrontation with the state's strongest point.

options.label: The rally. Nothing changes until people see how many of them there are, and the officials will not move until they do.

evidence.says: Kuran argues that under repression people conceal what they actually believe, so nobody can tell how much opposition exists; a visible crowd reveals it, and the revelation can cascade very fast.

options.label: Neither. Both invite the crackdown, and the people who suffer it will not be the ones who called for it.

evidence.says: Arendt distinguished power, which rests on numbers acting together, from violence, which is instrumental and can destroy power without ever producing it — and warned that provoking force is not the same as building support.

options.label: Refuse the framing. Deciding what a population should risk on their behalf is the thing the regime also does.

questions.prompt: The crackdown comes. Soldiers beat unarmed marchers, it is filmed, and support for the opposition doubles within a fortnight. An organiser tells you privately that the beating was the best thing that could have happened to the movement.

options.label: He is right, and saying so out loud is what people cannot stand about strategy. Repression that backfires is how these movements win.

evidence.says: Sharp named this political jiu-jitsu: violent repression of visibly nonviolent people shifts third parties, the regime's own supporters and sometimes its troops toward the resisters, turning the state's strength against it.

options.label: He is right and should never say it. A leadership that thinks this way will eventually arrange the beating.

evidence.says: Williams held that a politician who can do necessary but terrible things without cost to themselves is exactly the wrong person to trust with the power to do them; the reluctance is part of the qualification.

options.label: He is wrong. Those were people, not a mechanism, and describing them as a fortunate input is where movements start to resemble what they oppose.

evidence.work: Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals
evidence.says: Kant's second formulation forbids treating a person merely as a means; on that reading a strategy which counts the injuries of supporters as a benefit has already crossed the line it claims to defend.

options.label: It is not for me to judge from outside. The people taking the beating were not coerced, and they knew the arithmetic better than I do.

questions.prompt: Two years on, the movement has won. The new government proposes to bar the old party's officials from public office for a decade, on the grounds that a democracy cannot be staffed by the people who ran the secret police.

options.label: Support it. The pillars that held the old regime up are still standing, and leaving them in place is how restorations happen.

evidence.says: Sharp warned that a transition which leaves the old regime's institutional supports intact invites either a coup or the quiet reconstitution of the same arrangement under a new name.

options.label: Oppose it. A rule that disqualifies people by association is the instrument you just spent nine years objecting to.

evidence.says: Havel argued that the line between complicit and innocent runs through almost everyone under such a system rather than between two groups of people, which makes collective disqualification both unjust and untrue to how the system worked.

options.label: Oppose it, and offer amnesty in exchange for testimony. What the country needs is the record, not the punishment.

evidence.says: Tutu defended the South African commission's trade of amnesty for full disclosure as the price of a shared account of what happened, and was explicit that it cost the wronged something real.

options.label: It depends entirely on whether the new government expects to lose an election. A rule written by winners about losers is not a principle.

questions.prompt: A colleague argues the whole framework is naive: it worked in Serbia and the Philippines because those regimes still cared about legitimacy, and it would have achieved nothing against a state willing to kill at scale.

options.label: The objection holds, and the honest version of the theory is narrower than its popular version. It is a method for regimes that need consent, not all of them.

evidence.who: Erica Chenoweth and Maria J. Stephan
evidence.says: Their dataset found nonviolent campaigns succeeded markedly more often than violent ones across the twentieth century, while also identifying conditions — notably security-force defection — that the outcome depends on.

options.label: No regime kills at scale for long without people willing to do it. The theory holds; the timescale is what changes.

evidence.says: La Boétie's argument, four centuries earlier, was that a tyrant has only the power his subjects hand him, and that the puzzle is not how tyranny is imposed but why so many carry it willingly.

options.label: If it fails against the worst regimes, it fails where it is most needed, and the counsel to be patient is being given to people who will not survive it.

evidence.says: Fanon rejected the demand that the colonised confine themselves to methods their oppressors would find acceptable, and denied that the violence of the dominated can be judged by a standard never applied to the violence that made them.

options.label: Both of you are arguing about what works. Whether it is right to ask this of people is a different question and nobody has raised it.

outcomes.label: Power Is a Mechanism
outcomes.text: You treat a regime as a machine with inputs, and you look for the input that can be withheld. This is Sharp's actual contribution and it is more useful than the moral language usually wrapped around protest, because it identifies what to do on a Tuesday. Its exposure is that a mechanism has no view about who gets hurt operating it — the same analysis that identifies the tax office also identifies which supporters are worth spending, and nothing inside the framework tells you to stop.

outcomes.label: The Means Are Already the End
outcomes.text: You will not let the goal launder the method, and you apply that to your own side first — which is the harder direction and the one most movements skip. You are guarded against becoming what you opposed. What it costs you is efficacy in exactly the cases where efficacy matters most, and you owe an answer to the person who says your scruples are affordable because someone else is paying for them.

outcomes.label: What It Makes of the Organisers
outcomes.text: Your attention is on what the strategy does to the people running it. You notice that an organiser who can describe a beating as fortunate has undergone a change, and you treat that change as data about who will govern afterwards. Williams is with you. The objection is that reluctance is not a plan: when the crackdown comes, character has still not told anyone which street to march down.

outcomes.label: The People, Not the Lever
outcomes.text: You keep returning to who absorbs the cost, and you refuse to let them be described as inputs. That instinct is the correction the strategic literature most needs. It is most exposed when it becomes a reason to do nothing — the person who is never willing to let anyone bear a risk has effectively chosen the status quo, which also has victims, and quieter ones.

outcomes.label: What Could Be Agreed To
outcomes.text: You ask whether those bearing the risk accepted it and whether the rules afterwards could be accepted by the losers. That handles both the crackdown and the disqualification cleanly, and it is the standard the transitions that held tend to have met. Its weakness is the person who cannot be asked: the bystander in the street, the official who will be purged, the generation that inherits the settlement.

outcomes.label: It Depends Who Is Asking
outcomes.text: You read every rule proposed here as an artefact of who expects to hold power next, and you are frequently right — lustration rules really are written by winners. The difficulty is that this reading is available against every position including your own, and a critique that dissolves all standards leaves you nothing to object with when the new government does exactly what the old one did.

outcomes.label: Nobody Appointed You
outcomes.text: You will not decide on behalf of people who did not ask you to, and you notice that calculating other people's acceptable losses is the posture of the state as much as of the movement. That is a real scruple. It also cannot be acted on: declining to choose is a choice with consequences, and the people you declined to speak for absorb those too.

entries.title: Political Jiu-Jitsu
entries.gist: Gene Sharp gave the phenomenon its name in *The Politics of Nonviolent Action* (1973). **Political jiu-jitsu** is what happens when a government attacks people who are visibly not fighting back, and the attack rebounds on the government. The martial-arts metaphor is exact: in jiu-jitsu you do not meet an opponent's force, you let it carry him past his own balance. The regime's advantage in weapons is real and undiminished; what changes is that using them costs more than not using them.

questions.prompt: You are routing tomorrow's march. One route passes a precinct whose commander has beaten demonstrators twice this year, and the press will be there. The other route is quiet, legal and safe, and nobody outside the city will hear about it.

options.label: Take the route past the precinct. Repression that the country watches is the most powerful thing this movement will ever have, and wasting it is not kindness.

evidence.says: Sharp argued that violent repression of visibly nonviolent people can throw a regime off balance, shifting third parties, its own supporters and sometimes its troops toward the resisters — the state's strength turned against it.

options.label: Take that route, but only after telling every marcher precisely what is likely to happen and letting each of them decide whether to be there.

evidence.says: King described a stage of self-purification before any direct action, in which volunteers were asked in advance whether they could take blows without retaliating, so that nobody arrived at the confrontation uninformed.

options.label: The quiet route. Walking people into a beating you have forecast is using them, whatever the beating later achieves.

evidence.work: Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals
evidence.says: Kant's second formulation forbids treating a person merely as a means; on that reading, planning a route because of the injuries it will produce enlists the injured in a purpose that is not theirs.

options.label: Stop planning around the police entirely. A movement that needs bruises to be heard has already accepted that its arguments are not enough.

evidence.says: Rawls treated civil disobedience as a public address to the community's sense of justice — an appeal conducted in the open to shared principles, which is a different thing from an appeal conducted through the spectacle of being hurt.

questions.prompt: The government adapts. Arrests now happen at four in the morning with no cameras present, while plainclothes officers start scuffles that the state broadcasters film. Two of your marshals hit back when they were grabbed, and it is on every channel.

options.label: Make the hidden repression visible. Get the families of the night arrests on record; the whole counter-strategy depends on nobody seeing.

evidence.work: Justice Ignited: The Dynamics of Backfire
evidence.says: Martin catalogued the standard methods by which an injustice is stopped from backfiring — concealment, devaluing the victim, reframing the event, channelling grievance into official procedures, and intimidation — and argued that countering each of them is what makes backfire happen.

options.label: Expel the two marshals today and say so loudly. Nonviolent discipline is not a style choice; without it the entire mechanism runs in reverse.

evidence.says: Sharp treated nonviolent discipline as a strategic necessity rather than a moral ornament: once resisters use violence, sympathy among third parties and within the regime's own ranks collapses and the state's repression is retrospectively justified.

options.label: Do not expel them. Policing your own members so the footage stays clean is the state's work, and the people who fight back are usually the ones with the least protection.

evidence.work: This Nonviolent Stuff'll Get You Killed
evidence.says: Cobb argued that armed self-defence by ordinary Black southerners coexisted with and materially protected the nonviolent civil rights movement, and that the tidy image of uniform nonviolent discipline was partly written afterwards.

options.label: Notice what you have become. You are now managing your supporters' suffering as material, and you are good at it.

questions.prompt: A police lieutenant you have never met faces his own version of this. He is ordered to clear the square. If he obeys in view of the cameras the government is damaged; if he refuses he is dismissed and replaced within the hour by an officer known for enjoying the work.

options.label: Obey, and hold the line as gently as anyone can. Staying in post is the only way the person in that uniform is someone who will restrain it.

evidence.says: Hirschman argued that exit removes precisely the members most likely to press for improvement, so that departing on principle can leave an organisation worse than staying inside it and using voice.

options.label: Refuse, resign, and say publicly why. Defection by the people who hold the batons is the thing that actually ends this, and a private conscience ends nothing.

evidence.who: Erica Chenoweth and Maria J. Stephan
evidence.says: Their comparative study identifies defection or non-cooperation by security forces and civil servants as among the strongest correlates of a campaign's success, which puts unusual weight on the individual officer's choice.

options.label: Obey fully. An armed man who decides which lawful orders to carry out is a worse danger to citizens than a bad order, and far more common.

evidence.says: Hobbes held that once each person retains private judgement about which commands bind them, the common power dissolves and everyone returns to the insecurity the arrangement existed to end.

options.label: There is no clean option here, and the demand for one is the trap. Whatever he does, he is the one who has to carry it.

evidence.says: Sartre used the case of the student torn between his mother and the Resistance to argue that no doctrine ranks the options for you; you invent the answer in choosing, and you own it afterwards.

questions.prompt: A colleague argues the whole theory is survivor's bias. For every Selma there are ten crushed movements nobody can name, repression usually works, and the doctrine of backfire is a story told by the campaigns that happened to survive.

options.label: Largely right. Backfire needs conditions — witnesses, an audience that identifies with the victims, a regime that still needs to be liked — and the popular version drops all of them.

evidence.work: Unarmed Insurrections: People Power Movements in Nondemocracies
evidence.says: Schock argued that outcomes turn on a regime's dependence relations and a movement's resilience and leverage rather than on nonviolence in itself, and documented campaigns that were simply crushed.

options.label: Backfire is real but slow. It works on the loyalty of the regime's own people over years, not on the evening news, and that is invisible while it happens.

evidence.says: Sharp described loyalty shifts among a regime's administrators, business supporters and soldiers as cumulative and largely unobservable until the point where cooperation visibly fails.

options.label: Whether it works is not the question. Refusing to answer violence with violence is right when the cameras come and right when they do not.

evidence.says: Gandhi insisted that means and ends cannot be separated, and treated satyagraha as a commitment to truth borne by the resister's own suffering rather than as a tactic to be assessed by its yield.

options.label: Asking whether it works already concedes that the people beaten are an input. The unasked question is who has standing to spend them.

outcomes.label: The State's Own Weight
outcomes.text: You treat repression as a force that can be redirected, and you are asking what a given event will do to the loyalties holding the government up. This is Sharp's actual argument and it is more useful than most talk about protest, because it tells you what tomorrow's decision should be. Its exposure is structural: the analysis has no vocabulary for the person absorbing the blow, and the same reasoning that identifies the useful confrontation also identifies which supporters are worth spending.

outcomes.label: Not Through Them
outcomes.text: You hold that a person cannot be routed into an injury for what the injury will accomplish, and you hold it whether or not the accomplishment is real. That is the one constraint the strategic literature keeps stepping over. The price is that you are refusing the mechanism at the exact point where it works, and you owe an answer to the organiser who says the status quo is also producing injuries, just slowly and to people nobody films.

outcomes.label: Only What Was Agreed To
outcomes.text: Your test is whether the people carrying the risk were told and chose, and whether the rules being enforced are ones the enforcers could stand behind. This handles both the march and the lieutenant without contradiction, and it is close to how disciplined movements have actually organised. Its blind spot is everyone who cannot be asked: the bystander, the conscript, the shopkeeper whose window goes in.

outcomes.label: Whoever Takes the Blow
outcomes.text: You keep returning to the specific person who gets hit, and you resist every description that turns them into footage. It is the correction this subject most needs, and it also cuts against the tidy version of movement discipline, since you notice who is expelled for fighting back and who was never in danger. Where it fails you is when it becomes a reason to keep everyone home, which is a decision with victims of its own.

outcomes.label: What It Makes of You
outcomes.text: You watch what the strategy does to the person running it — the moment when forecasting your own supporters' injuries becomes a skill you have. That instinct catches the corruption early, and it is why some of the best organisers burn out and some of the worst do not. The objection is that character does not choose a route. Someone still has to decide which street the march goes down tomorrow morning.

outcomes.label: Nobody Decides for Him
outcomes.text: You refuse the idea that a doctrine settles these cases, and you are right that both the lieutenant and the marshal are choosing without cover. That is honest about how it feels from inside. The difficulty is that it gives no guidance to the person who has to answer by Tuesday, and it can shade into treating every choice as equally defensible because every choice was hard.

entries.title: The Participation Threshold
entries.gist: Erica Chenoweth and Maria Stephan's *Why Civil Resistance Works* (2011) did something the literature on protest had mostly avoided: it counted. They assembled a dataset of major campaigns from 1900 onward that pursued maximalist aims — removing a government, expelling an occupier, or seceding — and that could be observed to have at least a thousand participants. Then they coded each campaign as primarily violent or primarily nonviolent and asked which achieved its stated objective.

questions.prompt: Your campaign's own count says roughly 2.9 per cent of the country has turned out at peak. Reaching the figure people keep citing would mean bringing in villagers from three provinces who will be identifiable to the police afterwards and who cannot leave the country if this goes wrong.

options.label: Bring them. Participation size is the best-supported predictor anyone has, and declining to use the one thing that reliably matters is not caution, it is waste.

evidence.who: Erica Chenoweth and Maria J. Stephan
evidence.says: Across their dataset of twentieth-century campaigns, the size and social breadth of participation emerged as the strongest single correlate of success, working through defections, loyalty shifts and the range of methods a large campaign can sustain.

options.label: Do not treat a historical regularity as a target. The figure described campaigns that had already grown; it was never a recipe for growing one.

evidence.work: Questions, Answers, and Some Cautionary Updates Regarding the 3.5% Rule
evidence.says: Chenoweth has repeatedly cautioned that the threshold is a descriptive observation about her sample rather than a law or a strategic instruction, and that no campaign in the data mobilised that share by deciding to.

options.label: The number is a symptom, not a cause. Campaigns reach that size when the regime is already cracking, and you cannot manufacture the crack from below.

evidence.says: Tarrow argued that cycles of contention open when political opportunities appear — elite divisions, unstable alignments, weakened repression — so that mass mobilisation is often the visible sign of a shift that began elsewhere.

options.label: You are proposing to move human beings across a country to hit a statistical target. That is the wrong relation to have to the people who trust you.

questions.prompt: The president offers a negotiated early election in eighteen months, with the same electoral commission and the same state broadcaster. Half your coalition calls it a win; the other half says it is the concession that ends the campaign without changing anything.

options.label: Take it. A campaign that extracts a dated concession from a sitting president has done the thing campaigns are for, and holding out for total victory is how movements dissolve.

evidence.who: Erica Chenoweth and Maria J. Stephan
evidence.says: Their coding counts a campaign as successful when it achieves its stated maximalist objective within a year of peak activity, and much of the record consists of negotiated exits rather than collapses.

options.label: Refuse. What a database records as success is not what people marched for, and the coding is exactly where this literature is weakest.

evidence.says: Pinckney showed that campaigns which remove a ruler frequently fail to produce democracy afterwards, and that what follows depends on sustained mobilisation and on the transitional government not concentrating power — none of which the success coding captures.

options.label: Neither half of the coalition owns this. Put it to the people who have been sleeping in the square, and abide by what they say.
Accept and stay in the square. A promise from this government is worth exactly the pressure standing behind it on the day it comes due.

evidence.says: O'Donnell described elected executives who accept the ritual of elections while hollowing out the institutions that could hold them to account, which implies that a commitment from such an executive binds only while it is enforced.

questions.prompt: A television commentator makes the case against you plainly. Nine hundred thousand people is three per cent of the country; the president was elected with fifty-one per cent; and a movement that removes a government because it can fill a square is claiming a veto that no one voted to give it.

options.label: He is right. The remedy for a bad election is the next one, and removing an elected government by mobilisation writes a precedent your opponents will use against you within the decade.

evidence.says: Levitsky and Ziblatt document cases in which opposition attempts to remove elected leaders by extra-electoral means strengthened those leaders and accelerated democratic breakdown rather than preventing it.

options.label: He is wrong. A vote held under a captured court, a state broadcaster and a jailed challenger is not a mandate, and the street is the only check left standing.

evidence.says: O'Donnell's argument is that an electoral victory does not by itself confer democratic authority where horizontal accountability has been dismantled, since the election is then a plebiscite rather than a choice.

options.label: Both are counting the wrong thing. Neither a crowd nor a ballot box settles legitimacy; the question is whether the rules could be accepted by whoever ends up losing under them.

evidence.says: Rawls grounded legitimacy in principles that free and equal persons could accept in advance without knowing their own position, which makes both the headcount in the square and the margin at the polls evidence rather than the standard.

options.label: Whichever side wins will describe its own method as the legitimate one. This argument is about who expects to be on top, and everyone in it knows that.

questions.prompt: A statistician friend takes the finding apart over dinner: the dataset only includes campaigns that already reached a thousand observed participants, the success coding is generous, and the record since 2010 is far worse than the century it was drawn from.

options.label: Concede all of it. The honest claim is narrower than the one on the placards, and its own author has said so.

evidence.says: Chenoweth reported that the success rate of nonviolent campaigns has fallen sharply since around 2010, attributing it partly to smaller and more digitally organised campaigns and partly to regimes that have learned to counter them.

options.label: A weakened regularity is still the best comparison available, and the alternative it is being compared with is armed rebellion, which does worse on the same coding and costs more.

evidence.work: Civil Resistance: What Everyone Needs to Know
evidence.says: Chenoweth's summary of the field holds that even after every correction, the comparative record still favours nonviolent campaigns over armed ones on both success and post-conflict outcomes.

options.label: The measurement argument is a way of not noticing that actual people are being asked to risk their lives on a correlation drawn from other people's countries.
None of this decides anything. You do not consult a dataset to work out whether to refuse a government you cannot live under.

evidence.says: Havel's greengrocer stops displaying the slogan not because a calculation favours it but because continuing has become a lie he is telling with his own hands; the refusal is prior to any estimate of what it will achieve.

outcomes.label: The Arithmetic
outcomes.text: You want to know what actually moves outcomes, and you are willing to change your plan when the evidence changes. That is rarer in political argument than it should be, and it is the spirit in which Chenoweth and Stephan did the work. What it exposes you to is treating a correlation as an instruction: the dataset can tell you that big campaigns succeeded more often, and it cannot tell you that the forty people you bring in tomorrow will not simply be arrested.

outcomes.label: People Are Not the Denominator
outcomes.text: You refuse to let a person become a unit in a headcount, whatever the headcount predicts, and you hold to procedural limits even when they cost you the outcome. The strength of this is that it survives the moment when your side is winning and finds the shortcut tempting. The cost is that the constraint binds you and not the government, which is the standard complaint against it and has never been fully answered.

outcomes.label: Rules the Loser Could Accept
outcomes.text: Your test is what could be agreed to in advance by people who do not know whether they will win — which is why you distrust both the square and a rigged ballot, and why you want the risk-bearers themselves to decide about the deal. It is the most stable position here. Its weakness is speed: working out what everyone could accept takes time that a campaign at its peak does not have, and peaks do not recur on request.

outcomes.label: The People Being Counted
outcomes.text: You keep your attention on the identifiable villagers rather than the percentage they would constitute, and you notice when a strategic conversation has stopped being about anyone. That instinct is a genuine check on organisers who have started to think in aggregates. Where it leaves you stuck is that the status quo is also producing casualties, they are simply not gathered in one place where you can see them at once.

outcomes.label: Whoever Wins Writes It
outcomes.text: You read the legitimacy argument as a proxy for the power struggle underneath, and you are frequently right — the same commentators change sides on street mobilisation depending on who is in the street. The difficulty is that this reading also dissolves your own claim: if legitimacy language is only ever positioning, you have nothing left to say when the winners do what the losers were condemned for.

outcomes.label: Prior to the Estimate
outcomes.text: You think the decision to refuse comes before any calculation of what refusal will achieve, and that a person who resists only when the odds are good was not really resisting. Havel is with you, and so is most of the testimony of people who actually did it. The price is that this reasoning cannot be given to anyone else: it justifies your own risk and it cannot justify asking a village to take one.

entries.title: The Public Sphere
entries.gist: *The Structural Transformation of the Public Sphere* (1962) is Jürgen Habermas's habilitation thesis, and it is a history with a claim buried in it. The history concerns a peculiar development in eighteenth-century Britain, France and the German states: the appearance of coffee houses, salons, table societies, subscription libraries and journals like the *Tatler* and the *Spectator*, in which private persons came together **as a public** to reason about matters of general concern.

questions.prompt: The neighbourhood assembly on the harbour redevelopment is open to anyone. In practice it is attended by retired homeowners with time to prepare, and the tenants most affected work shifts, have children, and have started meeting instead in a messaging group of nine hundred people that refuses to send delegates.

options.label: Keep the assembly open and unweighted. Any rule you write to correct for this will be captured by whoever writes it, and an open room is the only thing nobody owns.

evidence.work: The Structural Transformation of the Public Sphere
evidence.says: Habermas identified the bourgeois public sphere's constitutive norm as the bracketing of status: participants were to argue as though social rank did not apply, so that the only authority in the room was the better argument.

options.label: Restructure it. Evening sittings, paid childcare, interpretation, and speaking time that is not first come first served. Formal openness to people who cannot come is not openness.

evidence.says: Fraser argued that bracketing inequality rather than eliminating it works to the advantage of dominant groups, because the protocols of polite public reason are themselves marks of the status they claim to set aside.

options.label: Treat the messaging group as a public in its own right, not a failure to attend yours. It is where those people are actually working out what they think.

evidence.says: Warner described counterpublics as publics that maintain an awareness of their subordinate standing and develop their own idioms, rather than as deficient attempts at the dominant public's style of address.

options.label: Stop pretending an assembly decides this. Tidal modelling and traffic load are not matters of opinion, and the forum's real function is to consent to what the engineers conclude.

evidence.says: Lippmann held that the omnicompetent citizen is a fiction and that the public cannot govern the substance of complex questions; its realistic role is to side with one faction of insiders against another at moments of crisis.

questions.prompt: A tenant begins describing her landlord's conduct — the boiler, the letters, the man who lets himself in. The chair rules it out of scope: this is a planning forum, and that is a private dispute for a tribunal.

options.label: The chair is right. A forum with no boundary becomes a place where everything is aired and nothing is decided, and the boundary is what makes it politics rather than grievance.

evidence.says: Arendt held that a political realm exists only where people speak about a world held in common, and that when the concerns of the household flood the public space what remains is administration and complaint rather than action.

options.label: The chair is wrong, and the ruling is the mechanism. Deciding which troubles count as public is how whole categories of harm were kept off every agenda for a century.

evidence.work: Feminist Critiques of the Public/Private Dichotomy
evidence.says: Pateman argued that the public–private division is not a neutral boundary but a political settlement, and that classifying domestic life as private removed from politics precisely the relations in which many people are least free.

options.label: He should have let her finish and then explained on the record why it falls outside. A procedure that never justifies itself is what empties rooms.
Chairs discover scope rules when the content is inconvenient. This is about Thursday's vote, and everyone in the room understood that.

questions.prompt: The developer offers to fund the assembly properly: hall hire, childcare, a professional facilitator, translation, and a printed summary posted to every household. There is no editorial condition, and nothing in writing about content.

options.label: Refuse. A deliberation funded by an interested party is publicity wearing the costume of a public, and everyone will know it even if nothing improper ever happens.

evidence.work: The Structural Transformation of the Public Sphere
evidence.says: Habermas traced a shift from a public that reasoned about power to a field of managed publicity, in which organised interests stage displays designed to secure acclamation rather than to be argued with.

options.label: Accept. The assembly is already captured — by time rather than money — and the childcare is the single thing on that list that would put the affected tenants in the room.

evidence.says: Fraser's standard is participatory parity, which she argued has material preconditions: without the resources that make attendance possible, a formally open forum reproduces the inequalities outside it.

options.label: Accept, with a published agreement, an independent chair, and the funder's submissions marked as such. Money is not the problem; unaccountable money is.

evidence.says: Ostrom found that durable collective arrangements were those whose rules the participants themselves shaped and could monitor, with accessible arenas for resolving conflict — the accountability structure mattering more than the source of resources.

options.label: It makes no difference. The planning department settled this in March, and the assembly is a ritual whose function is to have happened.

evidence.says: Michels argued that any large organisation, however democratic its charter, develops a directing minority whose interest in remaining in charge shapes outcomes before the membership is consulted.

questions.prompt: A historian on the panel says the whole framework is nostalgia. The coffee-house public was a few thousand propertied men in two cities; it excluded women, servants and the poor by design; and invoking it is how every generation condemns its own media.

options.label: She is right, and the myth does work. A golden age nobody can date is a convenient standard because nothing present can meet it.

evidence.work: Was There Ever a Public Sphere? If So, When?
evidence.says: Schudson argued that the American record shows little of the rational public discussion the model posits, and that the ideal is better understood as a recent normative invention projected backwards.

options.label: The description was always normative. What matters is the standard those rooms claimed and failed to meet, which is still the standard we use to convict them.

evidence.work: Further Reflections on the Public Sphere
evidence.says: Replying to his critics, Habermas conceded much of the historical case, including the plebeian and excluded publics he had underweighted, while holding that the normative content of the ideal is not disposed of by the failures of the society that first articulated it.

options.label: Both of you are arguing about 1750. The present problem is different in kind and needs its own description, not a verdict on coffee houses.

evidence.work: A New Structural Transformation of the Public Sphere and Deliberative Politics
evidence.says: In his late return to the theme Habermas argued that platform media dissolve the editorial filtering that once made a common agenda possible, so that the characteristic pathology is now fragmentation rather than manufactured consensus.

options.label: The exclusions were not a flaw in the achievement, they were its condition. Those men could reason calmly because nothing under discussion threatened them.

evidence.work: Women and the Public Sphere in the Age of the French Revolution
evidence.says: Landes argued that the republican public sphere was constructed in explicit opposition to the salon culture women had led, so that its universality was defined against them rather than merely failing to include them.

outcomes.label: The Open Room
outcomes.text: You care about what could be justified to everyone affected, and your instinct is to fix the procedure rather than the outcome: publish the rules, explain the rulings, declare the money. This is the closest thing to Habermas's own position and it is more robust than its critics allow, because it survives the discovery that your side is the one being ruled out of order. Its exposure is that a fair procedure can be fair and still be attended entirely by people with Tuesday evenings free.

outcomes.label: The Standard Holds
outcomes.text: You hold that some things are not for sale or for negotiation regardless of what they would buy — a deliberation funded by an interested party is compromised even if it is never interfered with. That keeps a public space recognisable as one. The price is visible in the childcare: refusing tainted money is a decision made by people who could already attend, and it is paid by people who could not.

outcomes.label: Whose Trouble Counts
outcomes.text: You track who is not in the room and what they were not allowed to say, and you treat the scope ruling as the substance rather than the housekeeping. Fraser and Pateman are with you, and the historical record is largely on that side. Where it strains is that a forum which admits every trouble as public business becomes one in which nothing is settled, and the people with the least time are the first to stop coming.

outcomes.label: What Actually Improves It
outcomes.text: You ask what will change who is in the room and what gets decided, and you will take compromised means to a better distribution of voice. That is the answer with the best chance of doing something by next month. It also has no natural stopping point: the same reasoning that accepts the childcare accepts the facilitator, the summary, and eventually the agenda, and no single step is the one that looks wrong.

outcomes.label: Publics, Not The Public
outcomes.text: You doubt there is one forum in which everyone could reason together, and you read appeals to it as the standpoint of whoever already sets the terms. The historical case for this is strong and the messaging group is genuinely a public. The difficulty arrives at the vote: if there is no shared arena, there is no procedure the losing side has any reason to accept, and you have described the situation without leaving anyone a way out of it.
