entries.gist: In 1902 Lenin published *What Is To Be Done?*, arguing that a workers' movement left to itself develops only trade-union consciousness — better wages, shorter hours — and that revolutionary understanding has to be brought to it from outside, by an organisation of disciplined professional revolutionaries. Under a police state, he added, this was not a preference but a condition of surviving at all. In 1904, after the split at the party's second congress, he defended a centralised organisational model in *One Step Forward, Two Steps Back*.

questions.prompt: A coalition of sixty local groups has lost a campaign it should have won, through three months of unresolved argument. A proposal on the table would create a small strategy committee whose decisions bind every member group.

options.label: Adopt it. Under real pressure, a movement that cannot decide anything is not democratic, it is simply available to be beaten.

evidence.says: Lenin argued that a movement left to develop spontaneously arrives only at trade-union consciousness, and that under conditions of repression an organisation of disciplined, full-time revolutionaries is the precondition of achieving anything at all.

options.label: Reject it. A committee that binds the membership begins by standing in for it and ends by replacing it, and no clause you write will prevent that.

evidence.work: Organizational Questions of Russian Social Democracy
evidence.says: Luxemburg held that the ultra-centralism Lenin proposed was the spirit of a night watchman rather than of a fighting movement, and that the mistakes a genuine workers' movement makes for itself are more valuable than the correctness of the best central committee.

options.label: The proposal only formalises what already exists. There is a group of eight people who make the decisions now, and none of them can be voted out.

evidence.says: Freeman argued that a group without formal structure does not lack a leadership; it acquires an informal one selected by friendship and availability, which cannot be held accountable precisely because it is not admitted to exist.

options.label: Any organisation of this size develops a ruling group whatever it writes down. The question is only whether you will be able to see it.

evidence.work: Political Parties: A Sociological Study of the Oligarchical Tendencies of Modern Democracy
evidence.says: Michels studied the most internally democratic parties and unions of his day and concluded that organisation as such produces an entrenched leadership, since expertise, continuity and control of information accrue to whoever holds the posts.

questions.prompt: Someone points out where this went last time: a party of professional revolutionaries took power and within five years the elected bodies were decoration and a dozen men decided everything.

options.label: That outcome was contained in the design. Substitution runs in one direction — the organisation for the class, the committee for the organisation, one man for the committee.

evidence.says: Trotsky, then opposing Lenin, predicted that the party organisation would come to substitute itself for the party, the central committee for the organisation, and finally a single dictator for the central committee.

options.label: Circumstances did it, not the structure. Civil war, blockade, famine and the physical destruction of the working class the party rested on.

evidence.says: Deutscher's account traces the single-party regime substantially to the emergencies of civil war and the collapse of the industrial working class, arguing that measures adopted as temporary hardened into a system.

options.label: The warning was given at the time by people inside the movement, and it named the mechanism: without free elections and free argument, public life dies and a clique is left ruling in the name of a class.

evidence.says: Writing in prison in 1918 while defending the revolution against its social-democratic critics, Luxemburg warned that suppressing elections, press and open dispute would leave a dictatorship of a handful of politicians rather than of a class.

options.label: It was predicted a generation earlier, and not by a Marxist: a state run in the workers' name would produce a new bureaucracy of former workers looking down from the height of the state.

evidence.says: Bakunin argued against Marx that a workers' state would be governed by ex-workers who, once in office, would cease to be workers at all and would look on the masses from above as a new privileged administration.

questions.prompt: The proposal passes, and the strategy committee is good: it wins two campaigns in a year. It now proposes suspending the annual conference during the dispute, on the grounds that the employer reads the minutes.

options.label: Refuse. This is the step, and it always arrives attached to a real operational reason, which is why it works.
Agree, with a fixed date to return. Secrecy during a dispute is not the same as rule by committee, and pretending otherwise loses disputes.
Agree only if the decision is taken by the membership rather than by the committee that benefits from it.
The winning record is the danger, not the reassurance. Competence is how a leadership acquires the standing to stop asking.

evidence.work: Political Parties: A Sociological Study of the Oligarchical Tendencies of Modern Democracy
evidence.says: Michels observed that leaders gain autonomy through demonstrated usefulness: the membership defers to those who have delivered, and gratitude does more to entrench a leadership than any constitutional provision.

questions.prompt: A ballot is held and the membership votes, by a large majority and with full information, to give the committee permanent binding authority.

options.label: Then it is legitimate. A movement that overrides its own members to protect them from their choice has already done the thing you were worried about.
A majority cannot vote away the next majority's ability to change its mind. That is the one decision a membership does not have standing to take.

evidence.says: Luxemburg's argument was that freedom which excludes those who think differently is not freedom, and that a movement's capacity to correct itself depends on keeping open the dispute a settled leadership has every reason to close.

options.label: Watch what happens to the people on the committee. The structure matters less than whether they still find it uncomfortable to be obeyed.
Leave, and organise elsewhere. Staying to be governed by something you predicted would go wrong makes you part of what it becomes.

outcomes.label: What Actually Wins
outcomes.text: You judge organisational form by what it can do under pressure, and you notice that most of the movements destroyed in the last century were destroyed while still arguing. That is the strongest thing in Lenin's case and it does not depend on agreeing with him about anything else. Its exposure is that this reasoning has no stopping rule: every further concentration of authority can be justified by the same argument that justified the first, and the emergency that licenses it is renewable.

outcomes.label: The Thing You Cannot Delegate
outcomes.text: You hold that some capacities — to elect, to dispute, to reverse — are not available for trade even in exchange for effectiveness, because they are what makes the body a body rather than a following. Luxemburg is with you, and she argued it while defending the revolution rather than from outside it. The cost is real and she paid part of it: the movement that keeps its procedures intact is slower, and it will sometimes be beaten by one that did not.

outcomes.label: Who Authorised It
outcomes.text: You keep asking who agreed, on what terms, and whether they can withdraw — which turns an argument about revolutionary theory into a set of answerable questions about mandate and recall. It is the version of this dispute that can actually be written into a constitution. Its limit is the case in q4: consent given once is used to close the route back, and a procedure cannot by itself tell you whether the people voting were in a position to refuse.

outcomes.label: What Leading Does to Leaders
outcomes.text: Your attention is on the people in the room and what a few years of being right does to them — the point where competence becomes entitlement and consultation starts to feel like an inefficiency. Michels found exactly this in the most democratic organisations available to him. On its own it is not a safeguard: character does not survive institutional incentives reliably, and a movement cannot be built on the hope of finding better people.

outcomes.label: It Happens Anyway
outcomes.text: You think oligarchy forms in any organisation of size, so the real choice is between one you can see and one you cannot. Michels and Freeman between them make this hard to dismiss, and it protects you from believing that flat structures are innocent. Where it leaves you is close to fatalism: if every arrangement produces a ruling group, you have no reason to resist the particular one in front of you, which is the argument that ruling group will make.

outcomes.label: The People It Is For
outcomes.text: You measure the structure by what it does to the members who are not in any committee — whether they are still participants or have become an audience that turns out when asked. That is the difference the theoretical argument usually loses, and it is visible long before any constitutional crisis. Its weakness is that attentiveness to the immediate membership can quietly become the movement's purpose, and the campaign it exists to win goes unwon.

outcomes.label: Leave and Build Elsewhere
outcomes.text: You would rather go than be governed by something you already believe will go wrong, on the reasoning that staying makes you a component of it. That is a serious position and it has been the right one more than once. It is also how a movement loses precisely the people who saw the problem, leaving the committee with a membership that never objected.

entries.title: The Narcissism of Small Differences
entries.gist: The phrase appears in *Civilization and Its Discontents* (1930), in the middle of Freud's argument about aggression, and it takes up about a page. He is asking why civilisation demands so much of people and why the demand is so unstable, and his answer is that human beings are constitutionally aggressive — that the instruction to love one's neighbour is issued against a standing inclination to exploit and humiliate him.

questions.prompt: Two charities in the same city provide respite care to the same families, from buildings a mile apart, and have not shared a platform in eleven years. They differ over whether the sitting should be done by trained volunteers or by paid staff. A funder offers three years of money on condition that they merge.

options.label: Merge. The disagreement is genuine and it is not worth what it has cost the families on both waiting lists for a decade.

evidence.says: Singer argued that the strength of an obligation to prevent serious harm does not vary with the agent's affiliations or distance from the sufferer, which makes an institutional loyalty a poor reason for a worse outcome.

options.label: Refuse. That difference is the whole method, not a preference, and people call it small because they have never had to deliver the service on a Tuesday night.

evidence.says: Williams held that a person's deep commitments are not one input among others to be traded against a better aggregate; requiring someone to abandon the project that organises their life alienates them from their own agency.

options.label: Merge the back office and keep both practices running as separate teams, with the difference documented rather than resolved.
The offer is the problem. A funder is using money to settle a professional disagreement it does not understand and has not had to work inside.

evidence.says: Scott argued that schemes imposed from above favour what is legible to the centre and routinely destroy the practical local knowledge that made the activity work, precisely because that knowledge cannot be stated in the centre's terms.

questions.prompt: Running a staff meeting, you notice something you have been avoiding. Your people are never more united, more good-humoured or more willing to cover shifts than in the ten minutes after somebody mentions the other charity.

options.label: That is the whole point, and it is a reason to distrust the enmity rather than to enjoy it. The rivalry is doing a job that has nothing to do with respite care.

evidence.says: Freud observed that a considerable number of people can be bound together in affection so long as there are others left over to receive their aggression, and that neighbouring communities most alike are the readiest to supply the role.

options.label: Cohesion from rivalry is ordinary and mostly useful. Every working group defines itself against an opposite number, and organisations that pretend otherwise go limp.

evidence.says: Simmel treated conflict as a form of sociation rather than a breakdown of it, noting that an external opponent consolidates a group's boundaries and internal solidarity in ways nothing else supplies.

options.label: The cohesion is real and so is the bill, and it is being paid by families neither organisation will name in the meeting where the joke is made.
Calling it psychology flatters everyone. Both organisations are bidding for one contract, and the doctrinal difference arrived after the competition did.

evidence.says: Tilly argued that categorical boundaries between groups are sustained because they organise the hoarding of opportunities and resources, so the belief content of a division is often downstream of what the division protects.

questions.prompt: A colleague objects to the phrase itself. Calling a difference small, she says, is something done by people who do not have to live on either side of it, and the term has been used to make other people's grievances sound like vanity.

options.label: She is right. "Small" is an outsider's measurement, and a word that converts a grievance into a personality defect is doing political work whatever its author intended.

evidence.says: Geertz described attachments of blood, language, custom and locality as experienced from within as ineffable and coercive rather than as preferences, which is why an observer's ranking of their size does not correspond to anything the participants recognise.

options.label: That mistakes the claim. Nobody says the difference does not matter to the people involved; the observation is about what the mattering is doing for them.

evidence.work: Group Psychology and the Analysis of the Ego
evidence.says: Freud connected group cohesion to a standing aversion toward the stranger, and took the intensity of that aversion to be evidence about the group's internal economy rather than a report on the stranger.

options.label: The pattern is real and the explanation is not. There is no reservoir of aggression needing discharge; there are conditions that reliably produce cruelty, and they can be changed.

evidence.says: Fromm rejected Freud's innate death drive and argued that destructiveness is a character formation produced by particular social conditions, which makes it historically variable rather than a constant to be drained off.

options.label: It is a description of something documented. Violence is commonest between neighbours who resemble each other, not between strangers, and refusing the word does not undo the finding.

evidence.says: Blok assembled comparative evidence that serious conflict clusters among adjacent and similar communities, and argued that boundaries require constant symbolic maintenance precisely where the underlying difference is thinnest.

questions.prompt: The merger goes through. At the first board meeting, a member of your old staff proposes that the other charity's founder be kept off the new board, citing what she wrote nine years ago about the volunteer model.

options.label: Support it. What she wrote has consequences for the people receiving the service, and treating a practice disagreement as a personality clash is how bad practice survives.
Oppose it. A merged body needs someone to be the stranger, and it has selected the nearest available candidate within four minutes of forming.

evidence.says: Bourdieu found the fiercest symbolic struggles between adjacent positions in social space, where the objective difference is smallest and the need to mark it is therefore greatest.

options.label: Neither side of this argument includes anyone who uses the service. Ask them, and be bound by it.
Whatever the merits, purging someone for a nine-year-old position tells every person in the new organisation exactly what will happen to them.

outcomes.label: What It Costs Outside the Room
outcomes.text: You keep asking what the division produces for the people who are not in it, and you will spend a loyalty to shorten a waiting list. That is the reading of Freud with the most practical purchase: the enmity is doing a job, and the job is not the one on the letterhead. Its exposure is that the same reasoning will trade away a distinction that turns out to have been carrying real information, and you will not find out which one it was until the service is worse.

outcomes.label: The Difference Is Real
outcomes.text: You resist having a considered position reclassified as a psychological symptom, and you are right that this move is available against any conviction whatsoever, including the one being used to dissolve yours. Held firmly, it is what stops good practice being merged away by people counting buildings. The cost is that it is indistinguishable from the inside from the thing Freud described, and everyone in an eleven-year feud believes their difference is the substantive one.

outcomes.label: What the Feud Makes of You
outcomes.text: Your attention is on what the rivalry does to the people inside it — the good humour that arrives with the joke, the speed with which a new body finds someone to exclude. You are watching character rather than argument, which is the register Freud was actually writing in. What it does not give you is a decision: noticing that a purge would be corrupting does not settle whether the position being purged was wrong.

outcomes.label: Ask the People It Is For
outcomes.text: You keep noticing that the argument is being conducted entirely by the people who are not on the receiving end of it, and you want the decision put to those who are. It is the cleanest way out of the trap, since it replaces a contest of self-descriptions with a question someone can answer. Its limit is that the people you would ask are dependent on both organisations and know it, which makes their answer harder to trust than the procedure assumes.

outcomes.label: Whose Difference Is Called Small
outcomes.text: You are alert to who gets to describe a grievance as trivial, and you notice that the word "small" is almost always applied downwards. That is the necessary corrective to a term with an ugly history of use. Where it strains is that the corrective, applied generally, protects every faction from every diagnosis: if no difference may be called small by anyone outside it, nothing can ever be said about a feud from outside a feud.

outcomes.label: Nobody Is Standing Outside
outcomes.text: You distrust the vantage point the term requires — the observer who can see that a difference is minor — and you suspect the funder, the consultant and the theorist alike of describing a conflict in whatever terms suit their position in it. This is well founded and it is also total. Applied to yourself it leaves you no ground from which to say the eleven-year feud was a mistake, which you plainly think it was.

themes.name: What Makes Right Right
themes.blurb: The ground floor. Whether morality is counted, commanded, cultivated or agreed — and whether it is anything at all.

themes.name: The Crowd
themes.blurb: What other people do to your judgement — obedience, conformity, the diffusion of responsibility, the mob that thinks it is a public.

themes.name: Righteous Hypocrisy
themes.blurb: The gap between the self you perform and the one that acts. Grandstanding, licensing, bad faith, and the comfort of an unexamined conviction.

themes.name: Power and Rule
themes.blurb: What a ruler may do that a person may not, whether the ends reach back and clean the means, and who gets to decide.

themes.name: Suffering and Compassion
themes.blurb: Whether pain is the only thing that finally counts, what you owe the person in front of you, and what you owe the one you will never meet.

themes.name: Truth and Lies
themes.blurb: Whether you may ever lie, what language does to what you can think, and whether some things should not be said at all.

themes.name: The Self and Freedom
themes.blurb: Whether you chose any of it, whether that matters for blame, and what is left of responsibility if the answer is no.

themes.name: Justice and Desert
themes.blurb: Who deserves what, whether luck should be allowed to decide it, and what a society owes the person it has ranked lowest.

themes.name: Loyalty and Attachment
themes.blurb: Whether the people close to you may count for more, and what impartiality costs when it is applied to a family.

themes.name: The Sacred
themes.blurb: Whether morality needs a ground outside us — and what changes if it turns out there is none.

themes.name: The Unborn and the Dead
themes.blurb: What is owed to people who do not exist yet, and whether more lives worth living is straightforwardly better.

themes.name: Machines and the Future
themes.blurb: What we are building, whether it can be given values, and whether anything we make could be owed something.

themes.name: Games and Strangers
themes.blurb: What happens to cooperation when nobody is watching, and why the rational move and the decent one keep coming apart.

philosophers.name: Socrates
philosophers.voice: You will not let a claim past without asking what it means, including your own — and you would rather end in honest confusion than comfortable agreement.

philosophers.name: Plato
philosophers.voice: You believe the good is something discovered rather than agreed, and that most disagreement is a failure to look hard enough.

philosophers.name: Aristotle
philosophers.voice: You sort before you judge, look for the mean between two ways of getting it wrong, and think a good life is a practice rather than a proof.

philosophers.name: Epicurus
philosophers.voice: You measure by whether it leaves a person less troubled, and you noticed that most of what people chase reliably fails that test.

philosophers.name: Epictetus
philosophers.voice: You draw a hard line around what is yours to control and refuse to spend a single thought on the other side of it.

philosophers.name: Marcus Aurelius
philosophers.voice: You hold yourself to a standard you never expect the world to meet, and you write it down at night because holding it is daily work.

philosophers.name: Seneca
philosophers.voice: You know exactly what the right life looks like and exactly how far your own has fallen from it, and you keep writing anyway.

philosophers.name: Diogenes of Sinope
philosophers.voice: You think most of what people call decency is theatre, and you would rather be indecent in public than complicit in private.

philosophers.name: Protagoras
philosophers.voice: Man is the measure. You take disagreement as the normal condition of moral life rather than a problem to be solved.

philosophers.name: Heraclitus
philosophers.voice: You do not think anyone steps into the same situation twice, so a rule fixed in advance is already describing a world that has moved.

philosophers.name: Cicero
philosophers.voice: You believe there is a law above the statute, and you spent a career arguing it in rooms that mostly did not care.

philosophers.name: Plutarch
philosophers.voice: You read a life for what it reveals about a person rather than for what it achieved, and you think the small anecdote is often the honest one.

philosophers.name: Confucius
philosophers.voice: You think character is built by practice inside real relationships, and that the forms people dismiss as empty are what make the feeling possible.

philosophers.name: Mencius
philosophers.voice: You saw the child at the well and concluded that the impulse to help is native to us, and that ethics is cultivation rather than construction.

philosophers.name: Xunzi
philosophers.voice: You think people are not naturally good and that this is no cause for despair — it is the reason institutions and ritual exist.

philosophers.name: Mozi
philosophers.voice: You care about the stranger exactly as much as the brother, and you regard the refusal to do so as the root of most avoidable harm.

philosophers.name: Laozi
philosophers.voice: You suspect most intervention makes things worse, and that the strongest move available is usually the one not made.

philosophers.name: Zhuangzi
philosophers.voice: You will not grant that your standpoint is the true one, and you find the confidence of moralists funnier than it is frightening.

philosophers.name: Han Feizi
philosophers.voice: You design for the person acting badly, because a system that only works when people are good is not a system.

philosophers.name: Sun Tzu
philosophers.voice: You judge by the outcome and you count the cost before the fight, holding that the finest victory is the one that never required a battle.

philosophers.name: Siddhartha Gautama
philosophers.voice: You begin from suffering rather than from rules, and you treat the craving underneath an act as the thing that actually needs addressing.

philosophers.name: Ved Vyasa
philosophers.voice: You put duty at the centre and then wrote the epic that shows how badly duty can conflict with itself, refusing to resolve it cheaply.

philosophers.name: Krishna
philosophers.voice: You hold that the act must be done and the fruit released — that attachment to the outcome, not the action, is where a person goes wrong.

philosophers.name: Shantideva
philosophers.voice: You cannot find the argument for why your own suffering matters more than a stranger’s, so you stopped acting as though it did.

philosophers.name: Nagarjuna
philosophers.voice: You dismantle every fixed position, including your own, and treat the emptiness that remains as liberating rather than bleak.

philosophers.name: Mahavira
philosophers.voice: Non-violence is not a policy you weigh against others; it is the boundary inside which everything else gets decided.

philosophers.name: Adi Shankara
philosophers.voice: If the separation between self and other is finally unreal, then harming another was always a confusion about who you are.

philosophers.name: Kabir
philosophers.voice: You have no patience for the priest or the mullah, and you think the whole apparatus of religious respectability gets between a person and the thing itself.

philosophers.name: Guru Nanak
philosophers.voice: You see one light in everyone and take the practical consequence seriously: the kitchen where all castes eat together is the argument.

philosophers.name: Chanakya
philosophers.voice: You think the statesman who refuses to get his hands dirty has simply exported the dirt to someone with less choice.

philosophers.name: Swami Vivekananda
philosophers.voice: You hold that service to a person in front of you is worship, and that a religion producing no such service has failed its own test.

philosophers.name: B.R. Ambedkar
philosophers.voice: You will not accept an order as legitimate because it is ancient, and you measure a society by what it does to the people it ranks lowest.

philosophers.name: Mohandas Gandhi
philosophers.voice: You hold that the means contain the end, so a just result reached by unjust means is not the result you were seeking.

philosophers.name: Rabindranath Tagore
philosophers.voice: You distrust every ideology that asks a person to become smaller in its service, including the patriotic ones.

philosophers.name: Jalal al-Din Rumi
philosophers.voice: You think the argument was never going to get anyone there, and that what changes a person is closer to love than to proof.

philosophers.name: Al-Ghazali
philosophers.voice: You went through doubt to the bottom and came back holding that the heart’s knowledge is not a lesser kind than the philosopher’s.

philosophers.name: Ibn Rushd (Averroes)
philosophers.voice: You refuse the choice between reason and revelation, holding that two true things cannot finally contradict and the fault is in our reading.

philosophers.name: Ibn Khaldun
philosophers.voice: You explain a people’s morals by the conditions that produced them, and expect those morals to soften exactly as the conditions do.

philosophers.name: Moses Maimonides
philosophers.voice: You rank charity by how far it protects the dignity of the person receiving it, which is a different question from how much was given.

philosophers.name: Hillel the Elder
philosophers.voice: What is hateful to you, do not do to another. You think the rest is commentary, and that the commentary still has to be studied.

philosophers.name: Augustine of Hippo
philosophers.voice: You do not trust your own motives, having watched them fail, and you think a moral theory that assumes good will has not met anybody.

philosophers.name: Thomas Aquinas
philosophers.voice: You believe reason can reach the moral law unaided and that revelation completes rather than replaces it, and you build the system to show it.

philosophers.name: Blaise Pascal
philosophers.voice: You take the wager seriously because you take the stakes seriously, and you think the heart has reasons the calculation does not reach.

philosophers.name: Martin Luther
philosophers.voice: Here you stand. You cannot do otherwise, and you regard the ability to do otherwise as the thing conscience is defined against.

philosophers.name: Thérèse of Lisieux
philosophers.voice: You think sanctity is available in the smallest ordinary kindness and that waiting for a large occasion is a way of avoiding all of them.

philosophers.name: Niccolò Machiavelli
philosophers.voice: You describe how power actually works rather than how it should, and you have been called wicked for the accuracy ever since.

philosophers.name: Michel de Montaigne
philosophers.voice: You noticed that everyone calls barbarism whatever is not their own custom, and you have never got over how much that explains.

philosophers.name: Thomas Hobbes
philosophers.voice: You start from what people are like without a common power over them, and everything you build is an answer to that picture.

philosophers.name: Baruch Spinoza
philosophers.voice: You think blame is mostly a failure of understanding, and that to grasp why someone acted is already to stop condemning them.

philosophers.name: John Locke
philosophers.voice: You hold that rights are not granted by government but predate it, which is why government can forfeit its claim on you.

philosophers.name: Jean-Jacques Rousseau
philosophers.voice: You think we were not born like this, that society did most of it, and that the general will is what freedom looks like among others.

philosophers.name: David Hume
philosophers.voice: Reason is the slave of the passions. You think moral judgement is a feeling first and an argument afterwards, and you are unbothered by that.

philosophers.name: Adam Smith
philosophers.voice: You test a judgement by whether an impartial spectator inside you would endorse it, which is stricter than it sounds.

philosophers.name: Mary Wollstonecraft
philosophers.voice: You will not accept a virtue defined so that half the species is praised for lacking the capacity to exercise it.

philosophers.name: Voltaire
philosophers.voice: You would rather live among people who are wrong and free than right and compelled, and you spent a career making that expensive for the compellers.

philosophers.name: Immanuel Kant
philosophers.voice: You ask whether you could will everyone to do it, and if the answer is no you stop — no matter what the consequences of stopping are.

philosophers.name: Jeremy Bentham
philosophers.voice: Each to count for one. You want the calculation made explicitly, because it is being made anyway and hiding it helps nobody.

philosophers.name: John Stuart Mill
philosophers.voice: You count consequences, and you draw the line at harm — over himself, over his own body and mind, the individual is sovereign.

philosophers.name: G.W.F. Hegel
philosophers.voice: You think an individual conscience abstracted from its community is an empty thing, and that freedom is realised through institutions rather than against them.

philosophers.name: Arthur Schopenhauer
philosophers.voice: You ground morality in compassion rather than in duty, holding that the person who acts well does it because another’s suffering became theirs.

philosophers.name: Søren Kierkegaard
philosophers.voice: You think the ethical can be suspended by something higher, and that the leap cannot be argued for without ceasing to be a leap.

philosophers.name: Karl Marx
philosophers.voice: You read a moral code as a set of arrangements that suit somebody, and you always want to know who.

philosophers.name: Henry David Thoreau
philosophers.voice: If the law makes you an agent of injustice, you think breaking it is not merely permitted but required, and you will take the night in jail.

philosophers.name: Ralph Waldo Emerson
philosophers.voice: You hold that the imitation of another’s virtue is a kind of suicide, and that what is true for you in private is what must be said.

philosophers.name: Leo Tolstoy
philosophers.voice: You take the Sermon on the Mount as a set of instructions rather than an ideal, and you find every institution that softens it complicit.

philosophers.name: Fyodor Dostoevsky
philosophers.voice: You are convinced that a morality resting only on reason collapses under pressure, and you wrote the collapse rather than asserting it.

philosophers.name: Friedrich Nietzsche
philosophers.voice: You ask where a value came from before asking whether it is true, and you suspect much of what calls itself good is weakness with a better name.

philosophers.name: William James
philosophers.voice: You want to know what difference a moral belief makes in practice, on the grounds that a difference which makes none is not a difference.

philosophers.name: Émile Durkheim
philosophers.voice: You think morality is a social fact before it is a personal one, and that a person cut loose from shared norms is in real danger.

philosophers.name: John Dewey
philosophers.voice: You treat a moral problem the way you would treat any problem — as something to be inquired into, tried, and revised in the light of what happened.

philosophers.name: Max Weber
philosophers.voice: You separate the ethic of conviction from the ethic of responsibility, and you think politics belongs to whoever can hold both without collapsing either.

philosophers.name: Sigmund Freud
philosophers.voice: You suspect the voice of conscience of being a great deal more punitive, and a great deal less rational, than it presents itself as being.

philosophers.name: Bertrand Russell
philosophers.voice: You will not hold a conviction more firmly than the evidence warrants, and you have gone to prison for one anyway.

philosophers.name: G.E. Moore
philosophers.voice: You think good is simple and indefinable, and that every attempt to reduce it to something natural has quietly changed the subject.

philosophers.name: Ludwig Wittgenstein
philosophers.voice: You suspect that what matters most in ethics cannot be said at all, and that the attempt to say it produces nonsense we should respect.

philosophers.name: W.D. Ross
philosophers.voice: You hold several duties at once, know they will conflict, and think judgement rather than a master rule is what settles which one wins today.

philosophers.name: A.J. Ayer
philosophers.voice: You think a moral claim expresses an attitude rather than stating a fact, and that the appearance of disagreement about truth is a mistake.

philosophers.name: Jean-Paul Sartre
philosophers.voice: There is no given answer and no one to hand you one; you are condemned to choose, and every appeal to circumstance is bad faith.

philosophers.name: Simone de Beauvoir
philosophers.voice: You take freedom as the ground of ethics and then ask, unlike your contemporaries, what it means for those whose freedom is structurally curtailed.

philosophers.name: Albert Camus
philosophers.voice: You accept that the universe supplies no meaning and refuse the two easy exits, holding that revolt has limits or it becomes what it opposed.

philosophers.name: Emmanuel Levinas
philosophers.voice: The face of the other person makes a claim on you before you have agreed to anything, and ethics begins there rather than in a principle.

philosophers.name: Martin Buber
philosophers.voice: You think the whole moral question is whether you are meeting a person or handling an object, and that most of the time we are handling.

philosophers.name: Hannah Arendt
philosophers.voice: You found the great evil of the century done by people who had stopped thinking rather than by monsters, which is far more frightening.

philosophers.name: Simone Weil
philosophers.voice: Attention, given fully to a person in affliction, is for you the rarest and most demanding thing anyone can offer another.

philosophers.name: George Orwell
philosophers.voice: You watch what political language does to the ability to think, and you hold that seeing what is in front of your nose is a constant struggle.

philosophers.name: Aldous Huxley
philosophers.voice: You think the more likely tyranny is the one people enjoy, and that a population can be made content on terms that cost it everything.

philosophers.name: Marshall McLuhan
philosophers.voice: You look past what is being said to what the medium is doing to the people using it, on the grounds that the second outlasts the first.

philosophers.name: Ursula K. Le Guin
philosophers.voice: You built the city whose happiness rests on one child’s misery, and you refused to tell the reader what walking away costs or achieves.

philosophers.name: Karl Popper
philosophers.voice: You prefer the reform you can reverse to the revolution you cannot, and you noticed that unlimited tolerance ends by destroying the tolerant.

philosophers.name: Isaiah Berlin
philosophers.voice: You think genuine goods conflict irreconcilably, and that any system promising to harmonise them all is preparing to sacrifice one quietly.

philosophers.name: Michel Foucault
philosophers.voice: You ask what a moral discourse is doing rather than whether it is true, and you look for the power arrangement it makes seem natural.

philosophers.name: Theodor Adorno
philosophers.voice: You doubt there is a right life inside a wrong one, and you distrust any comfort a damaged society is able to supply.

philosophers.name: Frantz Fanon
philosophers.role: of The Wretched of the Earth
philosophers.voice: You will not let the violence of the oppressed be judged by a standard that never applied itself to the violence that created them.

philosophers.name: Martin Luther King Jr.
philosophers.voice: An unjust law is no law at all — and you accept the penalty openly, because that acceptance is what distinguishes your disobedience from lawlessness.

philosophers.name: Malcolm X
philosophers.voice: You will not ask permission for a freedom that was never anyone’s to grant, and you reserve every means the situation requires.

philosophers.name: Václav Havel
philosophers.role: of The Power of the Powerless
philosophers.voice: You think the greengrocer who takes the sign out of his window has done something, and that living in truth is the whole of the politics.

philosophers.name: John Rawls
philosophers.voice: You ask what rules you would choose without knowing which life in the society would be yours, and you take the answer seriously.

philosophers.name: Robert Nozick
philosophers.voice: You hold that individuals have rights, and that there are things no person or group may do to them without violating those rights.

philosophers.name: Bernard Williams
philosophers.voice: You think a moral theory that requires a person to abandon what makes their life theirs has asked one thought too many.

philosophers.name: Derek Parfit
philosophers.voice: You follow the argument wherever it goes, including into conclusions you find repugnant, and you regard flinching as a failure of nerve.

philosophers.name: Alasdair MacIntyre
philosophers.voice: You think modern moral argument is interminable because it is using the fragments of a tradition it has forgotten, and shouting.

philosophers.name: Iris Murdoch
philosophers.voice: You think most moral work happens before the decision, in the quality of attention a person pays to what is actually in front of them.

philosophers.name: G.E.M. Anscombe
philosophers.voice: You hold that some acts are simply excluded from consideration, and that a philosopher who will debate them has already gone wrong.

philosophers.name: Philippa Foot
philosophers.voice: You built the trolley to test a distinction, not to settle a score, and you thought goodness in a human being was as natural a notion as health.

philosophers.name: Peter Singer
philosophers.voice: The drowning child is every child. You take the distance between you and a stranger to be morally irrelevant, and you live as though it is.

philosophers.name: Martha Nussbaum
philosophers.voice: You ask what a person is actually able to do and to be, and you think the emotions are part of practical reason rather than noise in it.

philosophers.name: T.M. Scanlon
philosophers.role: of What We Owe to Each Other
philosophers.voice: You test a principle by whether anyone could reasonably reject it, which puts the objection of the single worst-affected person at the centre.

philosophers.name: Christine Korsgaard
philosophers.voice: You think obligation comes from the identity you cannot act against without ceasing to be anyone in particular.

philosophers.name: Amartya Sen
philosophers.voice: You would rather remove a clear injustice now than specify the perfectly just institution first, and you think the second has swallowed the first.

philosophers.name: Kwame Anthony Appiah
philosophers.voice: You think we can owe something to strangers without agreeing with them about everything, and that conversation does more work than conversion.

philosophers.name: Michael Sandel
philosophers.voice: You ask what a market does to the good it is pricing, and you doubt that the answer is ever simply "distributes it more efficiently".

philosophers.name: Jonathan Haidt
philosophers.voice: You think the judgement arrives first and the reasoning is hired afterwards, and that people who disagree with you are running different foundations.

philosophers.name: bell hooks
philosophers.voice: You treat love as a practice with obligations rather than a feeling that happens, and you think naming domination is part of the practice.

philosophers.name: Angela Davis
philosophers.voice: You ask what the institution is actually producing rather than what it says it is for, and you are willing to conclude it should not exist.

philosophers.name: Cornel West
philosophers.voice: You think justice is what love looks like in public, and you refuse to let a critique become a substitute for tenderness.

philosophers.name: Ayn Rand
philosophers.voice: You regard self-sacrifice as the ethic that has done the most harm, and rational self-interest as the only basis on which people deal honestly.

philosophers.name: Jordan Peterson
philosophers.voice: You start from responsibility rather than rights, and you think the meaning people are looking for is on the other side of a burden voluntarily taken up.

philosophers.name: Sam Harris
philosophers.voice: You think moral questions have answers in the same way health questions do, and that deferring to intuition here is deferring to accident.

philosophers.name: Slavoj Žižek
philosophers.voice: You look past the visible outrage to the ordinary functioning that produced it, and you distrust the charity that keeps the machine comfortable.

philosophers.name: Judith Butler
philosophers.voice: You ask whose life would be mourned if it ended, and you treat the answer as the real measure of who currently counts.

philosophers.name: Byung-Chul Han
philosophers.voice: You locate the exhaustion inside the person rather than in the employer, and you notice the achievement subject supervising itself.

philosophers.name: Ted Chiang
philosophers.voice: You build the premise out honestly and let the moral weight arrive through consequence rather than assertion, and you never rig the ending.

philosophers.name: Toby Ord
philosophers.voice: You count the people who do not exist yet, and once you have counted them the present looks like a narrow and dangerous moment.

philosophers.name: Nick Bostrom
philosophers.voice: You take low-probability, unbounded-cost outcomes seriously when almost nobody does, and you accept how strange that makes you sound.

philosophers.name: Aldo Leopold
philosophers.voice: A thing is right when it tends to preserve the integrity of the biotic community — and you meant to include the community, not just its people.

philosophers.name: Thich Nhat Hanh
philosophers.voice: You think the peace has to exist in the person doing the work, or the work reproduces the thing it was meant to end.

philosophers.name: Desmond Tutu
philosophers.voice: A person is a person through other people. You chose truth and reconciliation over trials, and you knew exactly what that cost the wronged.

philosophers.name: Miranda Fricker
philosophers.voice: You identified the wrong done to someone simply as a knower — disbelieved because of who they are — and gave it a name people could use.

philosophers.name: Max Stirner
philosophers.role: of The Unique and Its Property
philosophers.voice: You treat every cause that asks for your service — God, nation, humanity, morality — as another master wearing a better coat.

philosophers.name: J.L. Mackie
philosophers.role: of Ethics: Inventing Right and Wrong
philosophers.voice: You think moral facts would have to be very strange entities indeed, and that their strangeness is good reason to doubt they exist.

philosophers.name: Jean Baudrillard
philosophers.voice: You suspect the moral outrage on display is a copy with no original, performed for an audience that also is not there.

philosophers.name: Emil Cioran
philosophers.role: of A Short History of Decay
philosophers.voice: You regard every conviction as a small tyranny in preparation, and the people with the fewest of them as the least dangerous.

philosophers.name: Richard Rorty
philosophers.voice: You gave up on grounding kindness in anything deeper than itself, and think solidarity is built by noticing suffering rather than by proving it matters.

philosophers.name: Hypatia of Alexandria
philosophers.voice: You taught pupils of every faction and refused to convert, holding that the reasoning is the thing shared and the rest is local weather.

glossary.name: Anchoring
glossary.definition: An arbitrary number you have just seen drags your subsequent estimate toward it, even when you know it is arbitrary.
glossary.example: Negotiators open high for this reason. The first figure on the table reshapes the range both sides then argue within, which is why "let them go first" is standard advice and why it is often wrong to comply.

probe.ask: The Mississippi is longer than 800 miles. Without looking it up, how long is it?

options.label: Around 1,000–1,500 miles
options.tell: Pulled toward the 800 you were just handed. The river is about 2,340 miles.

options.label: Around 1,500–2,000 miles
options.tell: Still short, and the anchor is the likeliest reason — it was the only number in the room.

options.label: Over 2,000 miles
options.tell: You resisted it, or you knew the answer. Only the first counts as evidence.

probe.reveal: The 800 carries no information — it was chosen to be low. Jacowitz and Kahneman found the anchor moves estimates even when subjects are told it was generated at random, and even when they are warned. Knowing about anchoring does not reliably protect you from it; deciding your range before you see anyone else's number does.

glossary.name: Availability Heuristic
glossary.definition: You judge how likely something is by how easily an example comes to mind, so vivid and recent events feel commoner than they are.
glossary.example: People consistently overestimate deaths from causes that make the news — shark attacks, plane crashes, terrorism — and underestimate the quiet ones that kill far more, because the quiet ones are not reported.

probe.ask: In an average year, which kills more people worldwide — sharks, or falling coconuts?

options.label: Sharks, clearly
options.tell: The vivid one. Sharks kill roughly 5–10 people a year worldwide.

options.label: Coconuts, clearly
options.tell: You have heard this one — the coconut figure is itself an unsourced legend, which is the deeper lesson.

options.label: I have no idea and would not guess
options.tell: The correct answer for both. Neither number is well measured, and the question was built to feel answerable.

probe.reveal: Both figures are folklore. What the question actually tests is whether a vivid category feels countable. Tversky and Kahneman's point was not that people are wrong about sharks, but that ease of recall substitutes for frequency without the substitution being noticed — which is why a plane crash reshapes risk perception and a year of car journeys does not.

glossary.name: Representativeness
glossary.definition: You judge probability by resemblance to a stereotype rather than by frequency.
glossary.example: Told someone is quiet and tidy, people guess "librarian" over "salesperson" — ignoring that salespeople outnumber librarians by an enormous margin, so even a small share of tidy salespeople outnumbers all librarians.

probe.ask: Someone is quiet, tidy and reads a great deal. Are they more likely to be a librarian or a lorry driver?

options.label: A librarian
options.tell: The description matches the stereotype. It does not match the population.

options.label: A lorry driver
options.tell: Correct, and for the unglamorous reason: there are far more lorry drivers.

probe.reveal: In most countries lorry drivers outnumber librarians by more than twenty to one, so even if the description is four times commoner among librarians, the tidy reader is still probably driving a lorry. Resemblance feels like evidence because it is evidence — it is just much weaker than the base rate it is competing with.

glossary.name: The Conjunction Fallacy
glossary.definition: Judging a specific combination more likely than one of its own parts, which is impossible.
glossary.example: The Linda problem: told she is outspoken and concerned with social justice, most people rate "bank teller and active feminist" as likelier than "bank teller" — though every feminist bank teller is already a bank teller.

probe.ask: A candidate wins a seat. Which is more likely — that they raised over £1m, or that they raised over £1m and had prior national media exposure?

options.label: Raised over £1m
options.tell: Correct. A set cannot be smaller than a set containing it.

options.label: Raised over £1m and had media exposure
options.tell: The second is a subset of the first, so it cannot be likelier. The story was doing the work.

probe.reveal: Adding detail makes a scenario more plausible-sounding and strictly less probable at the same time. Tversky and Kahneman found majorities picking the conjunction even among graduate students in decision science. This is why a forecast with a vivid causal chain attached should be trusted less than the vague one, not more.

glossary.name: Base Rate Neglect
glossary.definition: Ignoring how common something is in the population when interpreting a specific piece of evidence.
glossary.example: A test that is 99% accurate for a disease affecting one in ten thousand still produces far more false positives than true ones, because the rarity dominates. Clinicians and patients both get this wrong routinely.

probe.ask: A test for a disease affecting 1 in 1,000 people is 95% accurate. You test positive. What is the chance you have it?

options.label: About 95%
options.tell: The most common answer. It reads the accuracy figure as the answer.

options.label: About 50%
options.tell: Closer in spirit — you sensed the base rate mattered — but still far too high.

options.label: About 2%
options.tell: Right. In 1,000 people there is 1 true positive and about 50 false ones.

probe.reveal: The rarity of the disease dominates the accuracy of the test, and almost nobody feels this. Gigerenzer showed the error largely dissolves when the same problem is stated in natural frequencies rather than percentages — which suggests the failure is one of representation as much as reasoning, and that the fix is to restate the problem in counts.

glossary.name: The Gambler's Fallacy
glossary.definition: Believing an independent process is "due" to correct itself.
glossary.example: A roulette wheel landed on black twenty-six times running at Monte Carlo in 1913; the casino made a fortune from players certain red was overdue. The wheel had no memory then and has none now.

probe.ask: A fair coin has landed heads eight times running. What is the chance the ninth is tails?

options.label: Better than half — it is due
options.tell: The gambler's fallacy. The coin has no memory of the eight.

options.label: Exactly half
options.tell: Correct, if the coin is genuinely fair.

options.label: Worse than half — the coin may be biased
options.tell: The Bayesian answer, and defensible: eight heads is weak evidence against fairness.

probe.reveal: The stated answer is half, but the third option is the one worth arguing about. If you are not certain the coin is fair, a run is evidence, and updating toward more heads is correct. The fallacy is not "considering the streak" — it is expecting an independent process to compensate for its own past.

glossary.name: The Hot Hand
glossary.definition: Whether a streak of successes predicts the next attempt — famously debunked, then substantially un-debunked.
glossary.example: The 1985 paper found no hot hand in basketball and became a textbook case of human pattern-hunting. In 2018 Miller and Sanjurjo identified a subtle selection bias in that analysis; correcting it, evidence for a real hot hand reappears. A rare case of the debunking needing debunking.

probe.ask: Do you believe a basketball player who has just made three shots is more likely to make the next one?

options.label: Yes — streaks are real
options.tell: The intuition of nearly every player and coach, dismissed for thirty years, now partly vindicated.

options.label: No — it is a cognitive illusion
options.tell: The textbook answer since 1985, and the one the recent statistics have undercut.

probe.reveal: Gilovich, Vallone and Tversky found no hot hand in 1985 and it became the standard example of pattern-seeing. In 2018 Miller and Sanjurjo identified a selection bias in that method — conditioning on a streak biases the estimate downward — and correcting it restored a modest effect. Its size and how far it generalises beyond shooting remain disputed, so the lesson to take is not "streaks are real" but that a famous debunking can itself need debunking.

glossary.name: Regression to the Mean
glossary.definition: Extreme results tend to be followed by less extreme ones, for statistical reasons and not causal ones.
glossary.example: Israeli flight instructors told Kahneman that praise made pilots worse and criticism made them better. Both were regression: an exceptional flight is usually followed by an average one whatever you say afterwards.

probe.ask: Pilots praised after an excellent landing tend to do worse next time; pilots shouted at after a bad one tend to improve. What does this show?

options.label: Criticism works better than praise
options.tell: The conclusion the instructors drew, and the one Kahneman was told.

options.label: Nothing about praise or criticism at all
options.tell: Correct. Extreme performances are followed by less extreme ones whatever you say afterwards.

probe.reveal: Kahneman described this as the moment he understood that the world rewards punishing others and punishes rewarding them — not because it is true, but because regression guarantees the appearance. Any intervention applied only at the extremes will appear to work. This is why a control group is not a formality.

glossary.name: Survivorship Bias
glossary.definition: Drawing conclusions only from what made it through, ignoring what did not.
glossary.example: Wald was asked where to armour bombers, given the bullet holes on returning planes. His answer: armour where there are no holes. Planes hit there did not come back.

probe.ask: Returning bombers show most damage on the wings and fuselage. Where should the extra armour go?

options.label: Wings and fuselage — where the hits are
options.tell: The intuitive answer, and the one Wald was hired to overturn.

options.label: The engines — where the returning planes show no damage
options.tell: Correct. Planes hit there did not come back to be measured.

probe.reveal: Abraham Wald's insight was that the sample was assembled by survival. The same structure sits under most advice from successful people: the dropouts who founded nothing are not interviewed. The question to ask of any dataset is not what it contains but what could not have got into it.

glossary.name: Simpson's Paradox
glossary.definition: A trend that appears in every subgroup can reverse when the groups are combined.
glossary.example: Berkeley graduate admissions in 1973 looked biased against women overall, but department by department slightly favoured them. Women applied disproportionately to the most competitive departments, which reversed the aggregate.

probe.ask: A treatment has a better recovery rate than the alternative in mild cases and in severe cases, but a worse rate overall. Which should a patient choose?

options.label: The treatment — it wins in both groups
options.tell: Usually right, if severity is what drives assignment.

options.label: The alternative — the overall figure is the real one
options.tell: Almost always wrong: the aggregate is confounded by who received what.

options.label: Impossible to say without knowing why patients were assigned
options.tell: The rigorous answer. The causal structure decides which number to read.

probe.reveal: The reversal happens when the better treatment is given disproportionately to the sicker patients. Pearl's point is that no amount of staring at the table resolves it — you need to know how the groups were formed. Statistics alone cannot tell you which of the two contradictory answers is the one about the world.

glossary.name: Berkson's Paradox
glossary.definition: Selecting on a combination of two traits creates a spurious negative correlation between them.
glossary.example: Among people you have dated, attractiveness and kindness may seem inversely related — not because they are in the population, but because you filtered for having at least one.

probe.ask: Among people you have dated, the kind ones tend to be less attractive and the attractive ones less kind. What does that suggest?

options.label: There is a real trade-off between the two
options.tell: The intuitive read, and the one the sample cannot support.

options.label: It is an artefact of who you agreed to date
options.tell: Correct. You dated people who cleared a bar on the sum of the two.

probe.reveal: Selecting on a combination of two traits induces a negative correlation between them within the selected group, even when they are independent in the population. Berkson found it in hospital records. It quietly manufactures trade-offs in any dataset built from admissions, hiring, or anything else with a threshold.

glossary.name: The Prosecutor's Fallacy
glossary.definition: Confusing the probability of the evidence given innocence with the probability of innocence given the evidence.
glossary.example: A one-in-a-million DNA match in a city of ten million means roughly ten people match. Presented as "a one-in-a-million chance he is innocent", it has convicted people.

probe.ask: A DNA match has a 1-in-a-million false positive rate. A search of a 10-million-person database returns one match. How likely is it the right person?

options.label: Almost certain — one in a million
options.tell: The prosecutor's reading, and the one that has sent people to prison.

options.label: Roughly one in ten
options.tell: The right order of magnitude: about 10 false matches are expected in a database that size.

probe.reveal: The probability of the evidence given innocence is not the probability of innocence given the evidence, and a database search inverts the intuition entirely because you have given the rare event ten million chances to occur. Sally Clark's conviction turned on a version of this error and was quashed after the Royal Statistical Society intervened.

glossary.name: The Streetlight Effect
glossary.definition: Searching where it is easy to search rather than where the answer is.
glossary.example: Organisations measure what their systems already record — clicks, tickets closed, hours logged — and then manage those numbers, because the things that actually matter are harder to instrument.

probe.ask: You want to know whether a policy improved lives. Which do you actually measure?

options.label: The outcomes the department already collects monthly
options.tell: Available, comparable, and quite possibly measuring the wrong thing.

options.label: Something you would have to build an instrument to observe
options.tell: Expensive, slow, and the only version that answers the question you asked.

probe.reveal: Neither answer is wrong on its own; the failure is forgetting which one you took. The drunk under the streetlight is not stupid — searching where you can see is rational. The error is concluding that the keys are not there.

glossary.name: The McNamara Fallacy
glossary.definition: Treating what can be measured as the whole of what matters, and what cannot as unimportant.
glossary.example: US command in Vietnam tracked body counts because they were countable, and lost the war on variables nobody was counting. The name is a warning attached to a specific failure.

probe.ask: Your team's numbers are all up and morale is visibly collapsing. What do you report?

options.label: The numbers — morale is not measurable
options.tell: Defensible and how most reporting works. It is also how the failure begins.

options.label: Both, and say the second is unquantified
options.tell: Harder to write and the only honest version.

options.label: Morale — the numbers are lagging indicators
options.tell: Risky in the other direction: an unmeasured claim can be anything you want it to be.

probe.reveal: Daniel Yankelovich set out the sequence: measure what can be measured, disregard what cannot, presume what cannot be measured is unimportant, then say it does not exist. Body counts rose in Vietnam throughout. The fallacy is not measurement — it is the fourth step.

glossary.name: The Overconfidence Effect
glossary.definition: Confidence in your judgements systematically exceeds their accuracy.
glossary.example: Asked for ranges they are "98% sure" contain the true value, people are wrong far more than 2% of the time. Calibration training works, which is why forecasting tournaments now teach it explicitly.

probe.ask: Give a range you are 90% sure contains the wingspan of a Boeing 747. How wide did you make it?

options.label: A tight range — I know roughly
options.tell: Almost everyone does this, and almost everyone misses. It is about 68 metres.

options.label: A very wide range — 20 to 150 metres
options.tell: The correct behaviour for a 90% interval about something you do not know.

probe.reveal: Across calibration studies, ranges people label 90% confident contain the answer roughly 50% of the time. The fix is not to know more but to widen: a genuine 90% interval about an unfamiliar quantity should feel embarrassingly loose. If it does not feel absurd, it is not 90%.

glossary.name: The Dunning–Kruger Effect
glossary.definition: The claim that the least competent most overestimate themselves — real in its careful form, badly mangled in its popular one.
glossary.example: The original finding is about weak self-assessment across the board, not a special stupidity of the incompetent. Several statisticians argue the classic graph appears even in random data because of how the axes are constructed. The effect as usually cited online is not the effect that was found.

probe.ask: What do you take the Dunning–Kruger effect to say?

options.label: Incompetent people think they are experts
options.tell: The popular version, and not what the data show. Bottom-quartile performers rate themselves near average.

options.label: Everyone rates themselves near average, so the worst overestimate most
options.tell: Much closer to the published finding.

probe.reveal: The original paper found self-assessment is weakly related to performance across the whole range, which mechanically produces the largest overestimate at the bottom — and an underestimate at the top, a half of the finding the meme drops. Nuhfer and others have shown much of the curve can be reproduced from random data, so treat the effect as real but far smaller than the internet's version.

glossary.name: The Planning Fallacy
glossary.definition: Projects take longer than planned even when the planner knows that projects take longer than planned.
glossary.example: The Scottish Parliament building was estimated at around £40 million and finished near £414 million. Asking instead "how long did similar projects actually take?" — the outside view — is the one repair with evidence behind it.

probe.ask: Think of your current project. When will it be finished — and when was the last comparable one finished relative to its plan?

options.label: On time; the last one overran
options.tell: The signature of the effect: the past is treated as not applying to this case.

options.label: Late, by roughly the same margin as last time
options.tell: You are using the outside view, which is the only thing that has been shown to work.

probe.reveal: Buehler and colleagues found students predicting their own thesis completion missed even their "worst case" dates, while predicting other people's accurately. The correction is reference-class forecasting: ignore the plan, take the distribution of similar projects, and start there.

glossary.name: Hindsight Bias
glossary.definition: Once you know the outcome, it feels as though you knew it all along, and you cannot recover your earlier uncertainty.
glossary.example: Every inquiry into a disaster finds warning signs that were invisible in the noise beforehand. This is why post-mortems that ask "who should have seen it" tend to produce scapegoats rather than fixes.

probe.ask: Before you knew the outcome of the last election you followed, what probability did you give the winner?

options.label: High — it was fairly clear
options.tell: Check whether you wrote it down. Almost nobody's recalled forecast is lower than their actual one.

options.label: I recorded it and can check
options.tell: The only version of this answer worth anything.

options.label: I genuinely cannot reconstruct it
options.tell: The most honest answer available without a record.

probe.reveal: Fischhoff showed people cannot recover their prior uncertainty once they know the answer, and cannot suppress the knowledge when instructed to. This is why post-mortems find negligence everywhere, and why a forecast is worth almost nothing unless it was written down before.

glossary.name: The Curse of Knowledge
glossary.definition: Once you know something, you cannot model not knowing it.
glossary.example: In Elizabeth Newton's tapping study, tappers of well-known tunes expected listeners to identify them far more often than listeners could. Experts write documentation the same way.

probe.ask: Tap out a well-known tune on the table. What fraction of listeners will name it?

options.label: About half
options.tell: The typical estimate. The tune is playing in your head and you cannot subtract it.

options.label: Under 5%
options.tell: Right. Newton found listeners identified about 2.5%.

probe.reveal: Elizabeth Newton's tappers predicted 50% and got 2.5%. This is the mechanism behind most bad documentation and most bad teaching: the writer cannot simulate not knowing, so the gap reads as the reader's inattention rather than the writer's compression.

glossary.name: The Illusion of Explanatory Depth
glossary.definition: People believe they understand how ordinary things work until asked to explain them step by step.
glossary.example: Ask someone to rate their understanding of a zip, a flush toilet or a policy, then to explain the mechanism, then rate again. The second rating drops. It has been used to reduce political extremity, with mixed durability.

probe.ask: Rate your understanding of how a flush toilet works, then explain the mechanism step by step. Did the rating survive?

options.label: It dropped once I tried to explain
options.tell: The standard result, and the reason the probe asks you to attempt it.

options.label: It held — I could explain it
options.tell: Then you have knowledge rather than familiarity. The two feel identical from inside.

probe.reveal: Rozenblit and Keil found ratings fall sharply after an attempted explanation and stay lower. Fernbach extended it to policy: asking people to explain a policy mechanically, rather than justify it, reduced the extremity of their position — one of the few interventions on polarisation that has replicated at all.

glossary.name: Confirmation Bias
glossary.definition: Seeking and weighting evidence that fits what you already believe.
glossary.example: In Wason's 2-4-6 task, people test sequences that confirm their guessed rule and almost never test one that would break it. Falsification has to be taught; it is not the default.

probe.ask: Cards show A, K, 4, 7. The rule is "vowel on one side means even number on the other". Which cards must you turn?

options.label: A and 4
options.tell: The most common answer and wrong: turning 4 cannot break the rule whatever is behind it.

options.label: A and 7
options.tell: Correct. You must look for the case that would falsify.

options.label: A only
options.tell: Half the job — you checked the confirming instance and stopped.

probe.reveal: Wason found around 10% get this. The same people solve it instantly when it is phrased as "if someone is drinking beer they must be over 18" — identical logic, and now everyone checks the teenager. The deficit is not in logic but in which case occurs to you to check.

glossary.name: Myside Bias
glossary.definition: Evaluating arguments by whether they favour your prior commitments — and notably uncorrelated with intelligence.
glossary.example: Stanovich's finding is the uncomfortable one: cognitive ability predicts many reasoning skills but barely predicts resistance to this. Clever people are better at constructing the defence, not more likely to abandon the position.

probe.ask: A study finds a result you dislike. What is your first move?

options.label: Check the methodology
options.tell: Correct — and ask whether you check it as hard when the result pleases you.

options.label: Check who funded it
options.tell: Legitimate, and the most common asymmetrically applied test.

options.label: Update toward the result
options.tell: The rarest answer, and the one the word "evidence" is supposed to mean.

probe.reveal: Stanovich's finding is the uncomfortable one: myside bias is essentially uncorrelated with intelligence, education and open-minded thinking measures. Being clever does not protect you; it equips you to construct better objections to things you did not want to hear.

glossary.name: The Backfire Effect
glossary.definition: The claim that correcting a false belief strengthens it. Widely repeated; largely not found.
glossary.example: Wood and Porter tested thousands of participants across many issues and found corrections generally moved people toward accuracy. Nyhan himself has since described the effect as rare rather than general. If you have used this to justify not correcting anyone, the evidence does not support you.

probe.ask: Does correcting someone's false belief tend to strengthen it?

options.label: Yes — this is well established
options.tell: The widely repeated version. It did not survive.

options.label: No — corrections usually work a little
options.tell: What the larger studies found.

probe.reveal: Nyhan and Reifler reported a backfire effect in 2010 and it became folk wisdom about political argument. It did not replicate: Wood and Porter tested 52 issues with over 10,000 subjects and found it almost nowhere, and Nyhan himself has since described the effect as rare. Corrections mostly work slightly and rarely change votes — a duller finding, and the one to hold.

glossary.name: The Illusory Truth Effect
glossary.definition: Repetition increases believability, including for statements you know to be false.
glossary.example: It works even when the claim contradicts your own knowledge, which is why repeated slogans outperform single detailed corrections, and why fact-checks that restate the myth first can help it.

probe.ask: You have seen a claim four times and know it is disputed. Does it feel more true than the first time?

options.label: Yes, and that unsettles me
options.tell: The honest answer, and the effect operating in plain view.

options.label: No — knowing it is disputed inoculates me
options.tell: Fazio found repetition raised believability even for statements subjects knew to be false.

probe.reveal: Processing fluency is mistaken for evidence: the repeated claim is easier to think, and easy feels true. Fazio and colleagues showed the effect survives prior knowledge. This is the mechanism a disinformation campaign is actually buying, and why repeating a falsehood in order to debunk it is a genuine risk.

glossary.name: The Semmelweis Reflex
glossary.definition: Reflexively rejecting evidence that contradicts an established practice or identity.
glossary.example: Semmelweis cut maternal mortality dramatically by requiring handwashing, was ridiculed by a profession that heard it as an accusation, and died in an asylum. Germ theory arrived two decades later.

probe.ask: A junior colleague presents data showing your team's core practice is harmful. Your first response?

options.label: Question their competence and the data
options.tell: Reasonable in form. Note whether you would apply the same scrutiny to supporting data.

options.label: Ask what would need to be true for them to be right
options.tell: The move that keeps the question open rather than closing it.

options.label: Escalate it above them
options.tell: Procedurally sound and the most common way an inconvenient finding is buried.

probe.reveal: Semmelweis showed handwashing cut maternal deaths from around 18% to 2% and was rejected, dismissed, and died in an asylum. The rejection was not irrational in isolation — he had no germ theory to offer — which is what makes the reflex dangerous: it always has a respectable reason available.

glossary.name: Prospect Theory
glossary.definition: People evaluate outcomes as gains and losses from a reference point, not as final states, and weight probabilities non-linearly.
glossary.example: The foundation under most of behavioural economics, and the work cited in Kahneman's Nobel. Its core structure has held up better than many of the individual effects built on top of it.

probe.ask: Choose: a certain £900, or a 90% chance of £1,000. Then: a certain loss of £900, or a 90% chance of losing £1,000.

options.label: Certain gain, then gamble on the loss
options.tell: The modal pattern: risk-averse for gains, risk-seeking for losses.

options.label: The gamble both times
options.tell: Consistent, and closer to expected-value neutrality.

options.label: The certain option both times
options.tell: Consistently risk-averse, which costs you on the loss side.

probe.reveal: Both pairs have identical expected values, and most people switch. Kahneman and Tversky's value function is concave for gains and convex for losses, which is why the same person buys insurance and lottery tickets. The reference point, not the final state, is what is being evaluated.

glossary.name: Loss Aversion
glossary.definition: Losses loom larger than equivalent gains — the single most-cited idea in behavioural economics, and now seriously disputed in its strong form.
glossary.example: The popular "losses hurt about twice as much" ratio is not a constant; it varies enormously by context and often vanishes for small stakes. Gal and Rucker argue much of the evidence is better explained by status-quo inertia. The phenomenon is real in some settings; the universal multiplier is not.

probe.ask: How large is the loss-aversion coefficient — how much worse does a loss feel than an equal gain?

options.label: About twice as bad, universally
options.tell: The textbook 2.25 figure, now the disputed part.

options.label: It depends heavily on stake size and context
options.tell: Closer to where the argument currently stands.

probe.reveal: Gal and Rucker argued the strong form is not supported and that many classic demonstrations are better explained by inertia or by the endowment effect being about ownership rather than loss. Something real remains for large stakes; the universal 2:1 multiplier does not. This is the most-cited idea in behavioural economics and it is genuinely in dispute.

glossary.name: The Endowment Effect
glossary.definition: You value a thing more once it is yours.
glossary.example: The classic mug experiments found owners demanding roughly twice what buyers would pay. Later work shows the effect shrinks or disappears with trading experience and with certain procedures, so it is partly about unfamiliarity with the transaction rather than about ownership itself.

probe.ask: You are given a mug. What is the least you would sell it for? If you had not been given it, what is the most you would pay?

options.label: My selling price is clearly higher
options.tell: The classic gap — usually around 2:1 in the original studies.

options.label: They are about the same
options.tell: What tends to happen with experienced traders and with better-designed procedures.

probe.reveal: Kahneman, Knetsch and Thaler found a large gap; List found it shrinks or vanishes among people who trade regularly, and Plott and Zeiler argued much of it is an artefact of how the task is explained. The effect is real in inexperienced subjects and much less general than it was sold as.

glossary.name: The Framing Effect
glossary.definition: Logically identical options are chosen differently depending on how they are described.
glossary.example: The Asian disease problem: a programme "saving 200 of 600" is chosen far more often than one where "400 die", though these are the same. Ninety per cent lean beats ten per cent fat in every supermarket.

probe.ask: A treatment has a 90% survival rate. Another has a 10% mortality rate. Which sounds better?
