options.label: The 90% survival one
options.tell: The usual answer. They are the same number.

options.label: They are identical and I feel no difference
options.tell: Rare. Physicians shown these framings choose differently too.

probe.reveal: McNeil and colleagues found both patients and doctors preferred surgery over radiation when outcomes were framed as survival rather than mortality. The framing is not a communication problem to be tidied up — every presentation is a frame, so the question is always which frame was chosen and by whom.

glossary.name: The Sunk Cost Fallacy
glossary.definition: Continuing because of what you have already spent, which is gone either way.
glossary.example: Also called the Concorde fallacy, after two governments who kept funding an aircraft they knew would not pay back, precisely because they had funded it so far.

probe.ask: You are ninety minutes into a bad three-hour film you paid for. Do you leave?

options.label: Stay — I paid for it
options.tell: The money is gone whether you sit there or not. You are now spending time to honour it.

options.label: Leave
options.tell: The economically correct answer, and the one most people find genuinely hard.

options.label: Stay — I might still enjoy the ending
options.tell: A forward-looking reason, and therefore not the fallacy at all.

probe.reveal: Only the first answer is the fallacy: the third is a real expected-value judgement. Arkes and Blumer's theatre-ticket studies isolate this cleanly. Note that the fallacy has a defensible cousin — honouring commitments so that your future promises remain credible — which is a forward-looking reason wearing backward-looking clothes.

glossary.name: Hyperbolic Discounting
glossary.definition: Present rewards are over-weighted relative to future ones, and the discount is steeper near the present, producing preference reversals.
glossary.example: Most people take £50 today over £55 next week, but £55 in a year over £50 in fifty-one weeks — the same trade, moved. This is the shape of every failed diet and unpaid pension contribution.

probe.ask: Prefer £100 today or £110 next week? Then: £100 in a year, or £110 in a year and a week?

options.label: Today, then the later £110
options.tell: A preference reversal from the same one-week delay. This is the effect.

options.label: The £110 both times
options.tell: Consistent discounting, and unusual.

options.label: The earlier option both times
options.tell: Also consistent — a steep but stable discount rate.

probe.reveal: A week costs you £10 when it is this week and nothing when it is a year away, which means your preferences will reverse as the date approaches. This is why commitment devices work: your present self correctly does not trust the self who will be standing there on the day.

glossary.name: The Default Effect
glossary.definition: Whatever happens if you do nothing is what mostly happens.
glossary.example: Countries with opt-out organ donation register vastly higher consent than opt-in neighbours with similar cultures. Pension auto-enrolment works the same way, and it is the best-evidenced intervention in the whole nudge literature.

probe.ask: Organ donation consent rates are 15% in one country and 99% in a neighbouring one. What best explains it?

options.label: Cultural attitudes to death and the body
options.tell: The intuitive explanation, and mostly wrong for these pairs.

options.label: One country asks you to opt in and the other to opt out
options.tell: Correct. Johnson and Goldstein found the form design dominates.

probe.reveal: Austria and Germany, Sweden and Denmark: near-identical cultures, opposite rates, different default. The uncomfortable implication is that on questions where preferences are weakly formed, whoever designs the form is choosing the outcome — so "we just let people decide" is never a neutral position.

glossary.name: The Decoy Effect
glossary.definition: Adding a third, clearly worse option changes which of the original two people pick.
glossary.example: The Economist's notorious pricing: web-only $59, print-only $125, print-and-web $125. Nobody chooses print-only; its job is to make the bundle look free.

probe.ask: Digital £59, print £125, print+digital £125. Which do you take?

options.label: Print and digital — obviously
options.tell: The option the middle one exists to sell. Print-alone is there to be rejected.

options.label: Digital only
options.tell: What most people choose when the pointless middle option is removed.

probe.reveal: Ariely's Economist example: with the decoy, 84% took the bundle; without it, 68% took digital alone. The decoy is dominated and nobody buys it — its job is to make the target look like a win. Replications are mixed and the effect weakens with real money, but the pricing page you saw this morning was built on it.

glossary.name: Choice Overload
glossary.definition: More options can reduce the chance of choosing at all.
glossary.example: The famous jam study found a small display outsold a large one. A later meta-analysis found a mean effect near zero across many studies, with strong moderators. The phenomenon exists under specific conditions; the general claim does not.

probe.ask: Does offering more options make people less likely to buy?

options.label: Yes — the jam study proved it
options.tell: The famous result, and one that has not held up in aggregate.

options.label: Sometimes, under specific conditions
options.tell: Where the evidence actually sits.

probe.reveal: Iyengar and Lepper's 24-versus-6 jams study is one of the most cited in the field. Scheibehenne's meta-analysis of 50 experiments found a mean effect near zero, with large effects in both directions depending on time pressure, preference clarity and whether the options are hard to compare. Treat it as a moderator story, not a law.

glossary.name: The Peak–End Rule
glossary.definition: Retrospective judgement of an experience tracks its most intense moment and its ending, not its duration.
glossary.example: In the colonoscopy study, patients whose procedure was extended with a gentler final minute remembered it as less unpleasant — more total discomfort, better memory of it.

probe.ask: Which is worse: 60 seconds of hand in ice water, or the same 60 seconds followed by 30 seconds at a slightly less cold temperature?

options.label: The longer one — it is strictly more pain
options.tell: True by any additive measure, and not what people remember or choose.

options.label: The shorter one
options.tell: What subjects reported, and most chose to repeat the longer trial.

probe.reveal: Kahneman's cold-pressor study found the remembering self ignores duration almost entirely and averages the peak with the end. This puts the experiencing self and the remembering self in direct conflict about what to choose next — and it is the remembering self that books the holiday.

glossary.name: The Focusing Illusion
glossary.definition: Nothing in life matters as much as you think it does while you are thinking about it.
glossary.example: Californians and Midwesterners report similar life satisfaction, though both groups expect Californians to be happier. Attention to climate inflates its apparent weight; day to day, it is not what anyone is thinking about.

probe.ask: Would you be happier living in California?

options.label: Yes — the weather and the light
options.tell: The weather is what the question makes salient. It is a small part of a day.

options.label: Probably about the same
options.tell: What the data show: Midwesterners and Californians report near-identical life satisfaction.

probe.reveal: Schkade and Kahneman found both groups predicted Californians would be happier, and neither was. The illusion generalises: any factor you are asked to attend to inflates in importance while you attend to it, which is why the thing you are currently worrying about feels decisive and mostly is not.

glossary.name: Impact Bias
glossary.definition: You overestimate how long and how intensely future events will affect your happiness.
glossary.example: People predict a breakup, a promotion or a diagnosis will move their baseline mood for years. Measured, most return close to baseline far sooner, a process Gilbert calls the psychological immune system.

probe.ask: How long would a major setback — losing a job, a relationship ending — measurably lower your happiness?

options.label: Years
options.tell: The common prediction. Most events' measured effect decays much faster.

options.label: A few months
options.tell: Closer to the affective-forecasting data for most events.

probe.reveal: Gilbert and Wilson call the machinery the psychological immune system: people underestimate their own capacity to reframe. The exceptions matter — bereavement, chronic pain and long-term unemployment show much slower or incomplete adaptation — so this is a bias about typical events, not a promise about all of them.

glossary.name: The IKEA Effect
glossary.definition: You value things you built yourself out of proportion to their quality.
glossary.example: It explains why teams defend their own architecture, and why "not invented here" is so hard to argue with — the builder is not lying about the value they perceive.

probe.ask: You built a feature over three weeks. Usage data says nobody touches it. Do you remove it?

options.label: Keep it — it needs better discovery
options.tell: Sometimes true, and exactly what the effect predicts you would say.

options.label: Remove it
options.tell: The answer you would give instantly about someone else's three weeks.

probe.reveal: Norton, Mochon and Ariely found people paid substantially more for furniture and origami they had assembled themselves, and rated their own output close to experts'. Replications are mixed on size, and the effect depends on completing the task — abandoned builds do not get the premium.

glossary.name: The Scarcity Mindset
glossary.definition: Scarcity of money or time consumes cognitive bandwidth, degrading decisions in unrelated domains.
glossary.example: Their argument reframes poverty: not a failure of character producing bad decisions, but a condition that taxes attention and so produces them. Some specific findings, including a widely-cited IQ result, have faced replication difficulty.

probe.ask: Does being short of money make people worse at unrelated decisions?

options.label: Yes — scarcity itself consumes mental bandwidth
options.tell: Mullainathan and Shafir's claim, and the basis for a lot of policy argument.

options.label: The effect is smaller and less clear than reported
options.tell: Where several replication attempts have landed.

probe.reveal: The sugarcane-farmer study reported a cognitive gap before and after harvest equivalent to many IQ points. Subsequent replications have been mixed, and the effect size is disputed. The policy implication — that means-testing imposes a cost on exactly the people least able to bear it — survives on other grounds even where the specific finding wobbles.

glossary.name: The Zero Price Effect
glossary.definition: Free is not merely a low price; it changes the decision category.
glossary.example: Dropping a price from 1p to 0p produces a jump in uptake far larger than the penny warrants, which is why "free shipping" outperforms an equivalent discount.

probe.ask: Choose: a Lindt truffle for 15p, or a Hershey's Kiss for 1p. Now: the truffle for 14p, or the Kiss free.

options.label: Truffle, then Kiss
options.tell: The reversal. The price gap is identical in both pairs.

options.label: Truffle both times
options.tell: Consistent, and the minority.

probe.reveal: Shampanier, Mazar and Ariely found the truffle's share collapsing from 73% to 31% when the alternative became free, with the difference in price held constant. Free removes the downside entirely and so removes the comparison — which is why "free trial" and "free shipping" outperform equivalent discounts.

glossary.name: The Fundamental Attribution Error
glossary.definition: Explaining others by their character and yourself by your circumstances.
glossary.example: He is late because he is inconsiderate; you are late because of the traffic. The asymmetry is systematic, and it is stronger in individualist cultures — one of the more robust cross-cultural moderators in social psychology.

probe.ask: A driver cuts you up. Then you cut someone up. Explain each.

options.label: They are aggressive; I was in a hurry
options.tell: The asymmetry, verbatim. Character for them, circumstance for you.

options.label: Both of us were probably in a hurry
options.tell: The symmetric read, which requires deliberately supplying the situation you cannot see.

probe.reveal: Jones and Harris found observers inferred genuine attitudes from essays even when told the writer had been assigned the position. Note the asymmetry is partly informational — you know your own situation and not theirs — which is why the fix is to assume a situation exists rather than to assume good character.

glossary.name: The Self-Serving Bias
glossary.definition: Taking credit for successes and attributing failures outward.
glossary.example: Both parties to a failed project can be sincere and irreconcilable. It also inflates group contribution estimates: ask household members what share of chores they do and the total exceeds 100%.

probe.ask: Your team ships a hit and then a flop. Write the two post-mortems in your head. Do they use the same vocabulary?

options.label: No — the hit is "we", the flop is "the market"
options.tell: The bias in its ordinary form, and it is nearly universal in annual reports.

options.label: Yes, both name decisions we made
options.tell: The version that produces learning, and the rarer one.

probe.reveal: Studies of shareholder letters find the pattern reliably: good years are attributed internally, bad years to conditions. The bias is not lying — the causes really are mixed — it is that the search for causes stops at a different point depending on the result.

glossary.name: The Minimal Group Paradigm
glossary.definition: Groups assigned on a meaningless basis immediately favour their own.
glossary.example: Tajfel split boys by a coin flip, or a preference between two painters they had never heard of, and they promptly allocated more to their own group — sometimes preferring a smaller absolute gain that widened the gap.

probe.ask: You are assigned to Group A by a coin toss. You allocate money between an A and a B. Do you favour A?

options.label: No — the groups are meaningless
options.tell: What everyone predicts about themselves.

options.label: Probably a little, if I am honest
options.tell: What subjects actually did, on a basis as thin as a coin.

probe.reveal: Tajfel found favouritism on categories as arbitrary as a preference between two painters, and subjects often chose relative advantage for their group over maximum absolute gain for it. No history, no competition, no contact — the category alone was sufficient.

glossary.name: Out-Group Homogeneity
glossary.definition: "They are all the same; we are all individuals."
glossary.example: You can name a dozen kinds of person in your own profession or party and perhaps two in the opposing one. This is a perceptual fact before it is a moral failing, which is why it survives good intentions.

probe.ask: How many meaningfully different positions exist within the political side you oppose?

options.label: Two or three broad camps
options.tell: Compare with how many you would list for your own side.

options.label: As many as within my own side
options.tell: Almost certainly true, and almost never how it feels.

probe.reveal: The asymmetry is a sampling artefact with consequences: you meet your own group in variety and the other through its loudest representatives. It sustains the belief that the other side has a position rather than an argument, which is the precondition for treating disagreement as bad faith.

glossary.name: The False Consensus Effect
glossary.definition: Overestimating how many people share your beliefs and choices.
glossary.example: It is why an unpopular opinion feels like common sense to its holder, and why online communities produce catastrophic misreadings of national opinion.

probe.ask: What share of the country do you think agrees with you on the political issue you care most about?

options.label: A clear majority
options.tell: The usual estimate, and it correlates with your own position rather than the polling.

options.label: A minority
options.tell: Rarer, and where it happens it can invert into the false-uniqueness version.

options.label: I would have to look it up
options.tell: The only answer with a defensible method behind it.

probe.reveal: Ross, Greene and House found people on both sides of a question estimated their own side larger, and rated those who disagreed as more extreme and more revealing of their character. The estimate and the derogation come as a pair.

glossary.name: Pluralistic Ignorance
glossary.definition: Everyone privately rejects a norm while believing everyone else accepts it, so all continue to enforce it.
glossary.example: Studied in campus drinking, where most students privately disliked the drinking culture and each believed themselves unusual. Also the mechanism under sudden collapses of public support for a regime.

probe.ask: In a meeting, everyone nods at a plan you think is bad. What do you conclude?

options.label: I am missing something
options.tell: The inference that keeps the silence stable, especially when several people make it at once.

options.label: Others may be thinking the same and staying quiet
options.tell: The possibility that only costs one person something to test.

probe.reveal: Prentice and Miller found students consistently overestimated their peers' comfort with campus drinking, each privately uneasy and each reading the others' silence as endorsement. The norm was held in place by nobody's actual belief. One person stating a private view can collapse it.

glossary.name: The Spiral of Silence
glossary.definition: People who believe their view is in the minority fall silent, which makes it appear even more marginal.
glossary.example: A feedback loop between perceived and expressed opinion. It is the mass-communications sibling of preference falsification, and it explains why measured opinion can shift faster than anyone believed possible.

probe.ask: You hold a view you believe is unpopular in your workplace. Do you state it?

options.label: No — the cost is real and the benefit is not
options.tell: A rational individual calculation that aggregates into an inaccurate public picture.

options.label: Yes, and take the consequences
options.tell: What Noelle-Neumann called the hard core, who speak regardless of the climate.

options.label: Only to people I trust
options.tell: The most common answer, and it keeps the public estimate wrong while feeling like candour.

probe.reveal: Noelle-Neumann's theory holds that perceived minority status produces silence, which further shrinks the apparent minority. Evidence is mixed — effects are modest and depend on issue salience and how public the setting is — but the mechanism is visible in any organisation where the private and public distributions of opinion have come apart.

glossary.name: Social Proof
glossary.definition: In uncertainty, people take the behaviour of others as evidence about what to do.
glossary.example: Hotel towel-reuse cards saying "most guests in this room reused their towels" outperform environmental appeals. Descriptive norms move behaviour more reliably than moral ones.

probe.ask: Two restaurants, both unknown to you. One is full, one is empty. Which do you enter?

options.label: The full one
options.tell: Rational information aggregation — other diners know something you do not.

options.label: The empty one
options.tell: Also defensible: quicker service, and the crowd may be a cascade rather than evidence.

probe.reveal: Following the crowd under uncertainty is usually correct, which is what makes it exploitable — Cialdini's hotel-towel studies show descriptive norms outperform environmental appeals. The failure mode is that the crowd may be copying each other rather than knowing anything, which is the information cascade in this same glossary.

glossary.name: The Halo Effect
glossary.definition: One good trait bleeds into judgements of unrelated traits.
glossary.example: Thorndike found officers rating soldiers gave correlated marks for physique, intelligence and leadership. Attractive defendants get lighter sentences; a company that is profitable is described as well-managed until it is not.

probe.ask: A CEO is articulate, well dressed and tells a good story. How much does that shift your estimate of the company's finances?

options.label: Not at all — different things entirely
options.tell: What everyone says, and what the ratings data contradict.

options.label: Some, and I notice it happening
options.tell: The honest version. Noticing is the only available correction.

probe.reveal: Thorndike found officers' ratings of unrelated traits in their men correlated far too highly to be independent judgements. Rosenzweig's The Halo Effect applies it to business writing: performance is measured first, then the culture and leadership are described to match, and the resulting "causes of success" are largely the outcome read backwards.

glossary.name: The Mere Exposure Effect
glossary.definition: Repeated exposure increases liking, with no other reason required.
glossary.example: It works below conscious recognition, which is most of what advertising buys. It also explains why you prefer your mirror image and your friends prefer photographs of you.

probe.ask: Think of a song you disliked and now like. What changed?

options.label: I heard it enough times
options.tell: Zajonc's effect, unassisted by any new information about the song.

options.label: I understood it better
options.tell: Possible — and hard to distinguish from familiarity, which is the problem.

probe.reveal: Zajonc found liking rises with repeated exposure even for meaningless stimuli and even below the threshold of recognition. It is the cheapest thing advertising buys. It also means your sense of which ideas are reasonable is shaped by how often you have encountered them.

glossary.name: Groupthink
glossary.definition: Cohesive groups suppress dissent in favour of consensus, producing worse decisions than their members would make alone.
glossary.example: Janis built it from the Bay of Pigs. It is enormously influential and the experimental evidence is weaker than its fame suggests — the case studies are compelling, the controlled tests inconsistent.

probe.ask: Do cohesive, agreeable teams make worse decisions than fractious ones?

options.label: Yes — cohesion suppresses dissent
options.tell: Janis's claim, drawn from case studies chosen because they ended badly.

options.label: Not reliably; cohesion is not the key variable
options.tell: What the experimental literature has mostly found.

probe.reveal: Janis built the theory from famous fiascos — the Bay of Pigs, Pearl Harbor — and the method selects on the outcome. Laboratory tests find weak and inconsistent support for cohesion as the driver; directive leadership and insulation from outside information hold up better. The prescriptions are sensible even where the theory behind them is shaky.

glossary.name: Group Polarisation
glossary.definition: Discussion among the like-minded moves the group's average position further out, not toward the centre.
glossary.example: Deliberating juries award more than their median member initially favoured. Sunstein has argued this is the central dynamic of political sorting online, and the effect itself replicates well.

probe.ask: A group that mildly agrees on something discusses it for an hour. Where does the average position end up?

options.label: Nearer the centre — they will hear caveats
options.tell: The intuitive prediction and the wrong one.

options.label: Further out than where it started
options.tell: The reliable finding, across juries, judges and online groups.

probe.reveal: Sunstein's work on three-judge panels found judges voted more ideologically when sitting with two appointees of the same party than when sitting alone. The mechanism is not pressure but the argument pool: a like-minded group supplies mostly arguments in one direction, and hearing them is genuinely persuasive.

glossary.name: The Abilene Paradox
glossary.definition: A group takes an action none of its members wants, because each believes the others want it.
glossary.example: Harvey's family drove fifty miles in the heat to a bad diner, and afterwards discovered nobody had wanted to go. Distinct from groupthink: nobody here was persuaded, only silent.

probe.ask: Your team is going ahead with something you privately think is a mistake. How many others do you think agree with you?

options.label: Probably nobody
options.tell: The assumption that makes the paradox possible.

options.label: Possibly most of them
options.tell: Harvey's point: agreement is often unanimous and invisible.

probe.reveal: Harvey's family drove fifty miles to Abilene for a bad meal that nobody had wanted, each agreeing to spare the others. Unlike groupthink the problem is not pressure to conform but failure to manage agreement: nobody was persuaded of anything and everyone went along.

glossary.name: The Bystander Effect
glossary.definition: The more witnesses present, the less likely any individual is to help.
glossary.example: The Kitty Genovese story that popularised it was substantially wrong as the New York Times reported it. The laboratory effect on reporting-type tasks holds, but recent video studies of real public conflicts find intervention is common — in most recorded fights, someone steps in.

probe.ask: Are you less likely to be helped in an emergency if many people are present?

options.label: Yes — responsibility diffuses
options.tell: The textbook finding, from Darley and Latané and the Genovese story.

options.label: For non-dangerous situations; in real violence, more bystanders helps
options.tell: What the video evidence shows.

probe.reveal: Philpot and colleagues analysed CCTV of real public conflicts across three countries and found intervention in about 90% of cases, with more bystanders raising the chance someone acted — the opposite of the textbook prediction. The laboratory effect replicates for ambiguous, low-cost situations and does not generalise to danger. The Genovese reporting that launched the field was itself substantially inaccurate.

glossary.name: The Misinformation Effect
glossary.definition: Information encountered after an event alters the memory of the event.
glossary.example: Loftus showed asking how fast cars were going when they "smashed" rather than "hit" raised speed estimates and made witnesses recall broken glass that was never there. This work changed how courts treat eyewitness testimony.

probe.ask: Witnesses are asked how fast cars were going when they "smashed" versus "hit". A week later, who remembers broken glass?

options.label: The "smashed" group, though there was none
options.tell: Loftus and Palmer's finding. One verb rewrote the memory.

options.label: Neither — there was no glass
options.tell: What should happen, and did not.

probe.reveal: Loftus and Palmer found both speed estimates and later false memories varied with the verb. Memory is reconstructive, so every retelling is an opportunity to edit — which is why leading questions in police interviews are a procedural problem and not merely a stylistic one.

glossary.name: Flashbulb Memory
glossary.definition: Vivid, confident memories of learning shocking news — as inaccurate as ordinary memory, but held with far more certainty.
glossary.example: Studies that recorded people's accounts the day after major events and again years later found substantial drift alongside undiminished confidence. The vividness is real; the accuracy is not.

probe.ask: How confident are you in your memory of where you were during a major news event?

options.label: Very — I can see the room
options.tell: Confidence stays near ceiling. Accuracy does not.

options.label: Confident, but I know that means little
options.tell: The calibrated answer, and it takes effort to hold.

probe.reveal: Talarico and Rubin collected accounts the day after 11 September and again months later: consistency decayed at the same rate as ordinary memories, while confidence and vividness did not. Vividness is a feeling about a memory, not a property of its accuracy — which is why confident eyewitnesses are so persuasive and so unreliable.

glossary.name: The Spacing Effect
glossary.definition: Learning distributed over time is retained far better than the same time massed together.
glossary.example: One of the oldest and best-replicated findings in psychology, and among the most ignored: nearly every student crams, and nearly every curriculum is structured to let them.

probe.ask: You have six hours to learn something. How do you spend them?

options.label: Six hours the day before
options.tell: Feels more effective while doing it, and produces the worst retention.

options.label: One hour a day for six days
options.tell: Substantially better long-term retention for the same total time.

probe.reveal: One of the oldest and best-replicated findings in psychology, from Ebbinghaus onward. The trap is that massed practice feels more fluent during the session, so learners rate it higher while performing worse a week later. The subjective sense of learning is a poor guide to learning.

glossary.name: The Testing Effect
glossary.definition: Retrieving information strengthens memory more than re-reading it.
glossary.example: Students who self-test outperform students who reread, while reporting less confidence during study. The technique that feels worse works better, which is why it loses to highlighting.

probe.ask: You have read a chapter once. What next?

options.label: Read it again
options.tell: What most students do, and the weakest use of the time.

options.label: Close it and write down what you remember
options.tell: Retrieval practice, and substantially better retention.

probe.reveal: Roediger and Karpicke found students who re-read rated their own learning higher and performed markedly worse a week later than students who tested themselves. Retrieval is not measurement of learning; it is the mechanism of it. This probe is itself an application.

glossary.name: The Zeigarnik Effect
glossary.definition: Interrupted or unfinished tasks are remembered better than completed ones.
glossary.example: The premise of every cliffhanger. Replication has been inconsistent since the 1980s, and the effect appears to depend heavily on how much the person cared about finishing.

probe.ask: Do unfinished tasks stay in mind more than completed ones?

options.label: Yes, reliably
options.tell: The popular claim, used to justify cliffhangers and to-do systems.

options.label: Sometimes, and the replication record is uneven
options.tell: The more defensible position.

probe.reveal: Zeigarnik's 1927 waiter study is much cited and the follow-up literature is inconsistent, with several failed replications and effects that depend heavily on task involvement. Something in the vicinity is probably real — the specific, dependable effect that productivity writing invokes is not.

glossary.name: The Serial Position Effect
glossary.definition: The first and last items in a list are recalled best; the middle is lost.
glossary.example: It shapes interview order, ballot design and where the argument you most need remembered should go — which is not the middle of the email.

probe.ask: You interview eight candidates in a day. Which do you remember most clearly?

options.label: The first and the last
options.tell: Primacy and recency. Candidates four and five are structurally disadvantaged.

options.label: The best one, whenever they came
options.tell: What you believe, and what the recall curve does not support.

probe.reveal: The effect is among the most robust in memory research. The practical implication is that position in a sequence is a hidden variable in hiring, judging and grading — which is why structured scoring immediately after each candidate outperforms deciding at the end of the day.

glossary.name: Ego Depletion
glossary.definition: The theory that willpower is a finite resource depleted by use — a cornerstone of popular self-help that did not survive replication.
glossary.example: The 1998 radish-and-cookies study launched a thousand articles. A large pre-registered multi-lab replication found an effect indistinguishable from zero, and meta-analyses correcting for publication bias find little left. Baumeister has disputed the replications; the field has largely moved on.

probe.ask: Is willpower a finite resource that gets used up during the day?

options.label: Yes — this is well established
options.tell: The version in a decade of self-help books. It did not replicate.

options.label: No — the effect largely vanished under pre-registration
options.tell: What the multi-lab tests found.

probe.reveal: Baumeister's finding was supported by hundreds of studies and a meta-analysis. A registered replication with 23 labs and around 2,000 subjects found an effect near zero, and the earlier meta-analysis showed strong signs of publication bias. This entry exists as a warning about how much apparent evidence a false effect can accumulate.

glossary.name: Power Posing
glossary.definition: The claim that expansive postures change hormone levels and risk appetite.
glossary.example: The most-viewed TED talk of its era. In 2016 Dana Carney, the first author, publicly stated she no longer believed the effect was real and listed the analytic problems in the original study. Some later work finds a small subjective "felt power" effect; the hormonal claims did not replicate.

probe.ask: Does standing in an expansive posture for two minutes change your hormones and risk appetite?

options.label: Yes — the TED talk showed the data
options.tell: The talk has been viewed tens of millions of times. The hormonal finding did not replicate.

options.label: No, though it may change how you feel
options.tell: Where the evidence sits, including per one of the original authors.

probe.reveal: Ranehill and colleagues, with a much larger sample, found no hormonal or behavioural effect. Dana Carney, the first author of the original, publicly stated she no longer believes the effect is real and listed the methodological problems. Self-reported feelings of power do shift, which is a far smaller claim than the one that travelled.

glossary.name: Behavioural Priming
glossary.definition: The finding that reading words associated with old age makes people walk more slowly.
glossary.example: A famous demonstration of unconscious influence and one of the triggers of psychology's replication crisis. Direct replications failed, including one where the effect appeared only when experimenters knew the condition. Kahneman, who had cited this literature prominently, wrote an open letter warning the field.

probe.ask: Does reading words associated with old age make people walk more slowly?

options.label: Yes — a famous demonstration of unconscious priming
options.tell: It anchored a whole literature and failed direct replication.

options.label: No, and the replication explains why it looked real
options.tell: Correct. The follow-up is more instructive than the original.

probe.reveal: Doyen and colleagues failed to replicate with automated timing, then reproduced the original result when experimenters were told what to expect — implicating experimenter expectancy rather than priming. Kahneman's open letter to the field followed. Behavioural priming is the clearest case of a body of work that did not survive.

glossary.name: The Facial Feedback Hypothesis
glossary.definition: That holding a pen in your teeth, forcing a smile, makes cartoons funnier.
glossary.example: A seventeen-lab replication found no effect. A later large multi-lab project using different methods found a small one. The strong version taught in textbooks is not supported; something smaller may be there.

probe.ask: Does holding a pen in your teeth, forcing a smile, make cartoons funnier?

options.label: Yes — a classic result
options.tell: Strack's 1988 finding, taught for thirty years.

options.label: The evidence is now genuinely mixed
options.tell: The accurate summary after two rounds of multi-lab testing.

probe.reveal: A 17-lab replication found no effect. A later many-labs study using a different procedure and avoiding a camera found a small one. The current position is unresolved rather than settled either way — which is a more honest place to leave it than the confident version in either direction.

glossary.name: The Marshmallow Test
glossary.definition: That a child's ability to delay gratification predicts life outcomes decades later.
glossary.example: The 2018 replication with a larger, more diverse sample found the correlation roughly halved and largely explained by family background and early cognitive ability. Delay of gratification looks more like a marker of circumstances than an independent cause of them.

probe.ask: Does a four-year-old's ability to wait for a second marshmallow predict their adult outcomes?

options.label: Yes — famously, decades out
options.tell: The version in every parenting book. The original samples were tiny.

options.label: Weakly, and mostly through family background
options.tell: What the large replication found.

probe.reveal: Watts, Duncan and Quan retested with roughly ten times the sample and controls for family background: the association shrank to about a third and lost significance with controls. Waiting also tracks whether a child has learned that promises are kept — Kidd showed children in unreliable environments wait less, rationally.

glossary.name: Stereotype Threat
glossary.definition: That awareness of a negative stereotype about your group depresses performance under test conditions.
glossary.example: Enormously influential in education policy. Meta-analyses correcting for publication bias find much smaller effects, and several large replications found none. Specialists remain genuinely split; this is a live disagreement rather than a settled failure.

probe.ask: Does being reminded of a negative stereotype about your group lower test performance?

options.label: Yes — a well-established effect
options.tell: Widely taught and widely applied in education policy.

options.label: The literature shows strong signs of publication bias
options.tell: What the meta-analytic corrections suggest.

probe.reveal: Steele and Aronson's original result is heavily cited. Meta-analyses correcting for small-study effects find much smaller effects, and several large replications found none. The underlying phenomenon may be real in specific conditions; the general claim is not as solid as its presence in teacher training implies.

glossary.name: Growth Mindset
glossary.definition: That believing ability is malleable improves achievement.
glossary.example: Large-scale trials, including a US national study and a multi-school English trial, find effects that are real but very small and concentrated among lower-achieving students — far below what the popular literature and school assemblies promise.

probe.ask: Does teaching students that ability is malleable raise their achievement?

options.label: Substantially — it is transformative
options.tell: The claim that drove worldwide adoption.

options.label: Very slightly, and mainly for at-risk students
options.tell: What the large pre-registered trials found.

probe.reveal: The US National Study of Learning Mindsets, with over 12,000 students, found a small effect concentrated in lower-achieving students — real, replicable, and far below the headline. A large UK trial found no significant effect. The honest summary is a cheap intervention with a modest, targeted benefit, which is not what was sold to schools.

glossary.name: Broken Windows
glossary.definition: That visible disorder invites serious crime, so policing minor disorder prevents it.
glossary.example: It shaped policing across the world. The evidence is heavily contested: some field experiments support a disorder–disorder link, while studies of the crime drop attribute little of it to order-maintenance policing, and the enforcement costs fell very unevenly.

probe.ask: Does policing minor disorder reduce serious crime?

options.label: Yes — New York proved it
options.tell: The claim, made during a period when crime fell across cities that did nothing similar.

options.label: Disorder-focused community policing helps; aggressive stop-and-frisk does not
options.tell: Where the meta-analytic evidence points.

probe.reveal: Braga's meta-analyses find modest crime reductions from disorder-focused strategies, with the effect coming from community problem-solving rather than aggressive misdemeanour enforcement, which shows no consistent benefit and substantial social cost. New York's decline coincided with declines in cities using opposite policies.

glossary.name: Occam's Razor
glossary.source: attributed to William of Ockham, c. 1320
glossary.definition: Do not multiply entities beyond necessity: prefer the explanation with fewer assumptions.
glossary.example: A tiebreaker between explanations that fit the evidence equally, not a reason to prefer simple wrong answers to complex right ones — the misuse it most often gets.

probe.ask: Two theories fit the data equally well. One is simpler. Is the simpler one more likely true?

options.label: Yes — fewer assumptions, fewer ways to be wrong
options.tell: The usable version, and there is a formal argument for it.

options.label: No — reality is not obliged to be simple
options.tell: Also true, and the reason the razor is a heuristic and not a law.

probe.reveal: The Bayesian defence is real: a theory with more free parameters spreads its probability over more possible datasets, so it is penalised for flexibility. The razor is a tiebreaker among theories that fit equally, not a licence to prefer the simple story over the one that fits better.

glossary.name: Hanlon's Razor
glossary.definition: Never attribute to malice what is adequately explained by incompetence.
glossary.example: A useful default and a dangerous one: it is also how institutions absolve themselves, since sufficiently convenient incompetence is indistinguishable from policy.

probe.ask: You were left off an important invitation. What happened?

options.label: Someone made a point of excluding me
options.tell: Possible, and the hypothesis that costs most if wrong.

options.label: Someone copied last month's distribution list
options.tell: Usually right, and cheap to check.

probe.reveal: The razor is a prior, not a verdict — and it has a real failure mode: applied institutionally, "incompetence" becomes the standing explanation for patterns that are actually produced by incentives. Ask whether the same incompetence would have occurred if the error had gone the other way.

glossary.name: Hitchens's Razor
glossary.definition: What can be asserted without evidence can be dismissed without evidence.
glossary.example: A restatement of where the burden of proof sits. It settles who must argue, not who is right.

probe.ask: Someone makes a sweeping claim and offers no evidence. Must you refute it?

options.label: No — dismiss it
options.tell: Hitchens's rule, and it correctly places the burden.

options.label: Yes, or silence looks like agreement
options.tell: The practical reality in public argument, which is what makes the razor hard to use.

probe.reveal: The razor is epistemically right and rhetorically weak, which is the tension Brandolini's law describes from the other side. It also has a limit: not everything asserted without evidence in a conversation is unevidenced — sometimes the speaker simply has not been asked.

glossary.name: Goodhart's Law
glossary.definition: When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure.
glossary.example: Hospitals measured on waiting times keep patients in ambulances. Call centres measured on call duration hang up. The phrasing everyone quotes is Strathern's compression of Goodhart's monetary-policy point.

probe.ask: A hospital is measured on A&E waiting times. What happens?

options.label: Waiting times fall and care improves
options.tell: The intended outcome, and part of what happens.

options.label: Waiting times fall and patients are moved to trolleys in corridors
options.tell: The documented outcome. The measure improved; the thing it stood for did not.

probe.reveal: Strathern's formulation is the famous one. The law is not an argument against measurement — you cannot manage what you cannot see — but against using a single proxy as the target. The defence is multiple measures, changed periodically, with someone still looking at the corridors.

glossary.name: Campbell's Law
glossary.definition: The more a social indicator is used for decision-making, the more it will corrupt the processes it monitors.
glossary.example: The sharper, earlier sibling of Goodhart. Campbell was writing about educational testing, and the subsequent history of test-score scandals reads as confirmation.

probe.ask: Teacher pay is tied to test scores. What changes first?

options.label: Teaching quality
options.tell: The intent, and it is what happens in the first year, before the incentive is understood.

options.label: What is taught, then how scores are produced
options.tell: The documented sequence, up to and including erasure scandals.

probe.reveal: Campbell's version is specifically about social indicators used for decisions, and it predicts both narrowing and outright corruption of the measurement process. The Atlanta cheating convictions are the extreme case; curriculum narrowing is the ordinary one and is much harder to see in the data, because the data is what narrowed.

glossary.name: The Cobra Effect
glossary.definition: An incentive designed to solve a problem makes it worse.
glossary.example: The colonial administration is said to have paid a bounty for dead cobras in Delhi; people bred cobras. When the scheme ended they released them. The anecdote's sourcing is thin, but the pattern is thoroughly documented elsewhere.

probe.ask: A bounty is offered per venomous snake killed. What do you predict?

options.label: Fewer snakes
options.tell: The design intent, and it holds until someone notices the bounty is a business.

options.label: Snake farms, and more snakes when the bounty ends
options.tell: The story the effect is named for.

probe.reveal: The Delhi cobra anecdote is likely apocryphal, but the structure is well documented elsewhere — Hanoi's rat-tail bounty produced tailless rats, and paying for fossil fragments produced smashed fossils. Any bounty on a proxy creates a market for producing the proxy, and the market is often faster than the policy.

glossary.name: The Jevons Paradox
glossary.definition: Efficiency gains can increase total consumption rather than reduce it.
glossary.example: Jevons observed that better steam engines increased coal use. The same argument recurs in every debate about efficiency standards and data-centre power.

probe.ask: Engines become 30% more efficient. What happens to total fuel use?

options.label: It falls
options.tell: True if demand is fixed, which it rarely is.

options.label: It can rise, because efficiency makes use cheaper
options.tell: Jevons's observation about coal in 1865.

probe.reveal: Efficiency lowers the effective price of a service, and lower prices raise demand. Whether the rebound exceeds 100% is contested and depends on the sector — for domestic lighting and heating in rich countries it does not, for industrial energy it sometimes has. The paradox is a reason to price the externality rather than only to improve the technology.

glossary.name: The Streisand Effect
glossary.definition: Attempting to suppress information amplifies it.
glossary.example: Barbra Streisand sued to remove an aerial photograph of her house that had been downloaded six times; the suit made it famous. Now the standard argument against heavy-handed takedowns.

probe.ask: An unflattering article about you has 200 readers. Your lawyer offers to send a takedown notice.

options.label: Send it
options.tell: The takedown is itself news, and the story is now about the takedown.

options.label: Do nothing
options.tell: Usually right at 200 readers, and genuinely hard advice to take.

probe.reveal: Streisand's suit over an aerial photograph of her house took its downloads from six to hundreds of thousands. The asymmetry is structural: suppression is a costly signal that the material matters, and the signal travels further than the material would have. Note that the effect is invisible in the cases where suppression worked.

glossary.name: Brandolini's Law
glossary.definition: The energy needed to refute nonsense is an order of magnitude greater than to produce it.
glossary.example: The asymmetry that makes debunking a losing strategy at scale and prebunking a better one. Also the reason a confident wrong answer outcompetes a careful uncertain one.

probe.ask: A colleague makes six confident false claims in two minutes. What do you do?

options.label: Refute all six
options.tell: You will need twenty minutes and will look like the difficult one.

options.label: Pick the load-bearing one
options.tell: The only strategy that scales, and it concedes the other five by silence.

probe.reveal: Brandolini's asymmetry is why the Gish gallop works as a debate tactic and why fact-checking loses to production. There is no clean answer here — the law describes a cost structure, not a fix — but naming the asymmetry publicly is usually better than pretending you conceded on the merits.

glossary.name: Parkinson's Law
glossary.definition: Work expands to fill the time available for its completion.
glossary.example: Parkinson's original essay was satire backed by real Admiralty statistics: the number of officials rose steadily while the number of ships fell.

probe.ask: A task takes three hours. You are given a week. When is it finished?

options.label: In three hours, on the first day
options.tell: Rare, and usually reported by people misremembering.

options.label: Late on the last day, having taken a week
options.tell: Parkinson's observation, drawn from watching the Colonial Office grow as the empire shrank.

probe.reveal: Parkinson's original was satire with real data attached: Admiralty administrative staff rose while ships and sailors fell. The mechanism is not laziness but that work has no natural boundary — polish, consultation and re-checking expand to fill whatever is available.

glossary.name: The Peter Principle
glossary.definition: People are promoted on performance in their current role until they reach one they perform badly, and there they remain.
glossary.example: A study of sales workers found firms really do promote the best salespeople into management, where they underperform — the satire turns out to describe an observable practice.

probe.ask: Are people promoted until they reach a job they are bad at?

options.label: Yes — and that is why management is poor
options.tell: The satirical claim, and there is now real evidence for a version of it.

options.label: No — firms account for the different skills required
options.tell: What firms should do and, in sales data, mostly do not.

probe.reveal: Benson, Li and Lucas studied around 40,000 sales workers: the best salespeople were much more likely to be promoted and their teams then performed worse. Firms paid a real cost to use promotion as a reward rather than a match. It is one industry and one dataset, so the general claim remains contested — but Peter wrote it as a joke and the data partly vindicated him.

glossary.name: The Pareto Principle
glossary.definition: A large share of effects comes from a small share of causes.
glossary.example: Pareto noticed land ownership followed this shape. The "80/20" formulation is a later convenience: the ratio is not a law, and treating it as one is how the idea gets misused.

probe.ask: Your top 20% of customers produce 80% of revenue. What follows?

options.label: Focus everything on the top 20%
options.tell: The usual conclusion, and it ignores where the next top 20% comes from.

options.label: Nothing yet — this is the shape of many distributions
options.tell: The statistically literate answer.

probe.reveal: The 80/20 split is a feature of power-law-ish distributions and describes far more than it explains — the numbers need not sum to 100 and the exact ratio is arbitrary. It is useful as a prompt to check whether your effort is distributed like your returns, and useless as a justification on its own.

glossary.name: The Lindy Effect
glossary.definition: For non-perishable things, life expectancy grows with age: what has lasted fifty years may last fifty more.
glossary.example: An argument for reading old books and distrusting new frameworks. It applies to ideas and technologies, not to people or anything with a fixed lifespan — a distinction routinely dropped.

probe.ask: Two books: one published this year, one still read after 400 years. Which will still be read in fifty?

options.label: The old one
options.tell: The Lindy prediction, and a good bet.

options.label: Impossible to say
options.tell: True of any single pair — Lindy is a statement about distributions.

probe.reveal: For non-perishable things, survival is evidence of the properties that produce survival. The limit is that it only applies where the selection process still operates: Lindy says nothing useful about a technology whose environment has just changed, and it is frequently used to defend practices whose original conditions are gone.

glossary.name: The Black Swan
glossary.definition: Rare, high-impact events that are rationalised as predictable only afterwards.
glossary.example: Taleb's point is not that such events can be forecast but that systems should be built to survive not forecasting them. The term is now used, against his argument, to excuse foreseeable failures.

probe.ask: Your risk model has performed flawlessly for ten years. How much comfort should that give you?

options.label: Considerable — that is a long record
options.tell: The turkey's reasoning on day 999.

options.label: Little, if the model has not been tested by a crisis
options.tell: The point: absence of evidence in a fat-tailed domain is very weak evidence of absence.

probe.reveal: Taleb's argument is about domains where the tails carry most of the consequence, so the historical record systematically understates the risk. The trap is that it is unfalsifiable as stated — any quiet period is consistent with it — so its practical content is in the position sizing, not in the prediction.

glossary.name: The Narrative Fallacy
glossary.definition: Imposing a causal story on a sequence of events, which makes them feel explicable and predictable in hindsight.
glossary.example: Every business biography and every post-hoc market explanation. The story is generated from the outcome, which is why it is never available in advance.

probe.ask: A market falls 3% and the evening report explains why. How much should you learn from the explanation?

options.label: Something — journalists talk to traders
options.tell: A little, and note the same explanation is available for a 3% rise.

options.label: Nothing — the story is written after the number
options.tell: Closer to correct, and the reason the same news is reported as both cause and consequence.

probe.reveal: The fallacy is not story-telling but the compression: a story reduces a mess of causes to a chain you can remember, and the memorability is then mistaken for explanatory power. The test is whether the story would have predicted the outcome in advance, and it almost never would.

glossary.name: Antifragility
glossary.definition: Some systems gain from disorder rather than merely resisting it — the opposite of fragile is not robust.
glossary.example: Muscles, immune systems and competitive markets strengthen under bounded stress. The concept is often stretched to justify any disruption, which is not what a bounded stressor means.

probe.ask: Which system is better placed for an unpredictable decade?

options.label: One optimised for efficiency with no slack
options.tell: Best in the expected case and worst in the tails.

options.label: One with redundancy that gets stress-tested regularly
options.tell: Pays a running cost to gain from disorder rather than merely survive it.

probe.reveal: Taleb's distinction is between resisting volatility and benefiting from it: muscle, immune systems and evolutionary processes improve under the right dose of stress. The concept is often stretched past usefulness — most things are simply fragile or robust, and calling a preference for slack "antifragility" does not add anything.

glossary.name: Moral Hazard
glossary.definition: Insulation from the consequences of a risk changes behaviour toward that risk.
glossary.example: The central argument in every bailout debate. It cuts both ways: the same logic that warns against rescuing banks warns against rescuing anyone, which is why it needs an account of who bears the loss instead.

probe.ask: A bank is guaranteed rescue if it fails. What changes?

options.label: Nothing — bankers do not want to fail
options.tell: True of the individuals and irrelevant to the risk-taking calculus.

options.label: The optimal amount of risk to take goes up
options.tell: The mechanism, and it needs no bad intent to operate.

probe.reveal: Moral hazard is a change in the incentive structure, not a claim about character. The awkward part is that its clearest policy implication — let the failure happen — imposes the cost on people who did not take the risk, which is why the argument is more often deployed against benefits than against bailouts.

glossary.name: The Principal–Agent Problem
glossary.definition: Whoever acts on your behalf has their own interests and better information than you.
glossary.example: The structural fact under executive pay, fund management fees and every contractor relationship. Not a claim about dishonesty; it holds among entirely honest people.

probe.ask: Your estate agent advises accepting an offer £10,000 below your target. Whose interest is that?

options.label: Mine — they know the market
options.tell: Possibly. Their commission on the extra £10,000 is around £150.

options.label: Theirs — a fast sale is worth more to them than a high one
options.tell: The structure Levitt found in the data.

probe.reveal: Levitt and Syverson found agents kept their own houses on the market longer and sold them for about 3% more. No dishonesty is required: the agent bears all the cost of the extra weeks and captures a few per cent of the gain. Check what fraction of the upside your advisor receives.

glossary.name: The Shirky Principle
glossary.definition: Institutions will try to preserve the problem to which they are the solution.
glossary.example: Rarely a conspiracy, usually an incentive: the department that eliminates its own workload eliminates its own budget.

probe.ask: A charity could plausibly end the problem it addresses within a decade. What do you predict it does?

options.label: Works to end it and dissolves
options.tell: It happens — the March of Dimes had to reinvent itself after polio.

options.label: Broadens its mission and continues
options.tell: The far commoner path, and rarely a conscious decision by anyone.

probe.reveal: Shirky's formulation is about institutional incentives rather than motives: the people are sincere and the structure still selects for continuation. It is a useful prompt and an unfalsifiable accusation when used against a specific organisation, so use it on structures rather than on the people inside them.

glossary.name: Conway's Law
glossary.definition: Organisations design systems that mirror their own communication structure.
glossary.example: Four teams produce a four-pass compiler. Well evidenced in software architecture studies, and the reason reorganisations change codebases.

probe.ask: Four teams build a compiler. How many passes does it have?

options.label: Four
options.tell: Conway's joke, and the empirical studies find real support for the pattern.

options.label: However many the problem needs
options.tell: What the design document says.

probe.reveal: MacCormack and colleagues found open-source products, built by loosely coupled contributors, were measurably more modular than commercially built equivalents of the same function. The "inverse Conway manoeuvre" — reorganising teams to get the architecture you want — follows, and is more often talked about than done. The evidence is a handful of studies on a quantity that is hard to measure and has not been replicated widely, so treat the correspondence as a strong tendency rather than a demonstrated law.

glossary.name: Gall's Law
glossary.definition: A complex system that works is invariably found to have evolved from a simple system that worked.
glossary.example: The standing argument against ground-up rewrites and grand system designs, and the reason most of them fail.

probe.ask: You need a complex system. Where do you start?

options.label: Design the complete system, then build it
options.tell: The approach behind most large failed IT programmes.

options.label: Build the simplest thing that works, then grow it
options.tell: Gall's claim, and the one the failure record supports.

probe.reveal: Gall's stronger version is that a complex system designed from scratch never works and cannot be patched into working. The counter-example is that some systems — a bridge, an aircraft — cannot be grown incrementally, so the law is really about systems whose requirements are discovered through use.

glossary.name: Dunbar's Number
glossary.definition: A cognitive limit of roughly 150 stable social relationships, inferred from primate neocortex ratios.
glossary.example: Widely cited in management writing. A 2021 Stockholm University analysis argued the underlying extrapolation cannot support a specific number, with confidence intervals spanning an enormous range. Dunbar disputes this. Treat the specific figure with caution.

probe.ask: Is there a cognitive limit of about 150 stable relationships?

options.label: Yes — it follows from neocortex size
options.tell: The claim, extrapolated from primate group sizes.

options.label: The statistical basis is weak and the confidence interval is enormous
options.tell: What the re-analysis found.

probe.reveal: Lindenfors and colleagues repeated the regression with better methods and found a 95% interval of roughly 4 to 520 — wide enough to be useless as a specific number. The general point that social capacity is bounded is uncontroversial; the number 150, now embedded in management advice, is not supported by its own derivation.

glossary.name: The Matthew Effect
glossary.definition: Advantage accumulates: to those who have, more is given.
glossary.example: Merton observed that eminent scientists get disproportionate credit for collaborative work. It compounds in citations, wealth, and early school success, and it is a structural explanation rather than a moral one.

probe.ask: Two researchers publish the same idea. One is already famous. Who gets the credit?

options.label: Whoever published first
options.tell: The norm. Merton documented that this is not what happens.

options.label: The famous one
options.tell: The Matthew effect, named from the gospel line about those who have.

probe.reveal: Merton found eminent scientists receive disproportionate credit for joint or simultaneous work, and the effect compounds through funding and citation. Salganik's music-lab experiments showed the mechanism directly: with social influence on, early random advantage became durable success and outcomes across parallel worlds diverged sharply.

glossary.name: The Red Queen Effect
glossary.definition: Continuous adaptation is required merely to maintain position relative to competitors who are also adapting.
glossary.example: From Carroll: all the running you can do to stay in the same place. Applies to arms races, antibiotic resistance and product features nobody wanted.

probe.ask: Every firm in your sector improves its logistics by 10%. What is your competitive position?

options.label: Better — we improved
options.tell: Absolutely true and competitively irrelevant.

options.label: Unchanged, and you had to spend to stay level
options.tell: The Red Queen: all the running you can do to keep in the same place.

probe.reveal: Van Valen's original was evolutionary — extinction risk stays constant because competitors adapt too. The strategic corollary is that improvements every competitor can also make are table stakes rather than advantage, and the only durable positions come from something others cannot copy at the same cost.

glossary.name: Second-Order Thinking
glossary.definition: Asking "and then what?" — considering the consequences of the consequences.
glossary.example: Rent control lowers rents and reduces supply. Most policy disagreement is between people stopping at different orders, not between people with different values.

probe.ask: A city caps rents to help tenants. And then what?

options.label: Tenants pay less
options.tell: The first-order effect, and real for tenants already in place.

options.label: Supply, mobility and maintenance change too
options.tell: The second order, where most of the argument lives.

probe.reveal: Diamond, McQuade and Qian's San Francisco study found both: large benefits to protected tenants and a reduction in rental supply that raised rents overall. Second-order thinking is not a verdict against intervention — it is the requirement to count both, which partisans on each side reliably decline to do.

glossary.name: Inversion
glossary.source: Carl Jacobi; popularised by Charlie Munger
glossary.definition: Solve a problem backwards: ask what would guarantee failure, then avoid that.
glossary.example: Munger's standing method — "all I want to know is where I'm going to die, so I'll never go there." Often more tractable than asking what would guarantee success.

probe.ask: You want the project to succeed. What is the more productive question?

options.label: What would make it succeed?
options.tell: Generates a long list of pleasant things, most of which are not decisive.

options.label: What would guarantee it fails?
options.tell: Generates a short list of concrete, checkable items.

probe.reveal: Jacobi's "invert, always invert", and the formal version is Klein's pre-mortem: state that the project has failed twelve months from now and ask everyone to write why. Klein found this produces substantially more, and more specific, risks than asking for concerns directly, because it licenses pessimism.

glossary.name: The Map Is Not the Territory
glossary.definition: A model is a compression of reality and omits by design; confusing the two is a category error.
glossary.example: The dashboard is not the business, the diagnosis is not the patient, and the metric is not the thing measured — which is where Goodhart's Law comes from.

probe.ask: Your dashboard shows every metric green while a customer is telling you the product is unusable.

options.label: The customer is an outlier
options.tell: Possible, and the reflex that lets a model outlive its accuracy.

options.label: The dashboard is not measuring the thing
options.tell: The correction, and it costs something to accept.

probe.reveal: Korzybski's formulation. Every model omits by design — a map showing everything would be the territory — so the question is never whether it omits but whether what it omits matters here. The failure is not having a model; it is losing the memory that you chose one.

glossary.name: Chesterton's Fence
glossary.definition: Do not remove a fence until you know why it was put there.
glossary.example: A rule about the order of operations in reform, not a defence of every fence. Its failure mode is that a reason can always be sought, so it can stall any change indefinitely.

probe.ask: You inherit a process nobody can justify. Do you remove it?

options.label: Yes — nobody can explain it
options.tell: Chesterton's target: the reformer who takes absence of an explanation as absence of a reason.

options.label: Not until I find out why it exists
options.tell: The rule, and it has a cost — the search can take longer than the fence is worth.

probe.reveal: Chesterton's point was epistemic humility, not conservatism, and he says so: once you know why the fence is there you may well remove it. The failure mode in the other direction is real — "we have always done it this way" is the fence defending itself — so the rule is find out, with a time limit.

glossary.name: The Availability Cascade
glossary.definition: A self-reinforcing cycle in which a claim gains plausibility through repetition in public discourse.
glossary.example: Coverage raises salience, salience raises perceived importance, which generates more coverage. The authors' concern was risk regulation driven by what was recently vivid rather than by what harms most.

probe.ask: A risk is discussed everywhere for a fortnight. Has the underlying risk changed?

options.label: It must have — this much coverage means something
options.tell: Sometimes true, and coverage volume is a poor instrument for measuring it.

options.label: Not necessarily — coverage generates coverage
options.tell: Kuran and Sunstein's mechanism.

probe.reveal: Availability begets availability: each retelling makes the risk easier to recall, which makes it feel commoner, which justifies more retelling. Kuran and Sunstein traced the pattern through several regulatory panics where spending tracked salience rather than expected harm.

glossary.name: Information Cascades
glossary.definition: People rationally ignore their own information and copy predecessors, so a whole population can converge on something false.
glossary.example: Each individual is behaving sensibly; the aggregate is fragile, and a small early accident determines the outcome. The formal model behind bank runs and fashion.

probe.ask: Three people before you guessed the urn is mostly red. Your own draw is blue. What do you say?

options.label: Red — three signals beat mine
options.tell: Individually rational, and it destroys the information your draw carried.

options.label: Blue — report what I saw
options.tell: Individually worse and collectively far better.

probe.reveal: Anderson and Holt reproduced Bikhchandani's model in the laboratory: once two people agree, later subjects rationally ignore their own draw, so the whole population can converge on the wrong urn from two unlucky signals. Cascades are fragile for the same reason — one piece of public information can reverse everything.

glossary.name: Selection Effects
glossary.definition: How a sample was assembled often explains the pattern in it better than any causal story.
glossary.example: The most common single error in reading research: the difference between "successful founders drop out" and "we only interviewed successful founders".

probe.ask: A study finds people who meditate are happier. What is the most likely explanation?

options.label: Meditation raises happiness
options.tell: Possible, and not what a correlation in a self-selected sample shows.

options.label: People with the time and disposition to meditate were already happier
options.tell: Selection into the treatment, which is the default suspect.

probe.reveal: How a sample was assembled usually explains more of the pattern than any causal story about the variables in it. This is the single most reusable question in this glossary: before asking what caused the difference between the groups, ask what caused the groups.

glossary.name: Dose–Response Reasoning
glossary.definition: A real causal relationship usually shows more effect with more exposure.
glossary.example: One of Hill's criteria for inferring causation from association, and among the most useful quick tests when reading a claim of harm or benefit.

probe.ask: A study finds a small effect at one dose and nothing at higher doses. How much does that worry you?

options.label: Not much — effects can be non-monotonic
options.tell: True in specific biological cases and rare enough that it needs its own argument.

options.label: A lot — a real cause usually shows more effect with more exposure
options.tell: Hill's biological-gradient criterion.

probe.reveal: A dose–response gradient was among Bradford Hill's criteria and is one of the more useful filters available to a non-specialist: it is hard to produce by chance and hard to fake. It is not decisive — thresholds and saturation are real — but a claimed effect that appears only at one arbitrary dose deserves suspicion.

glossary.name: Status Quo Bias
glossary.definition: A preference for the current state, held beyond what its merits justify.
glossary.example: Distinct from the default effect, which is about friction: this is about the current arrangement acquiring a presumption of rightness merely by being current.

probe.ask: You inherit a portfolio of 70% bonds. Would you have chosen that allocation yourself?

options.label: No, but I would not restructure it
options.tell: The bias precisely: the current state acquires a defence it did not earn.

options.label: I would move it to what I would have chosen
options.tell: The consistent answer, minus transaction costs.

probe.reveal: Samuelson and Zeckhauser found subjects given a hypothetical inheritance stuck with whatever allocation they were told they already had. A clean test on any position you hold: if you did not have it, at what price would you acquire it? If that price is well below the current one, you are holding it out of inertia.

glossary.name: Mental Accounting
glossary.definition: Money is sorted into non-fungible mental categories and spent differently from each.
glossary.example: People carry credit-card debt at 20% while holding savings at 2%, because the accounts are separate in the mind though the arithmetic is not.

probe.ask: You lose a £40 ticket at the door. Do you buy another? Now: you lose £40 in cash on the way. Do you still buy the ticket?

options.label: No to the first, yes to the second
options.tell: The modal pattern. You are £40 down either way.

options.label: The same answer to both
options.tell: Consistent, and it treats money as fungible, which it is.

probe.reveal: Kahneman and Tversky found the split clearly: the lost ticket is charged to the "entertainment" account, making the evening feel like £80, while the lost cash is charged to general funds. The accounts are not real. They are also sometimes useful — a budget is mental accounting deliberately imposed as a commitment device.

glossary.name: Action Bias
glossary.definition: Preferring to act rather than wait, even where waiting has the better expected outcome.
glossary.example: Goalkeepers facing penalties dive left or right almost always, though staying central would stop more. Standing still and being scored past feels worse than diving and being scored past.

probe.ask: You are a goalkeeper facing a penalty. Statistically the best strategy is to stay in the centre. Do you?

options.label: Dive — staying still looks like doing nothing
options.tell: What keepers do about 94% of the time. Bar-Eli found the centre is the best third.

options.label: Stay
options.tell: Better expected outcome, and much worse if you are wrong.

probe.reveal: Bar-Eli and colleagues analysed 286 penalties: kicks go left, centre and right in roughly equal thirds, keepers stay central 6% of the time, and the save rate for staying is the highest. The norm punishes visible inaction more than invisible error, which is a structure repeated in medicine and in policy. This rests on one sport and one dataset, and attempts to find the same bias in other domains have been inconsistent, so read it as a vivid case rather than a law.

glossary.name: Omission Bias
glossary.definition: Judging harmful actions as worse than equally harmful inactions.
glossary.example: The mirror of action bias, and the two coexist: people act when acting is visible and refrain when refraining is defensible. Underlies much of the vaccination debate.

probe.ask: A vaccine will kill 5 in 10,000; the disease it prevents kills 10 in 10,000. Do you vaccinate your child?

options.label: No — I would be the cause of the harm
options.tell: The bias, and the moral intuition behind it is not empty.

options.label: Yes — half the deaths
options.tell: The consequentialist answer.

probe.reveal: Ritov and Baron found a substantial minority refused even at much better ratios, and the reason given was authorship of the harm. Whether killing and letting die differ morally is a live question in the corpus — Foot and Rachels disagree — so this is a case where a bias and a moral position are hard to separate.

glossary.name: The Identifiable Victim Effect
glossary.definition: People give far more to one named person than to statistical many.
glossary.example: Their study found donations dropped when a named child's story was accompanied by statistics about the scale of need. The number does not add urgency; it removes it.

probe.ask: Would you give more to save one named, photographed child, or to a programme saving eight thousand unnamed ones?

options.label: The named child
options.tell: What people do, by a large margin, in donation experiments.

options.label: The programme
options.tell: What almost everyone endorses on reflection, and rarely does at the moment of giving.

probe.reveal: Small, Loewenstein and Slovic found donations dropped when statistical information was added to a named case — including when both were presented together, so the statistics actively suppressed giving. Slovic calls the general pattern psychic numbing: our compassion does not scale, and it sometimes runs backwards.

glossary.name: Scope Insensitivity
glossary.definition: Willingness to pay barely rises with the size of the problem.
glossary.example: Respondents offered similar amounts to save 2,000, 20,000 or 200,000 birds. The mental image is one bird either way, and the image is what is being priced.

probe.ask: What would you pay to save 2,000 birds from oil ponds? And 20,000? And 200,000?

options.label: Roughly the same for all three
options.tell: The finding: the mean figures were about $80, $78 and $88.

options.label: Ten times more for each step
options.tell: What proportional valuation requires and almost nobody produces.

probe.reveal: Desvousges and colleagues found willingness to pay essentially flat across a hundred-fold change in scale. The mental image evoked — one bird in oil — is identical in all three cases, and the image is what gets valued. This has direct consequences for how charitable giving and public consultation are interpreted.

glossary.name: Reactance
glossary.definition: A motivational push against restrictions on freedom, sometimes toward the restricted behaviour itself.
glossary.example: Why bans can raise consumption, why "you must decide for yourself" outperforms instruction, and why heavy-handed public messaging can invert.

probe.ask: A sign says "absolutely do not write on this wall". What is the effect?

options.label: Less graffiti
