options.tell: The intent, and stronger wording feels as though it should produce more of it.

options.label: More, especially among those who feel entitled to decide
options.tell: Pennebaker and Sanders found the strongly-worded sign produced more.

probe.reveal: Brehm's theory holds that a perceived threat to freedom produces a motivational push toward the restricted behaviour. It is why mandates can backfire, why "you are free to refuse" raises compliance in field experiments, and why the strength of a message and its persuasiveness are not the same variable.

glossary.name: Naïve Realism
glossary.definition: Believing you see things as they are, and that anyone reasonable who looked would agree — so disagreement means bias, ignorance or bad faith.
glossary.example: The engine under most political contempt. It also predicts that both sides will see the same news coverage as biased against them, which they do.

probe.ask: Someone informed and intelligent disagrees with you on something you consider obvious. Why?

options.label: They have not looked at it properly
options.tell: The first branch of the naïve-realist triad: ignorance.

options.label: Something is distorting their judgement
options.tell: The second branch: their view is explained by interest or ideology rather than by reasons.

options.label: They weight a value differently from me
options.tell: The option the triad omits, and usually the true one.

probe.reveal: Ross and Ward describe the sequence: I see reality directly, reasonable people who look will agree, therefore those who disagree are ignorant, irrational or dishonest. The first two premises feel like perception rather than assumption, which is why the conclusion arrives without any sense of having reasoned to it.

glossary.name: The Hostile Media Effect
glossary.definition: Partisans on both sides perceive identical neutral coverage as biased against their own side.
glossary.example: Shown the same Beirut coverage, pro-Israeli and pro-Arab students each judged it hostile to them and counted more unfavourable references to their own side.

probe.ask: You watch a news segment on a conflict you care about. How does it seem?

options.label: Slanted against my side
options.tell: What partisans on both sides reported about the identical footage.

options.label: Reasonably balanced
options.tell: What neutral viewers reported.

probe.reveal: Vallone, Ross and Lepper showed pro-Israeli and pro-Arab students the same coverage: each group rated it biased against them, and each believed a neutral viewer would be turned against their side by it. Both cannot be right, which makes this one of the cleanest demonstrations that perceived bias is partly manufactured by the perceiver.

glossary.name: The Third-Person Effect
glossary.definition: People believe media affects others more than themselves.
glossary.example: It predicts support for censorship: the harm is always to someone more impressionable, which is what makes the restriction feel costless to the person endorsing it.

probe.ask: How much does advertising influence your purchases, compared with how much it influences other people's?

options.label: Much less than it influences others
options.tell: The near-universal answer, and it cannot be true of everyone.

options.label: About the same
options.tell: Arithmetically necessary in aggregate and rarely reported.

probe.reveal: Davison's effect is robust across media and topics, and its consequence is political: support for censorship correlates with the size of the gap, because people legislate for the vulnerable others they imagine. The belief that you are the exception is itself the effect.

glossary.name: Moral Licensing
glossary.definition: Having behaved well makes people more comfortable behaving badly afterwards.
glossary.example: The effect appears in several paradigms but meta-analytic estimates are small and publication bias is a live concern. The mechanism is plausible; the size is not what the popular version claims.

probe.ask: You have just donated to a good cause. Does the next small ethical decision get easier or harder?

options.label: Easier to cut a corner — I have credit
options.tell: The licensing pattern, and people rarely notice the accounting.

options.label: Harder — I want to be consistent
options.tell: The opposite prediction, and it also has support.

probe.reveal: Monin and Miller found subjects who first established non-prejudiced credentials then expressed more prejudiced views. Meta-analysis puts the effect as small, with replication problems, and consistency effects run the other way in other setups. Treat it as a real possibility rather than a dependable mechanism.

glossary.name: The Just World Hypothesis
glossary.definition: A need to believe people get what they deserve, which produces derogation of victims.
glossary.example: Lerner found observers who could not help a suffering person came to think less of them. It is a defence of the observer's sense of safety, paid for by the sufferer.

probe.ask: You read about someone who lost everything in a scam. What is your first thought?

options.label: How did they not see it?
options.tell: The derogation, and it arrives before any information about the scam.

options.label: That could be me
options.tell: The costlier thought, which is why it is less common.

probe.reveal: Lerner found observers who could not help a suffering person came to rate her as deserving it. The function is protective — a world where misfortune is earned is a world you can stay safe in — and the cost is paid entirely by victims. Recognising the motive does not remove it, but it does make the first thought inspectable.

glossary.name: System Justification
glossary.definition: A motivation to defend existing arrangements, sometimes strongest among those the arrangements disadvantage.
glossary.example: Contested in its strong form — whether the disadvantaged really justify more is disputed — but the general tendency to rationalise the status quo is well supported.

probe.ask: Who is most likely to defend an arrangement that disadvantages them?

options.label: Nobody — people defend their interests
options.tell: The assumption behind most political prediction, and it is often wrong.

options.label: Sometimes the disadvantaged themselves
options.tell: Jost's claim, and the most contested part of the theory.

probe.reveal: Jost argues that the motive to see existing arrangements as legitimate can outweigh self-interest, producing outgroup favouritism among low-status groups. The strong version is disputed — Brandt and others find little consistent evidence for the specific claim that the most disadvantaged justify most — while the general phenomenon of legitimation is well attested.

glossary.name: The Pygmalion Effect
glossary.definition: Expectations held by a teacher or manager influence the performance of those they hold them about.
glossary.example: The original classroom study has been criticised on measurement grounds for decades. Meta-analyses find a real but modest effect, largest where expectations are formed before any acquaintance.

probe.ask: If a teacher is told certain pupils are about to bloom, do those pupils improve?

options.label: Yes, substantially — expectations create reality
options.tell: The Rosenthal and Jacobson claim as popularly told.

options.label: A little, and mainly in the youngest children
options.tell: Where the meta-analytic evidence sits.

probe.reveal: The original assigned "bloomers" at random and reported IQ gains. Methodological criticism was immediate and replications inconsistent; meta-analyses find a small average effect concentrated in the first two years of school and in situations where the teacher does not already know the pupil. Real, and much smaller than the story.

glossary.name: The Hawthorne Effect
glossary.source: named for the Hawthorne Works studies, 1924–32
glossary.definition: People change behaviour because they are being observed.
glossary.example: Re-analyses of the original illumination data found the classic effect largely absent, and much of what was reported reflects small samples and selective telling. The general phenomenon of observation changing behaviour is real; this specific study does not demonstrate it.

probe.ask: Do people work harder simply because they are being observed?

options.label: Yes — the lighting studies showed it
options.tell: The textbook version. Re-analysis of the original data does not support it.

options.label: Observation effects exist but the famous study does not show them
options.tell: The accurate position: the phenomenon is real, the study named for it is poor evidence of it.

probe.reveal: Levitt and List recovered the original Hawthorne data and found the pattern largely explained by the day of the week and by productivity rising whenever lighting changed at all — including downward. Participation effects in trials are real and are why blinding exists; the named study is a poor demonstration of them, and the size of the general effect is contested.

glossary.name: Specification Gaming
glossary.definition: An optimiser satisfies the stated objective while defeating its purpose.
glossary.example: Documented across dozens of real systems: agents that pause a game forever to avoid losing, or exploit a physics bug rather than learn to walk. Goodhart's Law with a faster feedback loop.

probe.ask: A boat-racing agent is rewarded for points rather than for finishing. What does it learn?

options.label: To race well — points come from racing
options.tell: The designer's assumption.

options.label: To circle a lagoon hitting the same targets forever
options.tell: What OpenAI's CoastRunners agent actually did, scoring higher than any human.

probe.reveal: Specification gaming is Goodhart's law with a fast optimiser attached: the agent has no model of what you meant, only of what you wrote. Krakovna's catalogue runs to dozens of documented cases. The lesson generalises to any incentive scheme facing a sufficiently motivated participant.

glossary.name: The Forer Effect
glossary.definition: People accept vague, general personality descriptions as specifically accurate about themselves.
glossary.example: Forer gave students an identical horoscope-style profile assembled from a newsstand astrology book; they rated it as highly accurate about them personally. The standing warning about every personality test, including the one you are using.

probe.ask: "You have a great deal of unused capacity you have not turned to your advantage. You pride yourself on independent thinking." How accurate is that about you?

options.label: Quite accurate
options.tell: The average rating Forer's students gave was 4.26 out of 5. Everyone received the same text.

options.label: Too vague to rate
options.tell: The correct response, and one that requires suspecting the question.

probe.reveal: Forer assembled the description from a newsstand astrology book and handed every student the same sheet after a personality test. The statements work because they are true of nearly everyone and because the reader supplies the specifics. This site's own results are built to be falsifiable for exactly this reason — the entry below is the test of whether they are.

glossary.name: Moral-Emotional Contagion
glossary.source: Brady, Wills, Jost, Tucker & Van Bavel, 2017
glossary.definition: Messages containing moral-emotional language spread further within political groups than neutral ones.
glossary.example: Their analysis of political tweets found each additional moral-emotional word raised diffusion within a group, while doing little to cross between groups. It is a mechanism for why outrage travels and nuance does not, without requiring anyone to be acting in bad faith.

probe.ask: Two posts make the same argument. One adds the words "shameful" and "disgraceful". Which travels further?

options.label: The plain one — it is more credible
options.tell: What people say they prefer.

options.label: The moral-emotional one
options.tell: Brady found each such word raised retransmission by around 20%.

probe.reveal: Brady and colleagues analysed over half a million political tweets and found moral-emotional language raised diffusion by roughly 20% per word — and that the spread was concentrated within ideological groups rather than across them. The platform does not select for what is true or even for what is angry, but for what is angry about the right target.

glossary.name: The Falling Cost of Outrage
glossary.definition: Digital platforms reduce the personal cost of expressing moral outrage while raising its reward, changing how much gets expressed.
glossary.example: Crockett's argument is structural rather than accusatory: offline, condemning someone risked retaliation and took effort; online it is a tap and may bring approval. The same person expresses more outrage without having become more outraged.

probe.ask: Condemning something publicly used to cost you time, risk and social capital. Online it costs a few seconds. What follows?

options.label: More outrage expressed, of no lower sincerity
options.tell: Possible, and it does not follow from the cost change alone.

options.label: More outrage expressed, and it carries less information about the speaker
options.tell: The signalling consequence: a cheap signal separates types less well.

probe.reveal: Crockett's argument is that platforms lowered the cost of expression while raising its reward, so the amount rises and the informational value falls. Note this is a theoretical case with supporting evidence rather than a replicated finding — the causal claim is contested — and that it applies equally to outrage you agree with.

glossary.name: Moral Grandstanding
glossary.definition: Using moral talk to promote oneself — measured as an individual difference, and associated with status-seeking and conflict.
glossary.example: The researchers built a scale and found grandstanding scores predicted political conflict and, notably, appeared across the political spectrum rather than on one side. Self-report measures of a socially undesirable trait carry obvious limits.

probe.ask: When you post about a moral issue, how often is part of the motive how it will make you look?

options.label: Rarely — I post because it matters
options.tell: The modal self-report, and the scale finds grandstanding motives are common.

options.label: Often, and I would rather admit it
options.tell: The rarer answer, and it does not by itself make the position wrong.

probe.reveal: Grubbs and colleagues built a measure with prestige- and dominance-seeking subscales and found it predicts political conflict and social-media hostility — though it is a self-report measure of other people's motives as much as one's own, and its construct validity is disputed. The philosophical point from Tosi and Warmke stands regardless: grandstanding is about the motive, not the content, so a grandstander can be entirely right about the issue.

glossary.name: The Smartphone Generation Hypothesis
glossary.definition: That the arrival of smartphones around 2012 drove a sharp rise in adolescent depression, anxiety and self-harm, particularly among girls.
glossary.example: The trend data are real and steep in several countries. Whether phones caused it is genuinely disputed: Przybylski and Orben found the average association between screen use and wellbeing is tiny — comparable to eating potatoes — while Twenge and Haidt argue the effect concentrates in heavy social-media use by girls and that the timing is too sharp to be coincidence. Both camps are reading largely the same datasets.

probe.ask: Did smartphones cause the rise in adolescent depression after 2012?

options.label: Yes — the timing is unmistakable
options.tell: Twenge's claim. The timing is real; causation from timing is the disputed step.

options.label: The correlation is real, the causal claim is not established
options.tell: Where most of the field sits.

probe.reveal: Orben and Przybylski re-analysed the same datasets with specification-curve analysis and found the association between screen use and wellbeing about the size of the association with eating potatoes. Twenge disputes the aggregation and points to girls and social media specifically. The rise in measured distress is not in doubt; the cause is.

glossary.name: The Great Rewiring
glossary.definition: That a play-based childhood was replaced by a phone-based one, with measurable harm, and that the fix is collective rather than individual.
glossary.example: Haidt assembles international trend data and proposes four norms including no smartphones before high school. Candice Odgers and others reviewed the book critically, arguing the correlational evidence cannot bear the causal claim and that the focus may divert attention from poverty and services. The disagreement is about causation, not about whether the trends exist.

probe.ask: Is the evidence strong enough to justify collective restrictions on phones in schools?

options.label: Yes — the harm case is strong enough to act on
options.tell: Haidt's position, and it treats this as a collective-action problem.

options.label: No — the causal evidence is too weak for policy
options.tell: Odgers's and Przybylski's objection.

options.label: The policy is worth trying whatever the causal story
options.tell: A third position: cheap, reversible, and defensible on attention grounds alone.

probe.reveal: Odgers reviewed the book in Nature and argued the correlational evidence cannot bear the causal weight; Haidt maintains the experimental and quasi-experimental subset does. The causal question is genuinely unresolved. Both sides agree the collective-action framing is right — an individual family cannot opt out of a norm — which is why the third option is where the practical agreement is.

glossary.name: The Filter Bubble
glossary.definition: That algorithmic personalisation isolates people in self-confirming information environments.
glossary.example: The intuitive version has not held up well. Several studies find social media users encounter more cross-cutting content than offline peers, and Bail's experiment found that paying partisans to follow opposing accounts increased polarisation rather than reducing it. The sorting is real; the mechanism is not the one the metaphor suggests.

probe.ask: Does algorithmic personalisation isolate people from opposing views?

options.label: Yes — that is what the algorithm optimises for
options.tell: Pariser's thesis, and the most common assumption in press coverage.

options.label: Social media users encounter more opposing views than non-users
options.tell: What most measurement studies find.

probe.reveal: Bakshy's Facebook study and Flaxman's browsing data both found that people who use social media and search encounter more cross-cutting content than those who do not, while their most-consumed sources remain concentrated. Self-selection appears to matter more than the algorithm, and the strong version of the thesis is not supported by the measurement studies. Exposure is also not the same as persuasion — see the entry below.

glossary.name: The Exposure Experiment
glossary.definition: Paying partisans to follow opposing views for a month made them more extreme, not less.
glossary.example: Republicans became substantially more conservative; Democrats slightly more liberal. The finding cuts against the standing assumption that contact reduces polarisation, and suggests exposure without context reads as attack.

probe.ask: If partisans were paid to follow accounts from the other side for a month, what would happen?

options.label: They would moderate — contact reduces prejudice
options.tell: The contact-hypothesis prediction, and the basis of many depolarisation proposals.

options.label: They would become more extreme
options.tell: What Bail found, significantly so for Republicans and directionally for Democrats.

probe.reveal: Bail and colleagues paid around 1,600 Twitter users to follow a bot retweeting opposing elites for a month. Republicans became substantially more conservative; Democrats slightly more liberal. Exposure to the other side's worst representatives is not contact in Allport's sense — it has none of the conditions he specified — and it appears to entrench.

glossary.name: Context Collapse
glossary.definition: A single utterance reaching audiences with incompatible norms, none of which it was written for.
glossary.example: A remark that is ordinary among colleagues, read by strangers, family and employers at once. It explains a large share of online moral conflict without anyone having said anything unusual.

probe.ask: You write a joke for the twelve people who know the reference. Forty thousand strangers see it. Who is it for?

options.label: Still the twelve — the others are eavesdropping
options.tell: How it was written, and not how it will be read.

options.label: Everyone, so it should have been written for everyone
options.tell: The counsel of safety, and it makes writing anything specific impossible.

probe.reveal: Marwick and boyd named the problem: a single utterance reaching audiences with incompatible norms, none of which it was written for. There is no solution available to the writer, only trade-offs — which is why so much public writing has flattened into text that cannot be quoted against you.

glossary.name: Virtue Signalling
glossary.definition: Public moral expression read as being about the speaker's standing rather than the issue.
glossary.example: Signalling theory says costly signals are informative and cheap ones are not — so the useful question is what the statement cost the person making it. As deployed, the term is usually unfalsifiable: it explains any moral speech by anyone disagreed with, and its own use is itself a status move.

probe.ask: Someone posts sincerely about an injustice. When is calling it virtue signalling a fair criticism?

options.label: Whenever there is no personal cost
options.tell: This makes the charge unfalsifiable — it applies to every public moral statement.

options.label: When their behaviour elsewhere contradicts it
options.tell: A real test, and it requires evidence rather than inference from the posting.

options.label: Never — motives are unknowable
options.tell: Too strong: motives are inferable, just not from the fact of speaking.

probe.reveal: The term names something real, and it is almost always deployed as a way of not answering the argument. Tosi and Warmke are careful about this: grandstanding is a claim about motive, so it never bears on whether the moral claim is true. Notice that the accusation is itself usually costless and public.

glossary.name: Selective Outrage
glossary.definition: Condemning an act more when the person doing it belongs to the other side.
glossary.example: Ditto and colleagues' meta-analysis found partisan bias in evaluating identical evidence was substantial and roughly symmetrical across left and right — which is the finding both sides consistently expect to come out in their favour.

probe.ask: A politician you support and one you oppose commit the same offence. Do your reactions differ in kind, or only in degree?

options.label: Only in degree — I am consistent
options.tell: What everyone reports, and what the paired-vignette data contradict.

options.label: In kind: for mine I ask about context first
options.tell: The honest description of what asymmetric scrutiny looks like from inside.

probe.reveal: Ditto's meta-analysis of 51 studies found partisan bias in evaluating identical evidence to be substantial and roughly symmetrical between left and right — a symmetry each side reliably expects to come out in its favour. The Selective Outrage test on this page is built to show you the manipulation directly.

glossary.name: Parasocial Interaction
glossary.definition: A one-sided sense of relationship with a media figure who does not know you exist.
glossary.example: Named for television decades before social platforms, and far stronger now that the figure appears to reply. It is why an influencer's moral lapse feels like a personal betrayal, and why audiences defend them past the evidence.

probe.ask: A creator you have watched for years announces bad news. What do you feel?

options.label: Real concern, as for a friend
options.tell: The parasocial bond doing exactly what it does. It is not fake feeling.

options.label: Sympathy, as for a stranger
options.tell: The calibrated response, and harder to sustain after a thousand hours of their voice.

probe.reveal: Horton and Wohl named the one-sided intimacy in 1956 for television. The intensification is structural: the address is direct, the setting is domestic, the frequency is daily, and the figure appears to reply. The consequences run both ways — audiences grieve strangers, and creators are held to obligations they never entered.

glossary.name: Barnum Statements
glossary.definition: Statements broad enough to fit almost anyone, which feel personal because the reader supplies the specifics.
glossary.example: The reason a result is only informative if it could have come out differently. A test that flatters everyone has measured nothing, whatever its respondents report.

probe.ask: This site tells you which philosopher your answers most resemble. What would make that more than a Barnum statement?

options.label: That it feels accurate
options.tell: The Forer criterion, and it is worthless — the astrology sheet felt accurate too.

options.label: That different answers produce visibly different results
options.tell: The falsifiability test, and the one to hold this site to.

options.label: That it names what it cannot distinguish
options.tell: The stronger version, and why the results here name ties instead of ranking them.

probe.reveal: Every personality product faces this and most fail it by design, because a description that fits everyone gets the best ratings. The defences available are structural rather than rhetorical: make the mapping from answers to output inspectable, make contradictory answers produce contradictory results, and say out loud when two outputs are too close to separate.

glossaryStatus.robust: Replicated repeatedly, including by people who wanted it to fail.
glossaryStatus.mixed: Real, but smaller, narrower or more conditional than popularly told.
glossaryStatus.contested: Serious specialists actively disagree about whether it holds.
glossaryStatus.failed: Large or pre-registered replications did not find it.
glossaryStatus.—: Not an empirical claim: a principle, a law or a definition.

audit.title: An estimate

arms.preamble: Is the Nile longer or shorter than 800 kilometres?
Is the Nile longer or shorter than 12,000 kilometres?

audit.prompt: Now estimate: how long is the Nile, in kilometres?

reveal.says: The number in the first question was arbitrary and you were told nothing about its accuracy. Half of readers see 800 and half see 12,000, and the two groups produce systematically different estimates — the group shown the larger number guesses higher. Tversky and Kahneman found this even when participants watched the anchor being generated by a spinning wheel in front of them.
reveal.caveat: Your single answer proves nothing about you. The effect is a difference between groups, and you are in one group. What it should change is your confidence in any figure you produced shortly after hearing another one — in a salary discussion, a valuation, or an estimate of how long a piece of work will take.

audit.title: A description
audit.preamble: Linda is 31, single, outspoken and very bright. She studied philosophy, was deeply concerned with discrimination and social justice, and took part in anti-nuclear demonstrations.

options.label: Linda is a bank teller.
Linda is a bank teller and is active in the feminist movement.
They are exactly equally probable.

reveal.says: Every feminist bank teller is already a bank teller, so the second cannot be more probable than the first — it is a subset. The description is built to make the conjunction *representative*, and representativeness overrides the arithmetic. In Tversky and Kahneman's original, a large majority of respondents chose the conjunction, including many with statistical training.
reveal.caveat: There is a real linguistic objection: "Linda is a bank teller" can be read as implying "and not a feminist", under ordinary conversational rules. If that is how you read it, your answer was about pragmatics rather than probability, and the criticism has been made by serious people.

arms.preamble: An outbreak is expected to kill 600 people. Two programmes are proposed. Programme A will save 200 people. Programme B has a one-third chance of saving all 600 and a two-thirds chance of saving nobody.

An outbreak is expected to kill 600 people. Two programmes are proposed. Under Programme A, 400 people will die. Under Programme B there is a one-third chance that nobody will die and a two-thirds chance that 600 will die.

options.label: Programme A — the certain outcome.
Programme B — the gamble.

reveal.says: The two versions are numerically identical. Saving 200 of 600 is the same as 400 dying. Presented in terms of lives saved, most people take the certain option; presented in terms of deaths, most take the gamble. The preference reverses with the wording, which means it cannot be tracking the outcome.
reveal.caveat: You saw one frame only, so nothing here shows *you* would have switched. What it shows is that the wording of a choice is not neutral packaging, and that whoever writes the options has already made part of the decision.

audit.title: A positive result
audit.preamble: A disease affects 1 in 1,000 people. A test detects it correctly every time it is present, and has a 5% false-positive rate. Someone tests positive, with no other information about them.
audit.prompt: Roughly how likely is it that they have the disease?

options.label: About 95%
About 50%
About 2%
Cannot be determined from this

reveal.says: In 1,000 people, one has it and tests positive. About 50 of the 999 healthy people also test positive. So roughly 1 in 51 positives is a true positive — about 2%. The 95% answer confuses the test's accuracy with the probability of disease, which are different questions. When Casscells and colleagues put a version of this to Harvard medical staff, most gave an answer near the test accuracy.
reveal.caveat: This is arithmetic, not opinion, so this item is genuinely gradeable — unlike most of the others here.

audit.title: Which kills more?
audit.prompt: In a typical year worldwide, which causes more human deaths?

options.label: Sharks
Hippopotamuses
They are about the same

reveal.says: Hippos kill far more people than sharks, by a wide margin — but shark attacks are filmed, reported internationally and made into films, and hippo attacks are not. What comes to mind easily feels common. This is why people misjudge the relative risks of flying and driving, and why coverage volume shapes public risk priorities more than mortality does.
reveal.caveat: Precise annual figures for both vary a great deal by source and are not reliable enough to quote, so none is given here. The direction of the comparison is not in doubt; the exact numbers you may have seen circulated usually are.

audit.title: The unfinished thing
audit.preamble: Your company has spent £9 million of a £10 million budget developing a product. A competitor releases something better and cheaper. Your remaining £1 million would finish yours.

options.label: Finish it. We have come too far to abandon it now.
Stop. The £9 million is gone whatever we do; the question is what the last £1 million buys.
Finish it, because cancelling would damage credibility with staff and investors in ways that outlast this product.

reveal.says: The £9 million is unrecoverable and identical under both choices, so it cannot bear on the decision. Only the £1 million and what it buys are live. Arkes and Blumer showed that prior expenditure changes people's choices even when it is explicitly stated to be unrecoverable.
reveal.caveat: The third option is not the fallacy. Reputational and morale costs of cancelling are real forward-looking consequences, and someone choosing it is doing the analysis correctly with a wider frame. Only the first answer reasons from the money already spent.

audit.title: How much would you give?

arms.preamble: A conservation scheme would save 2,000 migrating birds a year from drowning in oil ponds.
A conservation scheme would save 200,000 migrating birds a year from drowning in oil ponds.

audit.prompt: What is the most you would personally pay, per year, to fund it?

reveal.says: Half of readers are shown a figure a hundred times larger than the other half. In the study this comes from, the amounts people offered barely moved with the number of birds. The explanation is that what is being priced is the mental image — one exhausted bird in oil — and the image is the same either way.
reveal.caveat: This is the item with the sharpest implication for charitable giving and public spending: if willingness to pay does not track the number helped, then feeling is not a usable guide to allocating, and Singer's and Parfit's arguments in the morality corpus start to bite.

audit.title: The rule
audit.preamble: Four cards are on a table. Each has a number on one side and a colour on the other. You can see: 3, 8, red, brown. The claim to test is: "If a card shows an even number on one face, its opposite face is red."
audit.prompt: Which cards must you turn over to test the claim?

options.label: 8 and red
8 and brown
8 only
3, 8 and red

reveal.says: You must turn 8 — if it is not red, the claim is false. And you must turn brown: if there is an even number behind it, the claim is false. Turning red can only confirm and never refute, which is why most people choose it. Fewer than one in ten get this right in Wason's original abstract version.
reveal.caveat: The same problem in a social setting — "if someone is drinking alcohol they must be over eighteen", with cards showing drinks and ages — is solved easily by most people. The logic is identical. What is hard is the abstraction, not the reasoning.

audit.title: A reading
audit.preamble: You have a need for other people to like and admire you, and yet you tend to be critical of yourself. While you have some personality weaknesses, you are generally able to compensate for them. At times you have serious doubts as to whether you have made the right decision or done the right thing. You prefer a certain amount of change and variety and become dissatisfied when hemmed in by restrictions. You pride yourself on being an independent thinker and do not accept others' statements without satisfactory proof.
audit.prompt: How accurately does that describe you?

options.label: Very accurately
Fairly accurately
Not especially — it would fit most people
Not at all

reveal.says: That passage is assembled from a newsstand astrology book, and it is the same passage for every reader. Forer gave an identical profile to a class of students as their individual result; they rated it as highly accurate about themselves personally. The statements are constructed to be true of nearly everyone while feeling specific, because you supply the specifics.
reveal.caveat: This item is aimed at this website. Every result the morality tests produce is vulnerable to exactly this: a description that feels penetrating because you furnished the examples. The defence built into those tests is that the arithmetic is shown and could have come out differently — but if a verdict ever feels true in a way you cannot check, this is the item to remember.

fallacies.name: Ad Hominem
fallacies.definition: Rejecting a claim by attacking the person making it rather than the claim.
fallacies.example: "You would say that, you work for an oil company" — offered as a reason the emissions figure is wrong, rather than as a reason to check it.
fallacies.notFallacy: Attacking credibility is legitimate when the person IS the evidence. If someone's testimony is the only support for a claim, their honesty and expertise are directly relevant. Calling that ad hominem is the most common misuse of the term.

fallacies.name: Tu Quoque
fallacies.definition: Deflecting criticism by pointing out that the critic is guilty of the same thing.
fallacies.example: "You are lecturing me about flying while you took three holidays last year."
fallacies.notFallacy: Hypocrisy is genuine evidence about a person's sincerity and about how demanding a standard really is. It is only fallacious when offered as a reason the CLAIM is false.

fallacies.name: Straw Man
fallacies.definition: Refuting a weakened or distorted version of an argument nobody made.
fallacies.example: Answering "we should reform the asylum process" with "so you want open borders".
fallacies.notFallacy: Drawing out an implication your opponent has not stated but is committed to is not a straw man — it is argument. The test is whether they would accept the implication as theirs.

fallacies.name: Appeal to Improper Authority
fallacies.definition: Citing an authority outside their field, or a contested claim as though settled.
fallacies.example: A Nobel laureate in physics quoted on nutrition, cited as though the prize transferred.
fallacies.notFallacy: Deferring to genuine expertise in its own field is not a fallacy; it is how anyone knows almost anything. The fallacy is in the mismatch, not in the deference.

fallacies.name: Argumentum ad Populum
fallacies.definition: Treating widespread belief as evidence of truth.
fallacies.example: "Most people think this, so it must be right" — the argument that would have settled every question wrongly for most of history.
fallacies.notFallacy: Widespread belief IS evidence in some domains — about language use, social norms, or where many independent judges have relevant information. The fallacy is treating consensus as decisive on matters of fact it cannot reach.

fallacies.name: Appeal to Emotion
fallacies.definition: Substituting an emotional reaction for a reason.
fallacies.example: A charity advertisement that establishes urgency without establishing that the intervention works.
fallacies.notFallacy: Emotion is often the appropriate response to a fact and can be part of a sound argument. The fallacy is when the feeling REPLACES the evidence rather than following from it.

fallacies.name: Appeal to Nature
fallacies.definition: Treating natural as equivalent to good, or unnatural as bad.
fallacies.example: "It is a natural remedy" — as though hemlock and radon were not.
fallacies.notFallacy: Evolutionary or ecological arguments about what a system is adapted for can be legitimate. The fallacy is the leap from "is natural" to "is therefore good", which is Hume's is–ought gap wearing a different coat.

fallacies.name: The Genetic Fallacy
fallacies.definition: Judging a claim by where it came from rather than whether it is true.
fallacies.example: Dismissing a statistic because of who funded the study, without examining the method.
fallacies.notFallacy: Provenance is legitimate evidence about RELIABILITY when you cannot check the claim directly. Funding source is a reason to scrutinise; it is not by itself a refutation.

fallacies.name: Whataboutism
fallacies.definition: Answering a charge by raising a different one against the accuser or their allies.
fallacies.example: "Before you talk about our prisons, what about theirs?"
fallacies.notFallacy: Raising comparable cases is legitimate when the question is about consistency of a standard, or about relative priority given finite attention. It becomes fallacious when used to avoid answering rather than to widen the frame.

fallacies.name: Appeal to Consequences
fallacies.definition: Arguing a claim is false because its truth would be unwelcome.
fallacies.example: "If that were true, everything we have built would be worthless — so it cannot be."
fallacies.notFallacy: Consequences bear legitimately on what to DO and on how much evidence to require before acting. They bear on what is TRUE only via evidence.

fallacies.name: Begging the Question
fallacies.definition: Assuming the conclusion within the premises.
fallacies.example: "It is wrong because it is immoral." The premise and conclusion are the same claim in different clothes.
fallacies.notFallacy: This does NOT mean "raises the question", which is now its dominant popular use. Correcting people on that is usually pedantry; using it correctly is still worth doing.

fallacies.name: False Dilemma
fallacies.definition: Presenting two options as exhaustive when others exist.
fallacies.example: "Either we accept this proposal or we do nothing."
fallacies.notFallacy: Some dilemmas are real. When the alternatives genuinely are exhaustive, insisting on a third way is not sophistication — it is wishful thinking. The work is in showing the third option exists.

fallacies.name: Loaded Question
fallacies.definition: A question whose form presupposes something not established.
fallacies.example: "When did you stop cutting corners?" — either answer concedes the premise.
fallacies.notFallacy: A question presupposing something already agreed is not loaded. The fallacy is smuggling a contested premise past the answer.

fallacies.name: No True Scotsman
fallacies.definition: Redefining a category mid-argument to exclude a counterexample.
fallacies.example: "No serious economist believes that." Presented with one who does: "Well, no SERIOUS one."
fallacies.notFallacy: Definitions can be legitimately tightened when the original was loose and the tightening is principled and stated. The fallacy is doing it only to escape, and only after the counterexample appears.

fallacies.name: Moving the Goalposts
fallacies.definition: Raising the evidential bar once the original bar is met.
fallacies.example: Asking for one study, then for replication, then for a meta-analysis, then for a mechanism — while never having said in advance what would settle it.
fallacies.notFallacy: Raising standards is legitimate when new information shows the old standard was too low, or in proportion to the size of the claim. Say the standard in advance and the difference becomes visible.

fallacies.name: Special Pleading
fallacies.definition: Exempting a favoured case from a standard applied everywhere else, without justifying the exemption.
fallacies.example: Applying strict scrutiny to research one dislikes and waving through research one likes.
fallacies.notFallacy: Exemptions can be justified — relevant differences between cases are real. What makes it a fallacy is the absence of a stated reason that would also apply to the other side.

fallacies.name: Motte and Bailey
fallacies.definition: Defending a strong controversial claim by retreating to a weak uncontroversial one, then returning.
fallacies.example: Advancing a sweeping thesis, and when challenged insisting only the obvious version was meant — then arguing from the sweeping one again.
fallacies.notFallacy: Named by Nicholas Shackel in 2005. Distinguishing which claim you are making, and staying there, is the fix. Clarifying a claim under challenge is not the fallacy; oscillating is.

fallacies.name: Unfalsifiability
fallacies.definition: A claim constructed so that no observation could count against it.
fallacies.example: A theory whose defenders explain both a result and its opposite, with equal confidence, after the fact.
fallacies.notFallacy: Some true claims are hard to test with current tools. The fallacy is the claim that cannot in PRINCIPLE be wrong, not the one that is merely difficult to check.

fallacies.name: Post Hoc Ergo Propter Hoc
fallacies.definition: Inferring causation from sequence.
fallacies.example: "Crime fell after we introduced the policy" — in a decade when crime fell almost everywhere.
fallacies.notFallacy: Temporal order is a NECESSARY condition for causation and therefore real evidence. It is simply not sufficient. What is missing is a control, not the observation.

fallacies.name: Cum Hoc Ergo Propter Hoc
fallacies.definition: Inferring causation from association.
fallacies.example: Ice cream sales and drownings rise together; both are caused by summer.
fallacies.notFallacy: Correlation is genuine evidence for causation, and in many fields the only evidence available. The error is treating it as conclusive, not as treating it as relevant — a distinction the popular slogan flattens.

fallacies.name: The Single Cause Fallacy
fallacies.definition: Assuming one cause where several are operating.
fallacies.example: Attributing a company's failure to one decision, when the market, the funding climate and three other decisions were all necessary.
fallacies.notFallacy: Sometimes one cause really does dominate, and insisting everything is multi-causal can be its own evasion. The test is whether removing the named cause would have changed the outcome.

fallacies.name: Slippery Slope
fallacies.definition: Claiming one step leads inevitably to an extreme outcome, without establishing the mechanism.
fallacies.example: "Allow this exception and there will be no rule left."
fallacies.notFallacy: Slopes are sometimes real and the mechanism can be shown — precedent in law works exactly this way. The fallacy is the ASSERTED inevitability with no account of how each step forces the next.

fallacies.name: The Texas Sharpshooter
fallacies.definition: Finding a pattern after the fact and treating it as though it had been predicted.
fallacies.example: Firing at a barn, then painting the target around the tightest cluster. In practice: choosing the subgroup and the endpoint after seeing the data.
fallacies.notFallacy: Exploratory analysis is legitimate and necessary. It becomes a fallacy when the hypothesis it generates is reported as though it had been tested. Pre-registration exists to make the difference visible.

fallacies.name: The Regression Fallacy
fallacies.definition: Attributing to an intervention a change that regression to the mean would produce anyway.
fallacies.example: The worst-performing schools improve after any intervention, because they were selected for being extreme.
fallacies.notFallacy: The intervention may still work. The point is that the design cannot tell, because a control group was needed and was not used.

fallacies.name: Hasty Generalisation
fallacies.definition: Drawing a general conclusion from too few or unrepresentative cases.
fallacies.example: Two bad experiences with a service, reported as what the service is like.
fallacies.notFallacy: Small samples are informative about LARGE effects — one case is enough to refute "never happens". The fallacy is in the size of the conclusion relative to the evidence, not in using few cases at all.

fallacies.name: The Anecdotal Fallacy
fallacies.definition: Preferring a vivid individual case to systematic evidence.
fallacies.example: "My grandfather smoked and lived to ninety."
fallacies.notFallacy: Anecdotes are legitimate for existence claims, for generating hypotheses, and for identifying failure modes a dataset averaged away. They cannot establish a rate.

fallacies.name: Survivorship Bias
fallacies.definition: Reasoning only from cases that made it through a selection process.
fallacies.example: Studying successful founders for the habits that caused success, without checking whether unsuccessful ones had the same habits.
fallacies.notFallacy: Studying survivors is fine when you have the base rate too. The fallacy is the missing denominator, not the interest in survivors.

fallacies.name: The Base Rate Fallacy
fallacies.definition: Ignoring prior frequency when interpreting evidence.
fallacies.example: A rare condition and an accurate test still produce mostly false positives.
fallacies.notFallacy: Base rates can legitimately be set aside when you have strong individuating evidence. What cannot be done is ignoring them by default.

fallacies.name: Cherry Picking
fallacies.definition: Presenting the subset of evidence that supports a position while omitting the rest.
fallacies.example: Citing the three studies that found an effect and not the eleven that did not.
fallacies.notFallacy: Selecting the highest-quality studies is not cherry picking — it is doing the review properly. The difference is whether the selection criterion is stated in advance and applied to both sides.

fallacies.name: The Nirvana Fallacy
fallacies.definition: Rejecting a real improvement because it falls short of a perfect solution.
fallacies.example: "That reform would not fix the whole problem, so it is not worth doing."
fallacies.notFallacy: Sometimes a partial fix genuinely does harm — by absorbing the pressure for a real one, or by legitimising the system. That is an argument, not the fallacy; the fallacy is the bare appeal to imperfection.

fallacies.name: Equivocation
fallacies.definition: Using a word in two senses within one argument.
fallacies.example: "Nothing is better than eternal happiness; a sandwich is better than nothing" — two meanings of "nothing".
fallacies.notFallacy: Words legitimately have several senses, and using one consistently is not a fallacy. The error is the shift mid-argument, usually unnoticed by the person making it.

fallacies.name: Amphiboly
fallacies.definition: An argument whose force depends on a grammatical ambiguity.
fallacies.example: Contract disputes turn on this constantly, and the ambiguity is often deliberate.
fallacies.notFallacy: Ordinary language is ambiguous; asking for clarification is the fix, not an accusation.

fallacies.name: The Definist Fallacy
fallacies.definition: Defining a contested term so that your conclusion follows by definition.
fallacies.example: Defining "violence" narrowly or broadly enough that a disputed case is settled without argument.
fallacies.notFallacy: Stipulating a definition for clarity is legitimate and necessary. The fallacy is stipulating one that does the argumentative work while presented as merely clarifying.

fallacies.name: The Fallacy Fallacy
fallacies.definition: Concluding a claim is false because an argument for it was fallacious.
fallacies.example: Someone defends a true statement badly; you conclude the statement is false.
fallacies.notFallacy: A bad argument gives you no reason to BELIEVE the conclusion, but no reason to reject it either. This one is worth knowing precisely because a list like this makes it easy to commit.

fallacies.name: Affirming the Consequent
fallacies.definition: If P then Q; Q; therefore P. Invalid.
fallacies.example: "If it rained, the pavement is wet. The pavement is wet. So it rained." The sprinkler is also available.
fallacies.notFallacy: This is the structure of most scientific inference, which is why it is not simply a mistake: theories predict observations, and observations support theories inductively. It is invalid as DEDUCTION, not worthless as evidence.

fallacies.name: Denying the Antecedent
fallacies.definition: If P then Q; not P; therefore not Q. Invalid.
fallacies.example: "If you study, you pass. You did not study. So you failed." You might pass anyway.
fallacies.notFallacy: The valid forms are modus ponens (P, so Q) and modus tollens (not Q, so not P). Confusing them with these two is the commonest formal error in ordinary reasoning.

fallacies.name: The Undistributed Middle
fallacies.definition: All A are C; all B are C; therefore all A are B. Invalid.
fallacies.example: "All authoritarians censor. This government censors. Therefore it is authoritarian." Sharing a property is not sharing an identity.
fallacies.notFallacy: The conclusion may be true. It just does not follow from these premises, and the argument needs different ones.

fallacies.name: Composition and Division
fallacies.definition: Assuming what is true of parts is true of the whole, or the reverse.
fallacies.example: Every player is excellent, so the team is excellent. Or: the company is profitable, so this division is.
fallacies.notFallacy: Some properties genuinely do transfer — a wall of steel bricks is steel. The fallacy is assuming transfer rather than showing it for the property in question.

fallacyFamilies.relevance: The premise does not bear on the conclusion.
fallacyFamilies.presumption: The argument assumes what it needs to establish.
fallacyFamilies.causal: The inference from evidence to cause does not hold.
fallacyFamilies.statistical: The evidence cannot support a conclusion of that size.
fallacyFamilies.ambiguity: The argument turns on a shift in meaning.
fallacyFamilies.formal: The structure is invalid regardless of content.

outrage.varies: Whether the traveller campaigns on the issue they are undercutting
outrage.act: takes eleven long-haul flights in a year for work and holidays

arms.actor: A climate campaigner with a large following
An oil-company executive

outrage.reveal: The act and its emissions are identical. Most people rate the campaigner more harshly, because hypocrisy is a separate offence from the harm and we price it separately. That is defensible — insincerity is real evidence about a person. It becomes a problem when the extra condemnation displaces attention from the larger emitter, which is the outcome the executive would choose if asked.

outrage.varies: Which political side the donor is on
outrage.act: gives £2 million to a political party and is later appointed to a public board

arms.actor: A donor to the governing party
A donor to the opposition

outrage.reveal: Identical in every respect except the party. Ditto and colleagues, meta-analysing 51 experimental studies, found that partisans on both sides evaluate identical evidence more favourably when it suits their side, and that the asymmetry between left and right was small — a finding each side reliably expects to come out in its favour.

outrage.act: posts a lengthy apology for a remark made eight years ago, after being criticised

arms.actor: A well-known influencer with two million followers
A colleague you have worked with for years

outrage.reveal: The same words carry differently depending on whether you can imagine the person as a whole life or only as a public surface. Horton and Wohl named the one-sided relationship in 1956 for television; the effect is stronger now that the figure appears to reply. Notice which way yours moved — some readers are harsher on the stranger, some on the colleague, and the second is its own kind of bias.

outrage.act: donates a substantial sum to a hospital appeal

arms.actor: A businessman who announces it in a press release with photographs
A businessman who asks that it not be reported

outrage.reveal: The hospital receives the same money. Maimonides ranked anonymous giving higher precisely because of what publicity does to the transaction — and a consequentialist will point out that publicised giving raises more from others, so the anonymous donor may have chosen their own moral comfort over the hospital's income. Both positions are in the corpus.

outrage.act: uses a legal arrangement to reduce a tax bill substantially

arms.actor: A multinational company
A self-employed plumber

outrage.reveal: Both are legal and both reduce public revenue. Most people rate the company far more harshly, which may track a real difference in scale and power — or may be the identifiable-victim effect in reverse, where a faceless entity absorbs condemnation that a person we can picture would not. If your answer would change on learning the plumber saved more in absolute terms, the judgement was about scale; if not, it was about the actor.

outrage.varies: Which cause the protesters were blocking the road for
outrage.act: blocks a motorway during rush hour, delaying an ambulance

arms.actor: Climate protesters
Farmers protesting fuel duty

outrage.reveal: The disruption and the ambulance are the same. Whether disruption is legitimate is a real question — Gene Sharp's framework treats it as a method with costs, and King's Birmingham letter argues that unwelcome disruption is the point. What that argument cannot do is apply to one cause and not the other; if your rating moved with the cause, the principle you reached for was not the one doing the work.

outrage.act: is dismissed by their employer for a strongly-worded political post made in a personal capacity

arms.actor: An employee whose post attacked immigration
An employee whose post attacked Israel

outrage.reveal: Whether an employer may sanction private speech is a question about power, contract and the chilling of expression, and it does not change with the content of the post. It is also the item on which most people discover they hold two positions, and the discovery is the purpose. Mill's harm principle and Popper's paradox of tolerance are both in the corpus and they do not settle it the same way.

outrage.varies: Whether you are invited to identify with the actor
outrage.act: gets a competitive job after their parent made a call to an old friend

arms.actor: A candidate you have never met
Your closest friend's child, who you know is genuinely talented

outrage.reveal: The mechanism is identical and the displaced candidate is equally real in both. This is the item where partiality is on trial rather than politics: Bernard Williams argued that a demand for total impartiality asks one thought too many, while Godwin's fire case says the stranger's claim is no weaker for being a stranger's. Both entries are in the corpus and they disagree.

outrage.varies: Which kind of institution took the money
outrage.act: accepts a large donation from a foreign state with a poor human-rights record

arms.actor: A university department
A football club

outrage.reveal: The money and its source are the same. The usual defences differ — research independence in one case, the fans and the town in the other — and both are arguments about what the money buys rather than where it came from. If one of those defences persuades you and the other does not, the deciding factor was the institution, not the donor.

outrage.varies: How long ago the remark was made
outrage.act: is found to have written something cruel and bigoted, which they no longer defend

arms.actor: A public figure who wrote it fifteen years ago as a student
A public figure who wrote it eighteen months ago

outrage.reveal: Whether people can change is not a question you get to answer differently depending on whether you like them. Most readers hold that time and repudiation matter, which is a real position — but it has to be applied to the person whose politics you dislike as well, and the honest way to test yourself is to name the figure you would not extend it to.

outrageTags.name: The Moral Police
outrageTags.blurb: Nearly everything was seriously wrong, and it was seriously wrong whoever did it. You apply a demanding standard evenly, which is the rarer half of that sentence.
outrageTags.caveat: The failure mode of an even, demanding standard is not unfairness — it is that condemnation stops carrying information. If almost every act scores four or five, the scale has no room left to say which of them was worse.

outrageTags.name: The Permissive
outrageTags.blurb: Little of it troubled you much, and it troubled you about equally regardless of who did it. Consistent leniency is a position, and it is one several thinkers in the corpus defend.
outrageTags.caveat: Worth checking whether it is a position or an absence of one. The test for that is whether there is any version of these acts you would have rated a five.

outrageTags.name: Consistent
outrageTags.blurb: The actor barely moved you. Across ten acts your two ratings stayed close, and where they parted it was not by much — which is what applying a principle looks like from the outside.
outrageTags.caveat: The honest caveat is that you saw both versions, and consistency is easy to produce deliberately once you notice the design. What this shows is that you can be consistent when the comparison is visible — not that you are when it is not.

outrageTags.name: The Hypocrite
outrageTags.blurb: A demanding standard, applied unevenly, in a direction that repeats. That combination is what the word means when it is used precisely rather than as an insult: not that you have failed to live up to a standard, but that you have applied one and then suspended it.
outrageTags.caveat: It is also the most common result, and the least interesting fact about it is that it is yours. The useful question is which of the pairs below produced the largest gap, and what you would have to believe for that gap to be justified.

outrageTags.name: The Partisan
outrageTags.blurb: You were forgiving in general and notably less forgiving of one side in particular. The pattern is not harshness — it is that your leniency has a boundary, and the boundary is political.
outrageTags.caveat: This is the shape Ditto found on both sides of the aisle, in roughly equal measure. The reliable finding alongside it is that each side expects the asymmetry to come out in its favour.

outrageTags.name: The Situationist
outrageTags.blurb: Who did it moved you a great deal, and it did not move you in a direction that repeats. Your gaps run both ways, which means what you are responding to is the particulars rather than a side.
outrageTags.caveat: Two readings and the test cannot separate them: either you are attending to morally relevant detail that a rule would flatten — the position Bernard Williams argues in the corpus — or you are responding to whatever was salient in each vignette. The tie-breaker is whether you can state the principle behind each gap.

options.label: None — I judge the act
One or two
Around half
